case_summary.text: Additions u/s 69C deleted as genuine diamond purchases can't be disallowed merely due to cash sales: HC

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, diamond trader, imported diamonds and purchases were executed through banking channels and in compliance with statutory provisions, furthermore sine purchases were accepted as genuine with proper supporting documents, expenditure on such purchases could not be treated as unexplained merely because sales were made in cash or buyers could not be fully identified, and thus, disallowance under section 69C was unjustified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery, claimed that cash deposited in bank account during demonetization period pertained to sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers, since assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences, impugned addition made under section 69A, read with section 115BBE treating cash sales as bogus was to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of gold and diamond jewellery deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs during demonetization period in his bank accounts and claimed that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales

INCOME TAX: Where AO made addition for unexplained cash purchases in diamond trading business solely based on third-party software recovered from search on another entity without providing corroborative material or opportunity for cross-examination to assessee who maintained proper books and banking records, such addition under section 69C could not be sustained.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of ornaments and jewellery, made cash sales of Rs. 9.24 crores during demonetisation, since assessee had provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make aforesaid sale even after announcement of demonetisation and moreover, assessee had shown sales in VAT returns, which had been accepted by VAT authorities, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer on account of said cash sales

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed that purchase of jewellery during year was made by her relative using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his savings, since onus to prove genuineness of transaction lay with assessee which had not been discharged, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made cash payments to K for two housing society projects, since said payment denoted cash generated outside books of accounts and explanation as regards source was bereft of any acceptable evidence, addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69C was justified

INCOME TAX: Where assessee’s long-term capital gains from sale of diamonds were supported by declaration under IDS, 2016 and valid holding period, additions under sections 68 and 69C treating sale proceeds and alleged commission as unexplained were unsustainable and liable to be deleted.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of trading in bullion and jewellery, deposited cash in its bank accounts during demonetisation period, since assessee had successfully explained source of such cash deposits as sales/advances duly recorded in its books of account and comparative sales data dispelled allegation of abnormal cash sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating same as unexplained cash credits under section 68

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in jewellery trading business, made cash deposits of Rs. 73.66 lakhs during demonetization, since assessee had furnished cash flow statements demonstrating a consistent and plausible cash trail and nature of assessee’s business inherently involved high-value cash transactions, addition made solely on basis of cash deposits in bank account was unsustainable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made cash payments to K for two housing society projects, since said payment denoted cash generated outside books of account and explanation as regards source was bereft of any acceptable evidence, addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69C was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made cash payments to D for purchase of cows for his farm, in view of facts that assessee had explained that cash was actually given and received back from D thrice, final time through R who was relative (spouse of sister in law) of assessee and it had no business transactions with R and D had also confirmed transactions, addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69C was to be deleted

IT: Where assessee made purchase of Jewellery worth Rs. 34.48 crores in cash by submitting that a group of bidders formed a syndicate and participated in auction and after successful bidding, money from prospective purchasers were collected and same was remitted to 'M' Ltd., since assessee could not demonstrate that he was representing any syndicate and, moreover, he also failed to demonstrate a situation which compelled him to make payment in cash, impugned disallowance made under section 40A(3) was to be confirmed

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited cash of Rs. 2.52 crores in bank account during demonetization period, since on entering into fresh agreement in June, 2016, assessee had made huge sales in cash which eventually stood deposited in bank account and entire cash sales made by assessee were duly reflected in VAT returns of assessee, addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69A was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals)

IT: Where assessee made purchase of Jewellery worth Rs. 34.48 crores in cash by submitting that a group of bidders formed a syndicate and participated in auction and after successful bidding, money from prospective purchasers were collected and same was remitted to 'M' Ltd., since assessee could not demonstrate that he was representing any syndicate and, moreover, he also failed to demonstrate a situation which compelled him to make payment in cash, impugned disallowance made under section 40A(3

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made additions under section 69C on account of payments made by assessee of Rs. 3.51 crores and Rs. 63.73 lakhs on ground that same were not recorded in his books of account, since out of total addition, Rs. 2.83 crores were recorded in books of assessee and, further, assessee had cash balance of Rs. 10.17 crores in hand as on 12-8-2014 to justify source of balance addition of Rs. 68.30 lakhs also, impugned additions were rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals)

IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made an addition of Rs. 1 crore out of total cash deposits of Rs. 1.34 crores during demonetisation period under section 69A read with section 115BBE, since cash deposited in bank account were part of sales of jewellery business of assessee, Assessing Officer was to be directed to assess income at rate of 8 per cent under section 44AD on Rs. 1 crore

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a tractor dealer, received cash payments exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs from farmers for purchase of tractors, since assessee furnished all details in respect of sales made by it to various farmers and kept particulars of farmers proving their identity, ID Proof, Aadhar No., land revenue record and agricultural land holding of all farmers, etc. and there was no allegation by Assessing Officer that unaccounted income and black money was introduced by assessee in form of cash

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited large cash sums during demonetisation and explained deposits as cash sales fully recorded in accepted books, with supporting documents provided and trading results not rejected, no addition under section 68 for unexplained cash credits was permissible.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee received sale proceeds of her flat in cash on five different dates, in view of explanation of assessee that she accepted payment in cash as she was in dire need of funds for marriage of her daughter and she could not rely upon purchaser to make payments by cheques which might or might not be honoured and that getting amount deposited by way of RTGS/Cheque in her bank account and then travelling with cash withdrawn at Jagraon to Delhi to make purchases was considered

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-jeweller claimed that substantial amount of cash deposited in bank account was with respect to cash sales made during demonetization period, since sales made by assessee were supported by commercial invoice reported in VAT return and accepted by VAT authority, and moreover AO did not reject assessee's books of account by invoking section 145, AO erred in not accepting declared cash sales as not verifiable merely on ground that purchases detail could not be verified and, thus, addition made under section 68 could not be sustained

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a dal manufacturer, made cash deposits into bank account during demonetization period, since assessee had pre-dominantly cash sales and he was able to file various evidences to prove availability of cash-in-hand as on 8-11-2016 and that there was no abnormal variation in total sales, cash sales and cash deposits, impugned addition made towards such cash deposited in bank account of assessee under section 69A read with section 115BBE was to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee received sale proceeds of her flat in cash on five different dates, in view of explanation of assessee that she accepted payment in cash as she was in dire need of funds for marriage of her daughter and she could not rely upon purchaser to make payments by cheques which might or might not be honoured and that getting amount deposited by way of RTGS/Cheque in her bank account and then travelling with cash withdrawn at Jagraon to Delhi to make purchases was considered to be unsafe/impractical, impugned penalty levied under section 271D was liable to be quashed

INCOME TAX : Where assessee during demonetization deposited substantial amount of cash in banks and claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers which were subsequently converted into sales of jewellery, since said trade advances were subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order passed by High Court that where assessee made purchase of Jewellery worth Rs. 34.48 crores by way of cash in auction, since assessee could not demonstrate that he was representing any syndicate and, moreover, he also failed to demonstrate a situation which compelled him to make payment in cash, impugned disallowance made under section 40A (3) was to be confirmed

INCOME TAX : Where assessee received cash from two parties during demonetization period and contended that subsequent sales were made for said amount, since assessee had neither furnished any confirmation from said parties nor any evidence of said two parties being assessed to tax, identity and creditworthiness of parties and genuineness of transactions were not proved, thus, additions made on account of said cash received by assessee was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee during demonetization deposited substantial amount of cash in banks and claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers which were subsequently converted into sales of jewellery, since said trade advances were subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills,

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order passed by High Court that where assessee made purchase of Jewellery worth Rs. 34.48 crores in cash by submitting that a group of bidders formed a syndicate and participated in auction and after successful bidding, money from prospective purchasers were collected and same was remitted to 'M' Ltd., since assessee could not demonstrate that he was representing any syndicate and, moreover, he also failed to demonstrate a situation

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected,
No Sec. 69A additions on deposits during demonetization as assessee had sufficient stock to justify cash sales: ITAT
No Sec. 69A additions on deposits during demonetization as assessee had sufficient stock to justify cash sales: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization period and claimed that same arose out of cash sales of jewellery, since other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT and books of account of assessee were accepted by AO, said deposits could not be said to be unexplained cash deposit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 75 lakhs in its bank account during demonitization and claimed same to be made out of cash sales, since assessee had maintained proper books of account and cash book justified for making such cash deposits during year, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69A was to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in diamond trading, was subjected to addition under section 69C for alleged bogus purchases from a concern based solely on information from investigation into another group, but assessee denied transactions and purchase records showed no such entries, in absence of cogent evidence against assessee, addition was unsustainable and had to be deleted
Purchase of jewellary in cash rightly disallowed as assessee failed to justify his compulsion for cash payment

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had purchased land and some part of consideration was made in cash and not disclosed for tax purposes, since payment to vendor was actually made in both cheque and alleged cash during financial year 2013-14, impugned transaction could not be related to assessment year 2015-16 and, thus, addition made under section 69C was to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed that entire amount of excess cash found from business premises was generated from undisclosed sale of medicine, since revenue was unable to show any other sources related to excess cash, excess cash was from business of assessee and, thus, application of section 115BBE on amount of excess cash was bad in law

INCOME TAX : Where AO made addition under section 68 on account of huge cash amount deposited by assessee-jeweller in its bank account post demonetization, since assessee had explained source of said cash deposits as sales of jewellery, produced sale bills and admitted same as revenue receipt as well as offered it to tax and assessee also represented outgo of stocks which was matching with sales, impugned addition was to be deleted
Addition for unexplained cash payment on jewellery purchase unsustainable as no incriminating evidence found in search: ITAT
Lump-sum addition upheld for unexplained cash deposit during demonetization as full sales explanation not satisfactory:ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where cash deposited post-demonetization by assessee was out of cash sales which had been accepted by Sales Tax/VAT Department and not doubted by Assessing Officer and there was sufficient stock available with assessee to make cash sales, sales made by assessee out of existing stock were sufficient to explain deposit of cash (obtained from realization of sales) in bank account and, thus, cash deposits could not have been treated as undisclosed income of assessee

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales,

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-jeweller claimed that cash deposited in bank account during demonetization period pertained to cash sale transaction of gold jewellery, since assessee had maintained regular books of account, bills, vouchers and day-to-day stock register having complete quantitative details of cash sale transaction of jewellery, addition under section 68 could not be made
No error in ITAT’s ruling deleting sec. 69C additions by holding that source of cash purchase was duly recorded: HC

IT : Where aggregate credits in undisclosed bank account of assessee were considered as cash sales, entire sales could not be considered as income but only profit embedded in it could be considered as income of assessee
No sec. 68 addition on mere suspicion of bogus entry; IT Act doesn’t bar an assessee from disclosing cash sales

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited huge cash during demonetization period in his bank accounts contending that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12] In light of above factual matrix, if one examines the issue, the Assessing Officer has rejected the contention of the assessee on two grounds. The first and foremost reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject the explanation of the assessee is that persons from whom assessee claims to have been received advance are not responded to summons issued under section 131(1) and in few cases, they have denied any kind of transactions with the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not discharge its onus cast upon as per the provisions of section 68, in respect of cash receipts, and thus, opined that cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee from various persons is unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has committed a fundamental mistake in examining the cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee towards sale of jewellery in light of provisions of section 68. [Para 13]

Be that as it may. The fact remains that, the assessee has furnished name and address of the customers from whom it has received cash for sale of jewellery. The assessee need not obtain confirmation and submit to the Assessing Officer, because, the law does not mandate collecting PAN details of the persons, if sale value of jewellery does not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs as per rule 114B of Income-tax Rules, 1962. In so far as compliance of KYC norms, it is mandatory under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with effect from 4-5-2023 onwards and not applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14]

of the case detailed above.

The whole controversy can also be seen from the another angle, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases to the tune of Rs. 48.78 crores during the subject assessment year as the payments for these purchases were stated to be made out of cash deposited in bank accounts out of so-called cash sales of gold made by the assessee of which identity of the buyers was not revealed by the assessee. The assessee in the instant case could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit of huge magnitude of more than Rs. 49 crores in his bank account which he claimed to be from cash sales from gold bars to the persons wherein the identity of the buyers are not revealed by the assessee. Thus, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit in the bank account and consequently sources of incurring expenditure by way of purchases claimed by the assessee in its profit and loss account of Rs. 48.78 crores could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee and onus cast under section 69C was not satisfied which would make amount covered by such expenditure represented by purchases of gold bars to be deemed income of the assessee under the deeming fiction of section 69C. The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. Thus, revenue succeeds on this ground while the assessee fails on this issue in their respective appeals. [Para 10]

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer called upon the assessee to file details of name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Out the above 50, summons issued to 40 persons returned by the Postal Authorities citing 'addressee cannot be located' or 'no such person' or 'no such address' or 'insufficient address' or 'no such address at the above place'. In response to summons, three persons were responded and out of three, two persons denied having any kind of transactions with the assessee. Further, one person confirmed having paid advance to the assessee company and also purchased jewellery from them. The Assessing Officer, on the basis of enquiry conducted under section 131(1), came to the conclusion that the assessee could not substantiate cash receipts received from various persons towards sale of jewellery before the date of demonetization. Therefore, vide letter called upon the assessee to file confirmation from all the parties and also called upon the assessee to show cause 'as to why' the credits should not be considered as unexplained cash credit under section 68. In response, the assessee submitted that as per law, it is not required to collect complete address and PAN from the persons to whom it has sold jewellery. Further, as per rules 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, if sale value of jewellery is in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs to a single person, then, it is required to collect PAN. Since, there is no requirement of collecting PAN, the assessee does not having details of PAN and correct postal address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Therefore, assessee submitted that the question of filing confirmation letter from the parties, from whom, it has collected advance for sale of jewellery does not arise, and consequently, cash receipts cannot be assessed under section 68. The assessee had also explained the Assessing Officer that it has sufficient cash balance as on 8-11-2016 as per books of account maintained for that assessment year and argued that the total cash deposits into bank account is explained out of cash in hand. The assessee has also made an alternative submission that it has sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12]

applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh in its bank account during the demonetisation period.

■

After taking into consideration the submissions and facts, there is substance in the contention of the Authorised Representative that without pointing out any discrepancy in the book of accounts as maintained by the assessee, the VAT returns, cash book, ledger, stock register, purchase register, sales register, sundry creditors and debtors, which were duly audited, the disallowance has been made. On the perusal of the documents which are on record it is crystal clear that the assessee was not having adequate infrastructure to handle such huge transactions in gold bars and had no experience to handle turnover in gold bars of such a huge magnitude, rather if the theory of assessee is accepted as to the sale and purchase of gold bars, then by not disclosing the names of ultimate buyers of gold who have allegedly bought gold through assessee, the assessee has in fact facilitated introduction of the undisclosed money of his buyers into the bank accounts of the assessee and its conversion into gold bars without disclosing their identity which also prevented end use of gold bars to be monitored. Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

Following the search on 23-12-2023, the AO alleged that the assessee paid cash on-money for Halol land purchases and made additions under section 69C of Rs. 78.82 lakhs (AY 2016-17), Rs. 87.97 lakhs (AY 2018-19) and Rs. 30.20 lakhs (AY 2023-24), aggregating about Rs. 1.97 crores, by estimating cash payment at 20 per cent of the agreement value. The AO principally relied on the statement of Rakesh Talati, alleging a customary 15-20 per cent cash component and cash delivery through an employee, and certain WhatsApp chats with Dharendra Pathak.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that Talati's statement was general, devoid of transaction-specific details and later retracted; no seller was examined; no cash trail or seized material evidenced cash payment; and all purchases were registered, made through banking channels and at or above stamp duty values. It was further shown that the WhatsApp chats related to a proposed Valsad transaction, whereas the additions concerned Halol lands. The CIT(A) found no corroborative evidence of cash payment, noted the absence of enquiry from sellers, accepted that the registered values were not below stamp duty values, held the chats unrelated to Halol and found the uniform 20 per cent estimation to be without factual basis. The additions were deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material placed before it. The entire addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash payment for purchase of land rests on a very narrow foundation, namely the statement of Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications. If the statement of Rakesh Talati is examined closely, it is evident that the statement is general in nature and lacks all essential particulars which are necessary for treating it as evidence of actual expenditure. The statement does not identify the specific land parcel in respect of which cash was allegedly paid. It does not identify the survey number. It does not identify the seller who allegedly received cash. It does not mention the exact amount paid in cash. It does not mention the date of payment. It does not identify the source from which the cash was generated. It does not identify the person who physically delivered the cash to the seller in relation to any particular transaction. Such a statement, at the highest, may give rise to suspicion and may justify further enquiry, but it cannot by itself constitute proof of actual expenditure incurred by the assessee. [Para 96]

■

The evidentiary weakness becomes more pronounced because the statement of Rakesh Talati was subsequently retracted. It is true that a retraction by itself does not automatically wipe out an earlier statement; however, once a statement is retracted and the assessee contests the factual correctness of the alleged admission, the burden lies on the revenue to corroborate the original statement through independent material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]

In the special facts and circumstances prevailing on 8-11-2016, after announcement of demonetization and the desperate situation that arose because of announcement of demonetization, it is quite understandable that customers rushed to use SBNs for making purchases without exercising selection and choice. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. FACT: ■

Pursuant to the search on 23-12-2023, the AO treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on the basis of statements of Nisha Singh (Rs. 30,000 per month) and Ramesh Kundnani (Rs. 1 lakh per month). Treating the aggregate monthly cash salary at Rs. 1.30 lakhs (Rs. 15.60 lakhs annually), the AO extrapolated the addition uniformly from AY 2015-16 to AY 2023-24, relying on Nisha Singh's cash deposits and rejecting both retractions. No parallel payroll, cash salary records, vouchers or cash trail was found.

■

On appeal, the assessee submitted that the search yielded no evidence of cash salary payments; Nisha Singh's retraction explained that the Rs. 30,000 represented remuneration of her brother, Vishal Singh, under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani routed through her, which the AO never verified; and Kundnani's retraction remained unrefuted. The CIT(A) held that no contemporaneous evidence established cash salary payments, the explanation regarding Vishal Singh was not investigated, the foundational requirement of proving expenditure under section 69C was absent, and the uniform extrapolation across years lacked year-wise evidence. On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and examined the entire material available on record. At the outset, it would be appropriate to observe that the revenue's case, when reduced to its essential components, rests solely upon the statements of two employees recorded during the course of search proceedings. There is no dispute that no document evidencing payment of cash salary was found during the search. There is no dispute that no parallel payroll register was recovered. There is no dispute that no employeewise cash salary sheets were discovered. There is no dispute that no vouchers, approvals, authorisations, electronic communications, payroll records or cash disbursement statements were found. In other words, despite an extensive search operation conducted in the case of the assessee company, the revenue has not brought on record a single contemporaneous document indicating existence of a parallel salary structure. This factual background assumes considerable importance because the addition sought to be made is not in relation to an isolated cash payment but on the premise that the assessee was maintaining a recurring system of salary payments outside its books of account. [Para 78]

■

The Tribunal shall first deal with the statement of Nisha Singh. The revenue seeks to rely upon her original statement to establish that she received Rs.30,000 per month in cash. However, the matter does not end with the original statement. The record reveals that she subsequently filed a retraction affidavit furnishing a specific and verifiable explanation. According to her, the amount in question pertained to her brother Vishal Singh, who was working on a part-time basis under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani, and the amount was routed through her and deposited in her bank account. Once such a specific explanation came on record, it became incumbent upon the Assessing Officer to examine its correctness. The revenue could easily have verified the role of Vishal Singh. It could have examined Inder Jaisinghani. It could have brought material demonstrating that the amount actually emanated from the assessee company. None of these steps were taken. Instead, the explanation was rejected without investigation. In the Tribunal's considered view, rejection of a specific factual explanation without any enquiry cannot elevate the original statement into conclusive evidence against the assessee. [Para 79]

Section  68,  read with sections  69A  and  153A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  102,  read with section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash credit (Unaccounted sales)  - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Assessing Officer, relying on parallel Tally data, WhatsApp chats and statements of Sunrise/SP Group personnel, alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash sales to SP Group aggregating Rs. 980.15 crores and brought profit at 14.75 per cent to tax - Assessee contended that entire case rested on third-party material; no incriminating evidence was found during search on assessee; and SP Group, by clarification and retraction affidavits, stated that cash transactions related to third parties and open-market purchases, not assessee - Whether since revenue failed to establish through cogent independent evidence that assessee was source of goods reflected in third-party records or recipient of alleged cash consideration, addition was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 68] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

A search was conducted on 23-12-2023 in the case of the assessee-company and connected persons. Separately, search in the Sunrise/SP Group yielded parallel Tally data ('Ka', 'Km' and 'CN'), coded ledgers, WhatsApp chats and statements. Relying solely on this third-party material, the AO alleged unaccounted cash sales by the assessee to the SP Group aggregating about Rs. 980.15 crores, applied an average profit margin of 14.75 per cent and taxed the profit element. The AO further alleged that Rs. 432.27 crores was routed to the assessee through Rashmikant Amin and Rs. 547.88 crores was paid towards the assessee's expenses, relying on coded ledger references such as 'Shankarbhai' and 'CKP'.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that the entire case rested on third-party material; no incriminating evidence was found during its search; the coded ledgers did not name the assessee; and the SP Group, by clarification dated 17-4-2024 and retraction affidavits, stated that the cash transactions related to third parties and open-market purchases, not the assessee. The AO neither examined the named third parties nor established any cash trail to the assessee. The CIT(A), noting absence of discrepancies in stock, production, dispatches or books, no undisclosed assets, and no beneficiary linkage between the 'Rashmi Amin' ledger and the assessee, deleted the profit addition.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of gold bullion/jewellery. A search under section 132 was carried out on 22-12-2016 at the residential premises of ‘K’ and ‘A’, partners of JMK Export. Consequently, a search and seizure operation was also carried out in the residential premises of ‘M’, erstwhile director of ‘RBPL’ on 23-12-2016. Simultaneously, survey action under section 133A was conducted at the business premises of some other entities namely, JMK Exports, Harrison Diamonds Pvt. Ltd., JMK Jewels Pvt. Ltd. and RBPL.

During the course of search and survey operations, a large number of incriminating materials including E-mail and SMS conversations amongst parties was found. During the course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of ‘M’, statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he stated that cash deposits amounting to Rs. 32.82 crores made in the bank accounts of RBPL post-demonetization, was given to him by ‘R’, one of the directors of assessee company, for depositing in the bank accounts and thereafter transferring funds to specified bank accounts on commission basis. Based on the statement of ‘M’ and other incriminating materials allegedly found in course of search and survey operations, the Assessing Officer, in the course of assessment proceedings of ‘M’, recorded a satisfaction note for initiation of proceedings under section 153C in the case of assessee for assessment years 2011-12 to 2016-17.

For the impugned assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 143(2) requiring assessee to furnish certain information regarding the alleged cash deposits of Rs. 32.82 crores in the bank accounts of RBPL and commission of Rs. 1.52 crore paid to ‘M’ for depositing the cash. In response to the query raised, the assessee furnished detailed submissions completely denying the allegation of cash deposits made into the bank accounts of RBPL through ‘M’.

one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102,  read with section  276,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Cash sales) – Assessment year  2017-18  – Assessee, engaged in trading of Supari and Kattha, deposited cash in bank during demonetization period claiming that deposits represented cash sales recorded in books and disclosed in VAT returns – AO, noticing a surge in cash sales and purchases from related concerns, treated balance cash deposits of about Rs. 2.64 crores as unexplained under section 68 – CIT(A) deleted addition – It was noted that assessee had inventories as per perpetual inventory method prepared on basis of VAT returns filed before demonetization and AO had neither rejected books of account nor pointed out any defect in purchases, stocks or sales – Whether a change or departure in trading patterns by itself could not justify an addition under section 68 and, since AO had failed to bring material on record to disturb trading results or establish that sales were not genuine or that stock for effecting such sales was unavailable, impugned addition was not justified – Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a private limited company engaged in trading Supari and Kattha, deposited cash of Rs. 2.83 crore during the demonetization period and explained that the deposits represented cash sales recorded in its audited books, supported by stock records and VAT returns.

■

The AO observed an abnormal surge in cash sales immediately before demonetization, questioned purchases from related concerns and other surrounding circumstances, estimated probable cash sales at only Rs. 19 lakh, and treated the balance cash deposits of Rs. 2.64 crores as unexplained cash credits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) accepted the assessee's cash-flow statement and records, noted that the audited books, purchases, sales and VAT returns had not been rejected or found non-genuine, held that the deposits stood explained as arising from recorded sales and that taxing them again would result in double taxation, and accordingly deleted the addition of Rs. 2.64 crores.

The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties.
