Attribution of income taxable under sub-section (4) of section 45 to the capital assets remaining with the specified entity, under section 48

.

8AB. (1) For the purposes of clause (iii) of section 48, where the amount is chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under sub-section (4) of section 45, the specified entity shall attribute such amount to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in a manner provided in this rule.

(2) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of the balance in his capital account, chargeable to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45, relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of clause (iii) of section 48 shall be the amount which bears to the amount charged under sub-section (4) of section 45 the same proportion as the increase in, or recognition of, value of that asset because of revaluation or valuation bears to the aggregate of increase in, or recognition of, value of all assets because of the revaluation or valuation.

(3) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 does not relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of clause (iii) of section 48.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (2) or (3), where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 relate only to the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of clause (iii) of section 48.

(5) The specified entity shall furnish the details of amount attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in Form No. 5C.

(6) Form No. 5C shall be furnished electronically either under digital signature or through electronic verification code and shall be verified by the person who is authorised to verify the return of income of the specified entity under section 140.

(7) Form No. 5C shall be furnished on or before the due date referred to in the Explanation 2 below sub-section (1) of section 139 for the assessment year in which the amount is chargeable to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45.

(8) The Principal Director General of Income-tax (Systems) or the Director General of Income-tax (Systems), as the case may be, shall -

(i)

specify the procedure for filing of Form No. 5C;

(ii)

specify the procedure, format, data structure, standards and manner of generation of electronic verification code, referred to in sub-rule (6), for verification of the person furnishing the said Form; and

(iii)

be responsible for formulating and implementing appropriate security, archival and retrieval policies in relation to the Form No 5C so furnished.

Explanation 1: For the purposes of this rule, the amount chargeable to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 shall relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, if the revaluation is based on a valuation report obtained from a registered valuer as defined in clause (g) of rule 11U.

Explanation 2: For the removal of doubt it is clarified that revaluation of an asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill does not entitle the specified entity for the depreciation on the increase in value of that asset on account of its revaluation or recognition of the value of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill due to its valuation.

Explanation 3: For the purposes of this rule, the expressions "self-generated asset" and "self-generated goodwill" shall have the same meaning as assigned to them in clause (ii) of Explanation 1 to sub-section (4) of section 45.]

The orders of AO as well as CIT(A) are completely silent as to for what purpose the earlier withdrawals would have been spent. As per the cash book maintained by the assessee, a sum of Rs. 10,000 was being spent for household expenses every month and the assessee has withdrawn from bank a sum of Rs. 2 lacs on 4th Dec., 2000 and there was no material with the Department that this money was not available with the assessee. It has been held by the Tribunal that in the instant case the withdrawals shown by the assessee are far in excess of the cash found during the course of search proceedings. No material has been relied upon by the AO or CIT(A) to support their view that the entire cash withdrawals must have been spent by the assessee and accordingly, the Tribunal rightly held that the assessment of Rs. 2.5 lacs is legally not sustainable under s. 158BC of the Act and the same was rightly ordered to be deleted."

On the basis of the above judgement of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court, the Hon'ble ITAT Delhi have recently deleted the addition made for inordinate delay in cash deposit in the case of 'NEETA BREJA v. ITO (IT Appeal No 524(D) of 2017, dated 25-11-2019)

(iv)

Rejection of the Cash Deposits being made out of Regular Business Cash Sales

The additions being made in the OCM/demonetisation cases by the assessing authorities on the basis of deviation/variance in cash deposits and cash sales ratio of the demonetisation period with that of the earlier periods, as contained in the CBDT Instructions concerning Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in OCM cases, may not hold legal sustainable ground in higher appellate forums as once an assessee establishes the authenticity and genuineness of the cash sales and corroborates and substantiates such cash sales with all relevant and supporting documents like sales invoices, bank statements, confirmations from buyers, VAT/Sales Tax Returns, co-relation of such cash sales with purchases and stock etc, then the authenticity of making the cash deposits out of such cash sales can't be disregarded and rejected merely on account of variation or deviation of the ratio of cash sales in the current period with that of an earlier period. There can't be a fixed sales pattern in any business.

Also, once an assessee has offered his cash sales as his business income, then again taxing the cash deposits being made out of his cash sales as unexplained cash credits amounts to double taxation, which is not permissible as per the canons of Income Tax Law.

The Hon'ble Delhi Tribunal in the case of AGSONS GLOBAL P LTD v. Asstt. CIT [2020] 115 tacmann.com 342 (Delhi - Trib.)have held that the addition being made on the sole ground of deviation in ratio of cash sales and cash deposits during the demonetisation period with that of earlier period, is not proper and lawful.

The Hon'ble Indore ITAT Bench in the case of DEWAS SOYA LTD, UJJAIN v. Income Tax (Appeal No 336/Ind/2012 has held that,

"the claim of the appellant that such addition resulted into double taxation of the same income in the same year is also acceptable because on one hand cost of the sales has been taxed (after deducting gross profit from same price ultimately credited to profit & loss account) and on the other hand amounts received from above parties has also been added u/s. 68 of the Act. This view has been held by the Hon 'ble Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Devi Prasad Vishwnath Prasad [1969] 72 ITR 194 (SC) that "It is for the assessee to prove that even if the cash credit represents income, it is income from a source, which has already been taxed". The assessee has already offered the sales for taxation hence the onus has been discharged by it and the same income cannot be taxed again."

Assessing Authorities' Stand in OCM/Demonetisation Assessment Cases concerning Assesses' Claims of Cash deposits being made out of Cash Sales in Business

5. In the cases of persons engaged in business and maintaining books of accounts, the most common and natural explanation and justification for the cash deposits being made by them in the post demonetisation period has been cash sales being made by them in their businesses.

The assessing authorities, in majority of the OCM assessment cases, have declined to accept the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made out of cash sales of business in post demonetisation period and have made huge income-tax demands under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in the regular assessment orders in such OCM/demonetisation cases. The most common arguments and contentions being made by the assessing authorities in rejecting the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made by the assessees out of their cash sales in business post demonetisation period are discussed as under:

i.

Since w.e.f. 8.11.2016 midnight, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes (SBNs) were declared invalid and were not to be considered as legal tender, therefore, for the assesses carrying on business, booking of cash sales and accepting such SBNs for transacting business transactions, during post demonetisation period, was prohibited.

ii.

The money measurement concept of accounting underlines the fact that in accounting and economics generally, every recorded event or transaction is measured in terms of money, i.e., the local currency monetary unit of measure. Since the SBNs were just a piece of papers and they bear no value on 9th November 2016 or after, as Central Government, the guarantor, had withdrawn its guarantee and hence, the receipt of these SBNs can't be journalized in books of account. Therefore, the transactions made in SBNs on or after 9th November 2016 cannot be entered into cash books.

iii.

Therefore, if the assessee has received any SBN notes after 09.11.2016 on account of any monetary transactions and utilizes the same for making cash deposits into the bank account, then the credit of the same into the books of accounts is not to be considered as valid and has to be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act and brought to tax.

In some other cases, where the cash deposits have been explained by the assessees as pertaining to cash sales being made by them prior to the demonetisation period, the assessing authorities have again rejected the genuineness and authenticity of such claims believing that the assessees might have backdated the cash sales just before the demonetisation period so as to reflect cash in hand as on 8.11.2016 consisting of banned notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000, which they have deposited in their bank accounts post demonetisation.

No person shall receive an amount of two lakh rupees or more—

in aggregate from a person in a day; or

in respect of a single transaction; or

in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account.

Assessments in OCM/ Demonetisation Cases

4. The demonetisation period i.e. period from 9.11.2016 till 30.12.2016, fell in the FY 2016-17 corresponding to the AY 2017-18. So, in the regular assessments for the AY 2017-18, a large number of scrutiny cases were pertaining to the issue of huge and abnormal cash deposits during the demonetisation period.

The earlier deadline for completing regular assessments for OCM/demonetisation cases was 30.9.2019. However, due to the paucity of time, the CBDT has extended the deadline for assessing officers to complete and conclude the assessments of such OCM/demonetisation cases by December 31, 2019, which in any case was the time barring deadline for completion of regular assessment cases for the AY 2017-18, other than transfer pricing cases.

The assessing authorities have segregated such OCM cases separately for business cases and non-business cases and have analysed these in terms of various criterion.

Further, cash deposits made in a financial year have been segmented into three parts, i.e. pre demonetisation period (1.04.2016 till 8.11.2016), post demonetisation period (9.11.2016 till 31.12.2016) and total in the financial year 016-17 and corresponding period in FY 2015-16. The assessing authorities have subjected these data to analytics and have worked out the percentage increase in cash deposits against all the three combinations to derive the meaningful inferences. The above provisions of TDS have taken care of the profit at the time of consideration paid to the resident either in cash/cheque or even crypto. It means when a person shifts from one crypto to another, the provisions are applicable, but this transaction cannot be mapped as the amount is not credited to the bank account.

Strengthening the Provisions One more method can be used to bring these exchanges in the ambit of regulation i.e. by bringing these exchanges under section 285BA and treating them as reportable entities (REs). By this, the obligation of disclosing the transaction lies with the exchange. For the time being, in the absence of the change in section 285BA, a special pilot project by Intelligence and Criminal Investigation (I&CI) can be launched to gather the information for such Specified Financial Transactions (SFT). There is no information available in the organized form that how many exchanges are dealing with crypto currencies. Similarly, only the exchanges located in a country can be brought to the scheme. The exchanges located outside are not obliged to comply either with the provisions of the Act or with any notices issued under Section 133(6) of the Act. At first, for the domestic exchanges, a master list is required to be prepared by collecting information from Google etc.Then these REs may be asked to furnish the SFT, which should contain data of all persons who have made these transactions. The entries during the gain period should be specifically checked. The collected information can be disseminated to the Assessing Officers for further verification or scrutiny. Similarly, Section 194S provides for a deduction of tax, even if the VDA is sold for another VDA. In case the sale is made in any recognised currency, the sale value is determined as per the realised value, but in case, the sale is made in another VDA, the issue of the valuation may arise. The fair market value has not been defined, which is another challenge.

Cash Transaction

The above mechanism is useful for transactions made through banking channels, but for cash transactions, it is near to impossible to catch them as the cash system works in the same fashion as 'hawala' works. The word 'hawala' is a local version of the English word 'reference'; this system works only on a reference basis. An anonymous person cannot go directly to the 'hawala' dealer for transfer of money between cities or countries. A reference from some known person is required. These dealers are not maintaining any written record; once a transaction is completed, the record is erased. Even if any record is found during the course of the survey or search, nothing can be made out of these jotted entries. Generally, these transactions are very smooth. Trust and risk are primary conditions. So dealing with cash crypto is almost like dealing with 'hawala' transactions. No separate provisions of the law are applicable, and no special expertise is required to crack these transactions. Traditional hawala methods were mainly operating through two methods. Firstly, the quantum of money of the sender and receiver should be the same. The second method is 'under-invoicing or over-invoicing' of import and export bills as required. But transfer through crypto is not based on any such conditions, the money can be sent unilaterally. So the emphasis is required only on those transactions which are done through banking channels.

Major Challenge

The main danger of cryptocurrencies is the convenience of transferring money to offshore places. A person can buy crypto in cash in India and transfer it to some person living abroad. That person would sell it and receive money in the local currency. Same as in the case of international debit or credit cards, where the deposits are made in one country in local currency, but ATM withdrawals can be made in any country. But these transactions contain heavy transaction fees, which is not there in the case of crypto. The central banks are honouring the transactions of debit and credit cards, as in the case of crypts also. The central bank has to honour at least in those countries that have given legal status to some cryptocurrencies. So why have some countries, like China, completely banned any transaction in these currencies. Section 194S comes into the picture when the amount is credited to a resident. Hence the money sent outside of the countries is out of the purview of these provisions. The first-time buyers of the crypto are also required to bring under these provisions.

31. Need for an enabling provision to deduct tax under Section 194N as cash withdrawn is not an income

Section 194N was introduced by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, which was subsequently substituted with a new provision by the Finance Act, 2020. This provision requires deduction of tax at source from the cash withdrawn by a person from his account maintained with a bank, cooperative bank or a post office.

Section 194N is covered under Chapter XVII which relates to the collection and recovery of tax. Section 4 and Section 190 contain the enabling provisions for the deduction and recovery of tax.

Section 4(1) provides that income tax shall be levied in respect of the total income of the relevant year. Section 4(2) provides that in respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income tax shall be deducted at the source or paid in advance, where it is so deductible or payable under any provision of this Act.

Section 190 relates to the deduction/collection of tax and payment of advance tax. Sub-section (1) of the said section provides that:

"Notwithstanding that the regular assessment in respect of any income is to be made in a later assessment year, the tax on such income shall be payable by deduction or collection at source or by advance payment or by payment under sub-section (1A) of section 192, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter."

This provision explicitly provides that the collection and deduction of tax shall be made in respect of the income of the assessee. If the amount received cannot be categorised as income in the hands of the receiver on which tax is leviable, no tax can be deducted/collected at source.

TDS on cash withdrawal was introduced to promote a cashless economy and discourage payments in cash. Section 194N requires tax deduction from the amount withdrawn from the accounts. However, it contradicts with provisions of Section 4 and Section 190. There is no income component in cash withdrawn from a bank account, thus, the question of TDS should not arise.

The Supreme Court has affirmed this proposition in the case of CIT v. Eli Lilly & Co. (India) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 178 Taxman 505 (SC) that if a particular income falls outside section 4(1), then TDS provisions cannot come in. The Madras High Court, in the case of Tirunelveli District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. JCIT [2020] 119 taxmann.com 21 (Madras),has also held that tax cannot be deducted under Section 194N if cash withdrawn is not an income of the account holder.

Thus, it is expected that Govt. may bring a suitable amendment under the law to end any possible litigation on this provision.

TAXMANN ADVISORY AND RESEARCH TEAM (INCOME TAX)

Introduction

1. Demonetization has encouraged people to shift towards digital mode of payment while making financial transactions. By adopting digital mode of payment, no financial transactions would remain undisclosed and Consequently, an enhanced turnover of business might get reflected in the books of account.

Under the circumstances, an apprehension has been caused that increased turnover in the current year may lead to reopening of earlier years' cases causing undue harassment to taxpayers.

Thus, CBDT and CBEC (vide Circular No. 40/2016 and Circular No. 137/155/2012-Service tax) have advised tax officials not to re-open past assessments in income-tax and indirect tax cases only because increased turnover is reflected in books of account of business on account of increased use of digital means of payment.

2. Points to be considered for interpreting such circulars:

It would be incorrect to construe the above Circulars as giving any amnesty to tax-evaders.

The above circulars do not say that any spurt in turnover reported in books of account of businesses of current financial year (and consequently in their ITRs or indirect tax returns) is not need to be explained.

The Circulars do not give businessmen a license to show their accumulated black money in the form of demonetized notes as current year's turnover and get away scot-free without any interest or penalty and by paying normal tax for current year. If such a license is given by the circulars, the proposed PMGKY Scheme and proposed amendments to section115BBE of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and proposed new section 271AAC of that Act would be redundant.

The two circulars clarify the following points which is mere re-iteration of the existing law:

Suppose any business reported Rs.1cr to Rs.1.5 cr as its turnover in service tax and VAT in last 5 years. If the business reports a turnover of Rs.5 cr in financial year 2016-17, then it is natural for any tax official to suspect that increased turnover;

However, such suspicion alone is not sufficient to entail reopening of past assessments in income-tax and well as service tax/customs;

The Circulars do not take away the powers of tax officials to make inquiries into the sudden spurt in reported turnover;

If the results of enquiries yield information which can form basis of "reason to believe" escapement of turnover/income in the past periods, the assessments can be reopened.

The Circulars are innocuous and merely caution tax officials to adopt systematic approach under the law to enquire into sudden jumps and reopen past assessment only if enquiry throws up reason to believe that past turnovers/incomes escaped assessment. Sudden jump in turnover may give reason to suspect that turnover/income had escaped assessment in past years. But that suspicion should not lead to reopening of past assessments without making necessary inquiries and verification regarding causes of the sudden increase.

Huge increase in reported turnover can be due to genuine reasons as well as due to book-keeping sophistry.

3. Examples of genuine reasons for increased turnover due to increased use of digital means of payments:–

(1)

Credit cards offer EMI terms on purchases made through credit cards. This may have resulted in increase in sales. So, a business which was selling only on cash basis may experience a jump in turnover on account of this reason.

(2)

Impolitic purchases through plastic cards

(3)

Special cash back schemes of mobile wallets/debit cards/credit cards.

(4)

Expansion of facility of service provider/increase in manpower enabling him to service more customers.

4. Comments

Increased turnover reflected in books of accounts may also be due to past unaccounted money now shown in current year's books as current year's turnover and thereafter these notes are banked.

Whatever be the reasons, taxpayers can (and should be) asked to explain the huge increase in current period's turnover. If they are able to explain the same by valid reasons and also show corresponding increase in stocks and purchases (or expansion in size of facilities/manpower), then their explanation will be believed and past assessments will not be reopened. If they cannot explain the sudden increase in reported turnover, they can always declare their huge unexplained cash/bank deposits in proposed PMGKY Scheme and pay 49.9% tax and deposit 25% in PMGKY deposit (no interest; 4 years lock-in). If they declare their unaccounted cash/bank deposits in PMGKY, then obviously, there would be no question of reopening their past assessments of income-tax or indirect taxes. If they do not declare in PMGKY and opt to show it as current year's turnover, then they should be able to justify it.

Section 43B deals with specified deductions which are to be allowed on a payment basis. Thus, even if an assessee follows the mercantile method of accounting, deduction pertaining to the specified expenses shall be allowed only when payment has been made.

Part A-OI (Other Information) consists of information wherein the assessee is required to furnish the details of any amounts disallowed under Section 43B in any previous year but allowable during the year.

The Finance Act 2023 has inserted a new clause (h) in Section 43B to provide that any sum payable to a micro or small enterprise beyond the time limit specified in Section 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act 2006 (MSME Act) shall not be allowed as a deduction.

Accordingly, a new column is inserted under Part A-OI (Other Information) to disclose the sum payable to Micro or small enterprises beyond the specified time limit per the MSMED Act.

9. Disclosure of information pertaining to the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme

[ITR 2, 3 and 5]

The Schedule-CG of ITR forms seeks information about the capital gains earned by the taxpayer. This schedule requires various details, including information about the capital asset sold, the particulars of the buyer, and specifics regarding the amount spent for claiming exemptions.

In the newly notified ITR Forms, Schedule-CG has been modified to gather more information pertaining to sums deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts scheme (CGAS). The revised schedule now requires the inclusion of the following additional details towards CGAS:

Date of deposit

Account number

IFS code

Until the previous Assessment Year, taxpayers were only required to provide details pertaining to the sum deposited in CGAS.

10. Disclosure of Winnings from online games chargeable under Section 115BBJ

[ITR 2, 3 and 5]

The Finance Act 2023 has inserted a new Section 115BBJ to tax winnings from online games, w.e.f. Assessment year 2024-25. A corresponding Section 194BA has also been inserted with effect from 01-04-2023 for the deduction of tax from the net winnings from online games. Thus, all winnings from online games on or after 1-4-2023 shall be taxable under Section 115BBJ and subject to TDS under Section 194BA.

To report such income in ITR form, Schedule OS has been amended to disclose income by way of winning from online games chargeable under Section 115BBJ.

11. New Schedule 80GGC seeks details of contributions made to political parties

[ITR 2, 3 and 5]

Section 80GGC allows for a deduction for contributions to a political party or electoral trust. The new ITR forms include a new Schedule 80GGC, which requires the furnishing of the following details:

Date of Contribution

Contribution Amount (with a breakdown of contributions made in cash and other modes)

Eligible Contribution Amount

Transaction Reference Number for UPI transfer or Cheque Number/IMPS/NEFT/RTGS

IFS Code of the Bank

Unlike the previous ITRs, the new ITR forms require disclosing additional information beyond just the amount eligible for deduction under Section 80GGC.

12. 'Schedule - Tax Deferred on ESOP' seeks PAN and DPIIT Registration Number of the eligible startup

[ITR 2 and 3]

When an employer allots securities to an employee under ESOP scheme, free of cost or at concessional rate, it is taxable as perquisite in the year of allotment of securities. However, the liability for payment or deduction of tax on such perquisite is deferred in the case of an employee of an eligible startup.

30. Time limit to pass an order under Section 201(3) if the assessee fails to deposit TDS

Section 201(3) of the Act prescribes the time limit for the Assessing Officer to pass an order deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default for failure to deduct the tax from a person resident in India. The said order can be passed before the expiry of 7 years from the end of the financial year in which payment or credit was made or 2 years from the end of the financial year in which the correction statement was furnished by the assessee.

The section prescribes the time limit for the assessee who has failed to deduct the tax at source. In contrast, no time limit has been prescribed where the assessee has failed to deposit tax after deduction.

As a deductor is considered an assessee-in-default under Section 201(1) in both cases, that is, failure to deduct tax and failure to deposit tax after deduction, there should be a time limit for passing an order of assessee-in-default in both circumstances.

Abstract

Gold has regained prominence as a universal store of value amid rising geopolitical uncertainty, inflation, and distrust in fiat currencies. Its surge to record highs in 2025 reflects both legitimate economic behaviour and increasing compliance challenges. This article analyses how global gold dynamics intersect with taxation, money-laundering laws, and white-collar crime, particularly within India's regulatory ecosystem. It also examines cross-border trade complexities, enforcement coordination, and the evolving standards of global financial governance. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for policymakers and corporate stakeholders to balance economic opportunity with legal responsibility.

Keywords: Gold, Taxation, Compliance, PMLA, FATF, GAAR, Cross-Border Trade, Corporate Governance, White-Collar Crime

I. Research Objective and Context

Gold remains more than a commodity. It is an emotion, a financial anchor, and a barometer of public confidence. In 2025, its value has soared not only because of market mechanics but also due to geopolitical tension and financial distrust. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the legal, tax, and compliance implications of gold's renewed prominence in the global economy.

The research aims to:

1.

Examine the global and Indian gold market trends shaping 2025.

2.

Analyse the legal and regulatory architecture governing taxation, anti-money-laundering, and cross-border transactions.

3.

Identify vulnerabilities that enable gold to be used for white-collar crime.

4.

Recommend policy and governance strategies that uphold transparency and accountability without impeding legitimate trade.

Gold's unique attributes such as liquidity, anonymity, and universal acceptance make it both an asset of stability and a tool of concealment. Understanding this duality is essential for designing laws that protect integrity while enabling commerce.

II. The Global Gold Surge: Economics, Emotion and Law

A. Price Trends and Market Forces

According to Reuters and the World Gold Council, gold prices in 2025 have risen nearly 50 percent year-on-year, reaching around US $3,950 per ounce internationally and crossing Rs. 1,25,000 per 10 grams in India. This dramatic rise stems from persistent inflation, high global debt, and growing investor preference for tangible assets.

Central banks across Asia and the Middle East have purchased record quantities of gold to diversify reserves. Goldman Sachs has forecast prices could approach US $4,900 per ounce by 2026 if inflation remains elevated and interest rates stabilise.

This global pattern underscores gold's transformation from a passive store of value into a geopolitical hedge. It reflects both market sentiment and institutional strategy.

B. India's Domestic Context

India's relationship with gold is historical and deeply cultural. Demand peaks during festivals and marriage seasons, creating a recurring impact on trade balances. India imports nearly all its gold, which has implications for the current account deficit and currency stability.

High import duties and fluctuating exchange rates have incentivised smuggling and under-invoicing. In March 2025, the government discontinued parts of the Gold Monetisation Scheme to limit fiscal exposure. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has since reported a notable increase in illegal inflows through land and maritime borders.

C. Geopolitical Context

Gold's rally cannot be separated from the global political landscape. The continuing Russia–Ukraine conflict, instability in the Middle East, and trade tensions between the United States and China have disrupted global supply chains. Sanctions against Russian bullion refineries have redirected trade to Asian hubs such as Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

As trade flows realign, enforcement agencies must address differing compliance standards among jurisdictions. Some free-trade zones have become conduits for gold trading with limited regulatory oversight, increasing risks of mis-invoicing and money laundering.

III. Legal Framework Governing Gold and Financial Compliance

A. Income-Tax and Disclosure Laws

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, unexplained gold holdings can be taxed as income under Sections 69 and 69B. High-net-worth individuals and corporations are required to declare gold holdings accurately to avoid reassessment and penalty.

Cross-border transactions in gold attract transfer-pricing scrutiny under Section 92F. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued guidelines requiring documentation that justifies arm's-length pricing.

Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor.

As a result the monetary threshold means little to the e-commerce operators who require mandatory registration under the proposed law. This is in view of the provisions under Section 43C of the proposed law requiring e-commerce operators to collect and deposit tax before or at the time of credit of the money collected to the retailers/service providers.

Provisions of tax collection at source and input tax Credit 6. As set out above, Section 43C of the proposed law brings in an unexpected liability for the e-commerce operators. It imposes some heavy burden of tax collection at source on all e-commerce operators, regardless of their scale of operations. Big e-commerce operators may have little trouble in ensuring compliance; but the small and evolving players are bound to suffer. Importantly, since the sellers may be spread cross the country, tax needs to be paid to the credit of the "appropriate government ", e-commerce players might require multiple registrations: as a matter of fact, in all states where the seller is located. This means more compliance burden, and more costs to all the e-commerce players involved.

Furthermore, there are strict deadlines imposed for collection and payment of tax to the credit of the appropriate government. Section 43C(3) requires every e-commerce operator to pay it to the credit of the appropriate government within ten days after the end of the month in which such collection is made, in the manner prescribed. This provision can cause several problems, as it overlooks the practice of customers returning goods. Assuming that a delivery is made, and money is received, and appropriate credits are made to the respective governments, how could one claim a refund of the money deposited if the goods sold are returned by the buyer. If a sale is made to a buyer in Karnataka, and tax is deposited with this government, and where the goods delivered are returned, and the buyer purchases goods from another buyer in Andhra Pradesh, things can get complicated for all the players involved. There seems to be no provision to accommodate this situation as yet.

Also, there are websites that act merely as pass-through, and neither receive payment online nor through any medium. Websites like Quikr and Magicbrikcs are examples worth quoting. These websites, although arguably covered under the proposed law as e-commerce operators, neither receive payment themselves nor through any other medium. The payments happen between the buyer and the seller, without any role being played by the e-commerce operator in such case. For such websites the revenue is largely from the advertisements and premium services, which alone can be taxed under the proposed law. In these case, one cannot help but wonder how the tax collection at source provisions shall apply.

Importantly, there are heavy duty procedural compliances under the proposed law. Section 43C(6) provides that the details of supplies and the amount collected by the e-commerce operator during a calendar month, and furnished by every operator shall be matched with the corresponding details of outward supplies furnished by the concerned supplier in his valid return for the same calendar month or any other preceding months. Any authority not below the rank of Joint Commissioner may by notice require the operator to furnish details like supplies of goods/and or services effected through such operator during any period, and stock of goods held by the suppliers making supplies through such operator in the godowns or warehouses. Where an e-commerce operator fails to respond to such notice appropriately, a penalty which may extend to rupees twenty five thousand rupees shall also be payable.

Provisions relating to input tax Credit

7. Section 43C(5) of the proposed law provides that amount collected in accordance with the provisions of this section and paid to the credit of the appropriate government shall be deemed to be payment of tax on behalf of the concerned supplier. The supplier shall claim credit in his electronic cash ledger of the tax collected and reflected in the statement of the operator filed. Now, in a situation where the e-commerce operators fails to pay the amount required to be paid to the credit of the appropriate government, or miscalculates the amount of liability and under-pays, the retailers shall have problems in claiming input tax credit. This is an issue that merits serious consideration.

Presently, non-fungibility of VAT and service tax are big problems for e-commerce operators. The extant indirect tax structure has simply failed to keep pace with growing business models in India. With the advent of the GST law, non-fungibility is no longer a problem. E-commerce operators shall be well-placed to claim GST credit on all services/goods they procure.

Other issues

8. E-commerce operators have a flurry of offers in the forms of discounts, cash-backs, referral fees, buy one get one deals. All these deals may be to be subject to tax under the GST Act. Valuing the transaction in such cases is bound to be crucial since everything could potentially be a supply under the proposed law; more so, when it's only known that they are exempt from the levy of GST under the proposed law. Besides above, e-commerce operators routinely offer wallet services, which allow users to retain money in a wallet, and use it to pay for purchases/services whenever the need be. Paytm for instance offers this service free of cost. This could be treated to be a supply under the proposed law.

The Committee notes that Clause 37(1) does not explicitly clarify whether expenses expressly disallowed under other provisions of the ITB can still be claimed under this clause on the grounds of actual payment. As per the ITA 1961

Section 269SU provides that every person carrying on a business whose total sales, turnover, or gross receipts exceed Rs. 50 crores during the immediately preceding previous year, is required to provide a facility for accepting payment through prescribed electronic modes.

As per the ITB 2025

Clause 187 of the ITB 2025 carries the same provision as mentioned in Section 269SU of the ITA 1961.

As per ITA 1961

Section 271A of the ITA 1961 levies a penalty on a person who fails to keep, maintain, or retain books of account, documents, and other records as required under Section 44AA. The Assessing Officer, JCIT(A) or CIT(A) may direct such a person to pay a penalty of Rs. 25,000.

As per ITB 2025

The provisions of the existing Section have been textually simplified and retained with the same intent in clause 441 of ITB 2025. However, the word 'may' has been replaced with the word 'shall' in respect to the levy of penalty by AO.

The Committee found that non-compliance with maintaining books of accounts could arise from genuine reasons. To address such cases, the Committee recommended replacing "shall" with "may" in Clause 441.

Clause 514 is a newly introduced provision in the ITB. Any person who possesses the prescribed qualifications to value a specific class of assets may apply for registration as a valuer to the relevant authority in the prescribed form, duly verified, and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The application must include a declaration confirming that the applicant will conduct fair and accurate valuations, furnish valuation reports in the prescribed format, charge fees within the prescribed limits, and avoid valuing any asset in which he has a direct or indirect interest.

A registered valuer is required to prepare the valuation report in the prescribed form and have it verified in accordance with the laid-down procedures.

27. Increase in the threshold limit for payment of advance tax

The liability to pay advance tax arises only when the estimated tax liability of a taxpayer for the financial year is Rs. 10,000 or more. The threshold limit of Rs. 10,000 was revised 10 year ago vide the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2009 wherein it was increased from Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 10,000. The Govt. should consider revising the threshold limit of estimated tax liability from Rs. 10,000 to minimum Rs. 25,000.

28. LTA for foreign travel

An employee is entitled to claim exemption for the leave travel allowance granted to him by his employer for the purpose of going on a vacation anywhere within India. This exemption is still allowed only for vacations within India. This provision may help to promote Indian Tourism but it is not in pari-materia with current scenario as travelling to some overseas destinations is cheaper than visiting tourist destinations in India. Therefore, it is recommended that the exemption should be allowed for both Indian destinations as well as for foreign destinations. Alternatively, the exemption should be allowed for both hotel and travel expenditure if the destination is in India and only for travel expenses if vacation happened in an overseas country.

29. Benefit of sections 54, 54F & 54EC to be allowed even if new investments are made in name of close relatives

The exemptions under Sections 54, 54F, 54EC and 54B are allowed only when an assessee makes investment in some specified assets. The assessee and Income-tax department are often at loggerheads in respect of relative for whom the new asset should have been acquired by assessee to claim the exemption.

The Assessing Officer often disallows the exemption if assessee purchases new asset in name of his close relative (i.e., son, daughter or spouse) and claims the exemption by contending that there is no requirement that the investment in new assets should be in the name of the assessee.

There is no clarity in the law whether exemption shall be available in case the new asset has been acquired by assessee in name of his close relatives. Thus it is suggested that Union Budget 2020 should bring about suitable amendments to end the litigations.

30. Allow more time to buy new house for Sec. 54 or 54F exemptions

Section 54 and 54F allows very little time to the taxpayers to invest in a new house. It allows 1 year before or 2 years after the date of transfer of old property in case of purchase of new property and 3 years if new property has to be constructed.

Generally, in township projects, the developers take minimum of 5 years before handing over the possession of the property to the buyers. In that case, if a buyer gets the possession of new house after 3 year, he is not allowed to claim Section 54/54F exemption. Therefore, suitable amendment is needed to allow section 54/54F exemptions to genuine taxpayers who invest in a project developed by a builder registered under RERA. Either the time limit to invest in new house should be increased to at least 5 years or a clarification should be issued that the taxpayer shall be allowed deduction for all investments made within the given time limit even if purchase or construction is not yet completed in that stipulated time limit.

The time limit for construction or purchase of a house property for deduction of interest on housing loan has also been increased from three years to five years by the Finance Act, 2016. Therefore, it has become necessary to increase the time limit under Section 54 and 54F.

31. Deposit in Capital Gain Scheme should not exceed the due date for filing of return

The provisions of section 54(2) stipulate that the amount of the capital gain which is not utilised by the assessee towards the purchase or construction of the new house before the date of furnishing the return of income under section 139, shall be deposited by him in capital gain account scheme. Section 54F(4) also provides exemption on similar lines.

Various Judicial authorities have held that for the purpose of Section 54/54F the due date for furnishing of return of income, as provided under Section 139(1), is subject to extended period as provided under Section 139(4). However, as the issue is not free from doubt and is likely to occur every now and then, it is recommended that a specific date (or a clarification in this regard) may be mentioned in sections 54 and 54F so that this type of uncertainty does not prevail.

53. Allowing utilisation of the input tax credit ledger balance for reverse charge payments

Under the GST law, certain provisions result in cash blockages without yielding any incremental revenue to the Government. For instance, in the case of imports of services, the recipient of services is liable to discharge GST liability in cash under a reverse charge mechanism, which will then be available to him as ITC. The mandatory cash payment leads to cash blockage.

The Government should consider allowing taxpayers to use their GST ITC balance for payment of tax under the reverse charge mechanism. The ability to use the ITC balance to discharge the RCM liability would not only address the cash flow issues but also streamline the tax administration process, making it more business-friendly without compromising the tax revenues for the Government.

54. Transfer of Input Tax Credit from one State to another

Under the existing GST framework, Form ITC-02 facilitates the transfer of unutilised input tax credit only between GST registrations located within the same State. The law does not currently envisage or provide any mechanism for transferring accumulated ITC in cases of inter-State business movement. Consequently, in situations such as business reorganisation, merger or restructuring involving different States, closure of operations or a branch in one State, and continuation of the same business from another State, the accumulated ITC remains locked with the original registration. This results in a loss of credit, a blockage of working capital, and procedural hardship, despite no change in the underlying business or tax incidence.

Recently, the Bombay High Court in the case of Umicore Autocat India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2025) 32 Centax 416 (Bom.), pursuant to a scheme of amalgamation, held that the transfer of unutilized ITC lying in the electronic credit ledger of transferor company to amalgamated company is allowed irrespective of fact that companies are located in different States.

It is recommended that a procedure be devised to allow for the transfer of accumulated ITC in such inter-state business transfers, to ensure seamless credit flow and avoid loss of legitimate credits to taxpayers.

55. Refund of the closing balance of the Input Tax Credit

Under the erstwhile VAT regime, taxpayers were permitted to claim a refund of unutilized input tax credit (ITC) at the end of the financial year. This ensured that taxes already paid on inputs did not become a permanent cost to businesses and supported adequate working capital management.

Under the GST framework, the refund of accumulated ITC is currently available only in limited circumstances, such as for zero-rated supplies (exports and supplies to SEZs) and for inverted duty structures. In most other situations, unutilized ITC remains blocked, even though it represents taxes already paid to the Government.

A critical situation arises when a taxpayer decides to close or exit a business. Currently, the GST law does not explicitly provide for the refund of unutilized ITC upon business closure, leaving taxpayers unable to recover legitimate credits accumulated over the course of operations. This creates an unnecessary financial burden, as the unutilized credit represents tax that has already been paid and should rightfully be refundable.

It is therefore recommended that a provision be introduced under GST allowing:

Refund of unutilized ITC at the end of a financial year, to ease working capital constraints.

Refund of accumulated ITC on business closure, enabling taxpayers to recover input taxes legitimately paid, thereby reducing stranded credit and avoiding penalisation of businesses for exiting operations.

56. Legislative misalignment in the case of ECOs who are required to pay tax on supplies listed under section 9(5) as if they are the suppliers of notified services

The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has issued Circular No. 240/34/2024-GST, providing much-needed clarification regarding the Input Tax Credit (ITC) availed by E-Commerce Operators (ECOs) in scenarios where services specified under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, are supplied through their platform. This circular extends the principles previously clarified in Circular No. 167/23/2021, dated December 17, 2021, to restaurant services and other services notified under Section 9(5).

The circular draws upon the principles established in Circular No. 167/23/2021-GST, dated December 17, 2021, which clarified the ITC treatment for restaurant services provided through ECOs. These principles are now explicitly extended to other services notified under Section 9(5).

Questions that remain unanswered

Section 158BC mandates that a person subjected to a search on or after 01-09-2024 must file a return of income in response to a notice issued by the Assessing Officer. The notice requires a person to furnish the return within the prescribed period but not exceeding 60/90 days2. Rule 12AE, which prescribes Form ITR-B for filing such returns, has been made applicable retrospectively from 01-09-2024. However, this Rule was notified only on 7th April 2025, and until this date, Form ITR-B did not exist in Income-tax Rules, 1962. Even after its notification, the form is not yet functional on the e-filing portal, creating a procedural gap in compliance with the requirement of Section 158BC.

This raises a critical issue if a notice under Section 158BC is issued on or after 01-09-2024 but before the notification of Rule 12AE, i.e., 07-04-2025, the assessee was legally required to file a return, but no prescribed form was available to comply with this obligation. This effectively places the assessee in a compliance dilemma, where a statutory obligation exists, but no practical mechanism to fulfill it has been provided.

The Rule fails to address how relief will be extended to taxpayers when a search is conducted after 01-09-2024 and a notice under Section 158BC is issued. Further, Rule 12AE does not provide any solution where an assessee is considered a defaulter because the due date for filing a return under Section 158BC had lapsed before the availability of an online mechanism to file Form ITR-B.

31. Condition to pay emoluments by specified modes under section 80JJAA should be applicable in case of new businesses also

Section 80JJAA of the Income-tax Act provides that every assessee earning business income and liable to the tax audit can claim a deduction under this provision for additional employee cost. The deduction shall be allowed for 30% of the additional employee cost in three assessment years.

However, such deduction shall be allowed only if the assessee fulfils certain conditions. One of the conditions is that emoluments must be paid by any of the following modes:

(a)

An account payee cheque;

(b)

Account payee bank draft;

(c)

By use of electronic clearing systems through a bank account; or

(d)

Other prescribed electronic modes, i.e. Credit/debit card, IMPS, RTGS etc.

This condition is applicable in the case of an existing business only. To move towards digital India initiative, it is expected that the above condition regarding payment of emoluments through the above modes may be extended in the case of new businesses also.

32. Seller for the purpose of TCS under Section 206C(1F) should include Individual or HUF

The Finance Act, 2016 inserted sub-section (1F) to Section 206C to bring high-value transactions within the tax net. This provision provides that every person, being a seller, who receives any amount as consideration for the sale of a motor vehicle of the value exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs, shall collect tax from the buyer at the rate of 1% of the sale consideration.

The term 'seller' has been defined under clause (c) of Explanation to Section 206C. This clause defines the meaning of seller with respect to sub-section (1) and sub-section (1F) of Section 206C. However, to include an individual or a HUF within the meaning of 'seller', it provides that total sales, gross receipts or turnover of such individual or HUF from the business or profession carried on by him should exceed Rs. 1 crore in case of business or Rs. 50 lakh in the case of the profession during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the goods of the nature specified in the Table in sub-section (1) are sold. This Explanation has inadvertently omitted to give a reference of sub-section (1F) of Section 206C.

It is recommended that clause (c) of the Explanation to Section 206C should be amended to mention the reference of sub-section (1F) also. This Explanation should read as under:

(a) "seller" with respect to sub-section (1) and sub-section (1F) means the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority or corporation or authority established by or under a Central, State or Provincial Act, or any company or firm or cooperative society and also includes an individual or a Hindu undivided family whose total sales, gross receipts or turnover from the business or profession carried on by him exceed one crore rupees in case of business or fifty lakh rupees in case of profession during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the goods of the nature specified in the Table in sub-section (1) or sub-section (1F) are sold.

Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

12.12-1 Evidence for ascertaining the value of investments

During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee. Assessee submitted a bill in respect of purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges. However, AO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee. Held once the identity of the diamond jewellery found during the course of search had been accepted as explainable from the purchase voucher and labour charges bill produced by the assessee at the time of search as well as during the course of regular assessment proceedings, the addition of the difference could be made by the AO only by establishing the fact that the value stated in the purchase invoice was fictitious. The burden clearly lay upon the department to prove that the value shown in the purchase invoice was not the real value. The department had not brought any material whatever on records to prove that the value of such diamonds embedded in the diamond jewellery at the time of its purchase in the month of July 1981 was understated in the purchase invoices. Such a burden was required to be discharged by the department by bringing clinching and conclusive evidence on record. The AO had not even examined the jeweller from whom these diamonds were purchased. The assessee had successfully discharged the initial burden of proving the source of acquisition of aforesaid diamond jewellery by producing the aforesaid bills at the time of search. The AO had completely failed to bring any evidence on record to show that the cost of ornaments shown by the assessee did not represent the real cost. Therefore, the addition on account of the difference in value of diamond ornaments in question is not justified and deserves to be deleted. - Gautam Laljibhai Gajjar v. ITO [1991] 37 ITD 514 (Ahd.)

During assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer after recording the assessee's statement regarding source of purchase of drafts amounting to Rs. 4,49,527, observed that the assessee claimed to have purchased drafts from cash available during normal business transactions, but it had made credit sales to almost all the parties whose accounts were obtained under section 133(6) and, therefore, there was no possibility of the assessee having heavy cash in hand. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, treated the amount as investment out of unexplained sources and added it back to the assessee's total income. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed (a) that the assessee was doing very good business in garments and had also daily sale proceeds, (b) goods released by custom authorities, after payment of customs duty and demurrage charges, were indeed available for sale and (c) the assessee utilised the sale proceeds for making further remittances to the Customs Collector for releasing more goods. Therefore, the according to the Tribunal, the entire amount of Rs. 4,49,527 representing the five drafts could not be said to be available in the hands of the assessee at a time; the drafts having been sent during the course of four months, the money must have rotated and it was appropriate to at best adopt the peak amount of Rs. 1,95,000 as money available from unexplained sources. On application under section 256(2) the High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision. - Wadhwa Ram v. CIT [1997] 93 Taxman 487 (Punj. & Har.)

Section 206C

Finance Act, 2013

13.3 Tax Collected at Source - Section 206C

13.3-1 Existing Provisions

In order to reduce the quantum of cash transaction in bullion and jewellery sector and for curbing the flow of unaccounted money in the trading system of bullion and jewellery, the Finance Act, 2012 inserted new sub-section (1D) in section 206C with effect from 1-7-2012 to provide for TCS on cash sale of jewellery and bullion to be collected by the seller.

According to new sub-section (1D), every person, being a seller, who receives any amount in cash as consideration for sale of bullion (excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less) or jewellery, shall, at the time of receipt of such amount in cash, collect from the buyer, a sum equal to 1% of sale consideration as income-tax, if such consideration,—

(i)

for bullion, exceeds two hundred thousand rupees; or

(ii)

for jewellery, exceeds five hundred thousand rupees.

13.3-2 Amendments

The Finance Act, 2013 has omitted the words "(excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less)" with effect from 1-6-2013.

13.3-3 Impact

So cash sale of gold coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less will also attract TCS with effect from 1-6-2013 if consideration exceeds Rs. 2,00,000.

To put in other words, with effect from June 1, 2013, consideration of "any coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less" shall not be excluded while calculating the monetary limit of Rs. 2,00,000.

Press release dated 1-5-2013 read as under :—

Currently, sale in cash of bullion (excluding coin or any other article weighing 10 grams or less) in excess of Rs. 2 lakh or jewellery in excess of Rs. 5 lakh is subject to Tax Collection at Source (TCS) @ 1%. As coins were neither included in bullion nor in jewellery, therefore, coins, even when amounting to more than Rs. 2 lakh in value, were being sold in cash without TCS.

The Finance Bill, 2013 proposes to delete exclusion of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less from bullion. Hence, the sale of bullion (including coins/articles) in cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%. Similarly, sale of jewellery in cash in excess of Rs. 5 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%.

It is not a new levy of tax but continuation of old levy except withdrawal of exemption in the case of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less.

| Introducing own black money in books as credits in the names of fictitious creditors or persons of inadequate means is no longer advisable in view of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act,1988. Better show it as own money by crediting capital account and bringing on books the relevant assets and pay 78% tax and disclose in ITR under section 115BBE(1)(a). If own black money introduced in books in names of fictitious persons/persons of low means, it will attract additions u/s 68, tax of 78% and penalty as also confiscation under the Benami Act. If assessee of limited means acts as benamidar and shows huge black money credited in books of someone else as his own, he can't get away paying 78% tax under section 115BBE(1)(a) with voluntary disclosure in ITR. It will be liable for confiscation under Benami Act. Credit of any sum in the books of the assessee in order to be cash credit u/s 68 should be capable of being treated as his income-Ali Hussain Abdeali Lokhandwala v. ITO [1991] 36 ITD 247 (Indore) Although section 68 heading is 'Cash Credits', it is not limited to cash receipts. The expression 'any sum' in section 68 is wide and would cover all credits including loans, receipts, trade credits, credits in capital account or in the name of third party. Assessee bound to offer satisfactory explanation as to the nature and source of credit in his books of account. There is no bar on assessee offering an alternative explanation. If either of them is accepted by AO, then, no additions can be made by AO. Explanation as to source does not mean assessee has to explain source of the source. However, to this rule, there is an exception. . . . credits in respect of share application money or share capital or share premium in the books of closely-held company. If assessee fails to offer any explanation or the explanation offered is unsatisfactory, then the amount of credit shall be assessable u/s 68 read with section 115BBE. Explanation must be a factual explanation and not merely a legal argument. It is one thing to say that credits are out of intangible additions in past periods. This is a factual explanation and must be proved. It is quite another thing for the assessee to say that intangible additions were made in the past and these be deemed to be/treated as source of cash credits. This is not an explanation as to source and is merely a legal argument and doesn't discharge the onus of explanation which section casts on the assessee. If assessee's explanation is not satisfactory, AO can make additions. AO is not bound to prove that unexplained credit is from a particular source. |

The intention to use the "cash" in the first proviso, in a negative sense, is to discourage the cash transactions. Thus, to compute the 5% threshold, only cash receipts should be considered, and any receipts by way of journal entry should not be considered in the 5% threshold. Similarly, sales made on a credit basis, even if funds are not realised, should not form part of the 5% threshold.

BLOCK PERIOD M/s XYZ could be assessed on UnI from assessment years 1986-87 to 1994-95 and for the period 1st April, 1995 to 10th October, 1995 under Chapter. 2. PROCEEDINGS IN CASE OF OTHER FIRMS AND THE PARTNERS Along with the books of account and assets of firm, assets of other firms AB and CD and partners P, Q and R were also seized. Accordingly, the AO of XYZ will have to hand over books and assets of M/s AB, M/s CD and of partners P, Q and R to the Assessing Officers having jurisdiction over the said Firms and partners as per section 158BD of the Act. Accordingly, all the aforesaid firms and partners would also be assessable in respect of UnI, if any, under Chapter. 3. TREATMENT OF CASH FOUND (a) As entries of Rs. 3.5 lacs were found in books of account, it could not be considered as UnI by virtue of section 158BA(3) and accordingly it would not form part of UnI No doubt, income, if any, embedded therein would be taken into consideration for determining DL (b) Diaries would not constitute books of account maintained in normal course, as discussed in para 1.3-2c above and therefore the cash of Rs. 1 lac would be considered as UnI. (c) The amount belonging to the partners cannot be regarded as UnI of XYZ under section 158BD, and as explained above, proceedings would be initiated in the hands of partners under Chapter to assess the amount as UnI. (d) The balance amount of Rs. 4 lacs remain unexplained and accordingly it would be includible as UnI in the hands of XYZ for the previous year to end on 31st March, 1996. 4. JEWELLERY (a) Jewellery found to be purchased in the year 1982 beyond the period of 10 years, cannot be considered as part of UnI, as the year would not form part of block period. Even under normal procedure the assessment cannot be re-opened. Accordingly, the cost of purchase of Rs. 20,000 cannot be included as UnI of M/s XYZ. (b) The jewellery purchased in the year 1987 of Rs. 3 lacs and in the year 1991 of Rs. 4 lacs would constitute UnI of M/s XYZ for the assessment years 1988-89 and 1991-92, respectively, in terms of provisions of sections 68, 69, etc., read with section 158BB(2). (c) That part of the jewellery which was reflected in the returns, etc., of the partners, cannot be considered as UnI, within the meaning ascribed to it in definition of UnI under section 158B(b). (d) That part of the jewellery explained as belonging to the partners would not constitute UnI of the firm in view of section 158B(b) to the extent it is explained. 5. SHARES (a) The shares acquired in the year 1980 cannot be considered as part of UnI as it falls beyond the block period defined in section 158B(a). (b) Dividends of Rs. 10,000 received every year would be considered as UnI and accordingly includible in determining TI for the assessment years 1986-87 to 1996-97. (c) The shares which were acquired in the year 1987 can be included as a part of UnI at the value thereof in the year 1987 of Rs. 3 lacs, in the assessment year 1988-89, by virtue of sections 68, 69, etc., read with section 158BB(2). In addition to the above dividends thereon would also be includible in the subsequent years, which are estimated at, say, Rs. 15,000 per year from assessment years 1989-90 to 1995-96. (d) Shares valued at Rs. 5 lacs, which are found; but, date of acquisition whereof cannot be ascertained can be treated as UnI of the previous year to end on 31st March, 1996 and could be valued at Rs. 5 lacs. Thus, to compute the 5% threshold, only cash receipts should be considered, and any receipts by way of journal entry should not be considered in the 5% threshold. Similarly, sales made on a credit basis, even if funds are not realised, should not form part of the 5% threshold. The term "receive" or "received" has been judicially explained as follows:

(a)

"To come into possession of, get, acquire, or the like, from any source outside of oneself." [In re McCullough's Estate, 193 Wash. 145, 74 P.2d 877 (1928)]

(b)

"To receive means to get by a transfer, as, to receive a gift, to receive a letter, or to receive money and involves an actual receipt." [The Major Law Lexicon by P. Ramanatha Aiyar, 4th Edn., Vol. 5; College Law Dictionaries by Dr. Avtar Singh, 2nd Edn.]

(c)

"The 'receipt' of income refers to the first occasion when the recipient gets the money under his own control." [Keshav Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 230 (SC)].

Thus, the term "received" means an amount (money) actually received by the assessee during the previous year. The proviso contemplates actual receipt of amounts by the assessee during the previous year. So, in this context, the term "received" may not include "receivable". The Supreme Court in CIT v. Moon Mills Ltd. [1966] 59 ITR 574 (SC) held that there is no scope for holding that the expression "received" means "receivable".

48.4.5-9 How to reckon the limit of Rs. 2,00,000? - Section 269ST is applicable when any payment is received of Rs. 2,00,000 or more

(a)

in aggregate from a person in a day;

(b)

in respect of a single transaction; or

(c)

in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person. Illustration 1 - Suppose Mr. X had made credit sales of Rs. 1,00,000, Rs. 1,50,000 and Rs. 50,000 on three different dates against different orders and different bills to Mr. Y. Mr. Y pays Rs. 3,00,000 by cash on 01.04.2023 against these bills. This will amount to receiving Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in aggregate from a person in a day" and thus violate section 269ST. If suppose Rs. 1,00,000 cash is paid on 01.04.2023 and Rs. 1,00,000 cash is paid on 02.04.2023 and Rs. 1,00,000 cash on 03-04-2023, it will not amount to a violation of section 269ST as Rs. 2,00,000 limit is not made up in either of the three ways in (a) or (b) or (c) above.

Illustration 2 - Suppose a caterer takes an order for a wedding and receives Rs. 15,00,000 in cash from his customer and gives item-wise bills for various services, and each bill doesn't exceed Rs. 2,00,000 and Rs. 15,00,000 is received in cash on different dates and cash received on any one day is less than Rs. 2,00,000. This splitting of bills and payments day-wise will not help as all these payments are "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person".

Illustration 3 - Suppose a credit sale of Rs. 2,00,000 is made, and the buyer makes two cash payments of Rs. 1,00,000 per day to the seller on two different dates. Section 269ST is attracted as Rs. 2,00,000 cash limit is reached "in respect of a single transaction".

Illustration 4 - Suppose X, a contractor, undertakes a contract for the renovation of a house and charges Rs. 5,00,000 (Rs. 2,00,000 related to civil work and remodelling, Rs. 2,00,000 related to woodwork, Rs. 50,000 for plumbing and Rs. 50,000 related to electrical work). He bills separately for each of these and receives three cash payments of Rs. 1,50,000 each on 2-9-2023, 3-9-2023 and 4-9-2023 and balance Rs. 50,000 in cash on 5-9-2023. Section 269ST is attracted as the sum received in cash is Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person"

Illustration 5 - Suppose in Illustration 4 above the contractor receives Rs. 1,99,000 in cash and a balance Rs. 3,01,000 in cheque. In this case, section 269ST is not attracted as the cash receipt is less than Rs. 2,00,000.

Illustration 6 - Suppose the owner of a house demolishes it and sells the resulting debris (malba) for cash amounting to Rs. 3,00,000. Section 269ST is attracted whether the transaction is business or personal.

Illustration 7 - Suppose I sell my old car for Rs. 2,50,000 and receive a cash advance of Rs. 75,000 on 2-10-2023 and Rs. 1,75,000 in cash on 3-10-2023 on delivery. Section 269ST is contravened here as the sum received in cash is Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person" as also "in respect of a single transaction" even though aggregate sum received in cash in a single day is less than Rs. 2,00,000.

In light of the above, an attempt is being made to explain various provisions of Chapter XIV-B.

Block Period

The block period to assess the undisclosed income shall be from:

(a)

Assessment years relating to the previous years 2018-19 to 2023-24.

(b)

01-04-2024 to 15-10-2024

Proceedings against

Since, along with the books of account and assets of XYZ, the assets of other firms AB and CD and partners P, Q and R were also seized, the assessment proceedings shall be done against:

(a)

M/s. XYZ under Section 158BC.

(b)

M/s. AB and M/s. CD under Section 158BD read with Section 158BC.

(c)

Partners P, Q and R under Section 158BD read with Section 158BC.

Treatment of cash found during search

(a)

Rs. 3.5 lakhs found in books of account could not be considered as undisclosed income. Income, if any, embedded therein would be taken into consideration for determining disclosed income.

(b)

Diaries would not constitute books of account maintained in normal course. Therefore, the Rs. 1 lakh cash would be considered undisclosed income for the previous year 2024-25 (AY 2025-26).

(c)

The amount belonging to the partners cannot be regarded as undisclosed income of XYZ. Proceedings would be initiated in the hands of partners under Section 158BD, read with Section 158BC, to assess if these are undisclosed income.

(d)

The balance of Rs. 4 lakhs remains unexplained, and accordingly, it would be included as undisclosed income in the hands of XYZ for the previous year 2024-25 (AY 2025-26).

Treatment of jewellery found during search

(a)

Jewellery purchased in 2012 is beyond the block period of 6 years. Hence, it cannot be considered undisclosed income. Even under normal procedure, the assessment cannot be re-opened to inquire about such jewellery.

(b)

The jewellery purchased in July 2019 for Rs. 14 lakhs and in August 2021 for Rs. 22.50 lakhs would constitute the undisclosed income of M/s. XYZ in terms of provisions of Sections 68, 69, etc., read with Section 158BB(2).

(c)

The part of the jewellery explained as belonging to the partners would not constitute the undisclosed income of the firm. That part of the jewellery will be dealt with according to Section 158BD read with Section 158BC.

Treatment of shares found during search

(a)

The shares acquired in 2012 cannot be considered as undisclosed income as it falls beyond the block period.

(b)

Dividends of Rs. 10,000 received every year would be considered undisclosed income for the previous years 2018-19 to 2023-24 (AYs 2019-20 to 2025-26).

(c)

The shares acquired in September 2018 whose market value was Rs. 3 lakhs in that year, shall be the undisclosed income of the assessment year 2019-20, by virtue of Sections 68, 69, etc., read with Section 158BB(2).

(d)

The dividend of Rs. 15,000 received yearly will be considered as undisclosed income for the previous years 2018-19 to 2023-24 (AYs 2019-20 to 2025-26).

(e)

Shares worth Rs. 5 lakhs, the date of acquisition of which cannot be ascertained, can be treated as undisclosed income of the previous year ending on 31-03-2025.

(f)

The tax-free bonds of Rs. 5 lakhs will be included in the undisclosed income of the previous year 2019-20 (AY 2020-21). Interest on such bonds being exempt would not form part of undisclosed income.

>

Treatment of cash entries found in diaries

(a)

The profit on account of cash sales and purchases for the previous year 2023-24 (AY 2024-25) of Rs. 2 lakhs (Rs. 6 lakhs minus Rs. 4 lakhs) will be assessable as undisclosed income.

(b)

The profit on account of cash sales and purchases for the previous year 2024-25 (AY 2025-26) of Rs. 1 lakh (Rs. 3 lakhs minus Rs. 2 lakhs) will be assessable as undisclosed income.

CHAPTER ONE

Special procedure for assessment of search cases*

Introduction

1.1 The Finance Act, 1995 inserts a new Chapter XIV-B [consisting of eight sections (sections 158B to 158BH)] in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), with effect from 1 -7-1995 and introduces a new procedure and concept for assessment of Undisclosed Income ('UnI') pursuant to a search under section 132 or a requisition under section

search or requisition and such other materials or information as are available with the Assessing Officer. [Section 158BB(1)]

■

While computing income under relevant heads, unabsorbed depreciation or unabsorbed losses should not be set off. [Explanation (a)to section 158BB(1)]

■

While computing undisclosed income, the following provisions shall apply having regard to the provisions of Chapter XIVB relating to block period. [Section 158BB(2)]

| Provisions | Nature |
| --- | --- |
| 68 | Cash credit deemed to be income, if not or not satisfactorily explained, in the year in which credit is found. |
| 69 | Unexplained investments not recorded in books, for which no explanation or satisfactory explanation about the source and nature is furnished, value of investment deemed to be income in the year in which investments are found. |
| 69A | Assessee found to be owner of unexplained money, bullion, jewellery or other valuables in any financial year, not recorded in the books, and not or not satisfactorily explained to AO, value deemed to be income. |
| 69B | Where amount of investment in any bullion, jewellery or other valuables is found not fully disclosed and if not or not satisfactorily explained to AO, excess to be deemed as income. |
| 69C | Unexplained expenditure - no or unsatisfactory explanation about the source of expenditure, the amount of expenditure may be deemed as income. (See also para 1.5-4d) |

■

The assessee would have to discharge the burden of proof with respect to any claim that UnI has been disclosed in any return before the commencement of search. [Section 158BB(3)]

■

In case of a firm and/or its partners, the method of computation and allocation should be the same as applicable to each of the previous years in the block. [Explanation.(b)to section 158BB(1)] (See para 1.5-5)
