The provisions certainly could not have contemplated two different bases for inclusion and exclusion of DI - inclusion for the purpose of determining TI and exclusion for the purposes of determining UnI. 1.5-4c Effect of computation as per Chapter IV - The objective is to ensure that no other deduction or relief available under the provisions other than Chapter IV can be taken into account for arriving at UnI

1.5-4c1 EXEMPTIONS UNDER CHAPTER III - The above provision, however, would not affect an exemption provided in Chapter IV itself or Chapter HI, that is, sections 10, 10A, 10B, etc.

To illustrate, suppose an assessee receives Rs. 2 lakhs in cash on sale of a house property. It was also noticed that the investment in a new house was in cash of about Rs. 3.5 lakhs. As the cash money was found to have been invested in a new house, in computing income under the head 'Capital gains', certainly, effect has to be given to exemption, which is not prohibited by Chapter.

1.5-4c2 DEDUCTIONS UNDER CHAPTER VI-A - If an assessee is entitled to a benefit or deduction under Chapter VI-A, in respect of UnI or against such UnI he would not be entitled to such deduction, having regard to the other view discussed in para 1.5-4b'.

To illustrate, suppose an industrial undertaking in a backward area, entitled to 100% deduction under section 80-IA, under invoices its goods and receives cash for sales effected. In the search, this is detected. While determining his income under Chapter IV of the Act, the cash receipts would be included as part of business profit in TI. He will not be eligible to a deduction under section 80-IA in respect of such receipts. Thus, although, the receipts could have been otherwise not taxed, would be taxed as UnI

1.5-4c3 ALLOWANCES/DISALLOWANCES - Computation of UnI is required under various heads. This implies that various allowances and expenses incurred and permissible as deduction under the said provisions would certainly be allowable. Similarly, if any provision for disallowance is attracted, like, section 40 or section 40A, such disallowance would also be made.

To illustrate:

If an undisclosed asset is found, depreciation and expenses on repairs, in respect of such undisclosed asset would be permissible deductions from UnI.

If there are borrowings in cash and interest is found to have been paid, such interest would be allowable in computing UnI

If it is found that a payment has been made to a non-resident; but, tax is not deducted, such payment would not be allowable on account of provisions of section 40(a) of the Act.

If any remuneration is paid to a partner and is not recorded in the deed, it would not be allowable.

If any cash payments are made in excess of Rs. 10,000 provisions of section 40A(3) may be attracted

Similarly, if a loss is incurred in respect of undisclosed transactions or source; such loss would be allowable against UnI, provided the loss is proved.

It may be clarified that all the above allowances or disallowances would be in respect of each of the previous year(s) in block period; they will have to be in terms of the applicable provisions; necessary conditions will have to be satisfied; and where a claim therefor is made, it would be upon assessee to discharge the burden of proof for making a claim for such allowance.

1.5-4c4 APPUCATION OF SECTION 32A/35(4) - Unabsorbed investment allowance is set off under section 32A. Unabsorbed expenditure on scientific research is allowed to be carried forward under section 35(4). No specific restriction has been placed on set off of such allowance or expenditure against UnI.

1.5-4d Assessment of undisclosed asset, etc.- Where any undisclosed asset, expenditure and the like are found, they are to be assessed having regard to provisions of sections 68, 69, etc., in terms of section 158BB(2) of the Act with suitable modification. Accordingly, the value thereof will have to be adopted having regard to the relevant previous year in the block in which they were found.

To illustrate:

If cash credit was found in the year 1987, it will have to be included in TI of the year 1987.

If land and buildings are found and is noticed that land was acquired in May 1989, value of the land would be includible in TI of previous year ending on 31 st March, 1990.

If in the above case expenditure on building, etc., was found to be incurred in subsequent years, amount of expenditure on building would be includible in TI of subsequent previous years.

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12] In light of above factual matrix, if one examines the issue, the Assessing Officer has rejected the contention of the assessee on two grounds. The first and foremost reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject the explanation of the assessee is that persons from whom assessee claims to have been received advance are not responded to summons issued under section 131(1) and in few cases, they have denied any kind of transactions with the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not discharge its onus cast upon as per the provisions of section 68, in respect of cash receipts, and thus, opined that cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee from various persons is unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has committed a fundamental mistake in examining the cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee towards sale of jewellery in light of provisions of section 68. [Para 13]

Be that as it may. The fact remains that, the assessee has furnished name and address of the customers from whom it has received cash for sale of jewellery. The assessee need not obtain confirmation and submit to the Assessing Officer, because, the law does not mandate collecting PAN details of the persons, if sale value of jewellery does not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs as per rule 114B of Income-tax Rules, 1962. In so far as compliance of KYC norms, it is mandatory under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with effect from 4-5-2023 onwards and not applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14]

The assessee in the instant case could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit of huge magnitude of more than Rs. 49 crores in his bank account which he claimed to be from cash sales from gold bars to the persons wherein the identity of the buyers are not revealed by the assessee. Thus, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit in the bank account and consequently sources of incurring expenditure by way of purchases claimed by the assessee in its profit and loss account of Rs. 48.78 crores could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee and onus cast under section 69C was not satisfied which would make amount covered by such expenditure represented by purchases of gold bars to be deemed income of the assessee under the deeming fiction of section 69C. The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer called upon the assessee to file details of name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. The assessee has filed a list of persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Out of list submitted by the assessee, the Assessing Officer has issued summons under section 131(1) to 50 persons to verify the genuineness of the assessee claim of receipt of cash from them. Out the above 50, summons issued to 40 persons returned by the Postal Authorities citing 'addressee cannot be located' or 'no such person' or 'no such address' or 'insufficient address' or 'no such address at the above place'. In response to summons, three persons were responded and out of three, two persons denied having any kind of transactions with the assessee. Further, one person confirmed having paid advance to the assessee company and also purchased jewellery from them. The Assessing Officer, on the basis of enquiry conducted under section 131(1), came to the conclusion that the assessee could not substantiate cash receipts received from various persons towards sale of jewellery before the date of demonetization. Therefore, vide letter called upon the assessee to file confirmation from all the parties and also called upon the assessee to show cause 'as to why' the credits should not be considered as unexplained cash credit under section 68. In response, the assessee submitted that as per law, it is not required to collect complete address and PAN from the persons to whom it has sold jewellery. Further, as per rules 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, if sale value of jewellery is in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs to a single person, then, it is required to collect PAN. Since, there is no requirement of collecting PAN, the assessee does not having details of PAN and correct postal address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Therefore, assessee submitted that the question of filing confirmation letter from the parties, from whom, it has collected advance for sale of jewellery does not arise, and consequently, cash receipts cannot be assessed under section 68. The assessee had also explained the Assessing Officer that it has sufficient cash balance as on 8-11-2016 as per books of account maintained for that assessment year and argued that the total cash deposits into bank account is explained out of cash in hand. The assessee has also made an alternative submission that it has sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12]

applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh in its bank account during the demonetisation period.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that there was an unusual increase in cash sales during October 2016 and held that the cash sales recorded immediately before demonetisation were non-genuine and represented unaccounted money introduced into the books.

■

After allowing credit for estimated cash-in-hand and estimated genuine cash sales, the Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and taxed the same under section 115BBE.

■

On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

■

In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the cash sales were duly recorded in regular books of account and supported by VAT returns, cash book, ledger accounts, stock register, purchase register, sales register and audited financial statements. It was further submitted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor disputed purchases or stock movement.

HELD: ■

After taking into consideration the submissions and facts, there is substance in the contention of the Authorised Representative that without pointing out any discrepancy in the book of accounts as maintained by the assessee, the VAT returns, cash book, ledger, stock register, purchase register, sales register, sundry creditors and debtors, which were duly audited, the disallowance has been made. It is the considered view of the Tribunal that abnormal growth in the cash sales and that certain parties were not identified to whom the cash sales were made, are vague grounds, to make addition when assessee has demonstrated that there was direct co-relation cash outflow and from the books of account the cash deposits in the bank account were made. It is found outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected and was not inquired into or otherwise disturbed by the AO. Once the AO has accepted the sales and assessee had substantially established on the basis of financials that there is a direct nexus of the cash sales with the closing stock, then addition u/s 68 is not justified. During demonetization period it was quite possible that the cash sales would increase for the reason also that customers holding the demonetized currency wanted to use the same for making cash investment in gold. CIT(A) has fallen in error to sustain the addition merely on the basis of suspicion. [Para 5]

■

Consequently the appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 6]

On the complete appreciation of the facts and also touchstone of human probabilities, the story of sale of gold bars appears to be a smokescreen while real objective was to introduce undisclosed income into banking system by way of deposit of cash in bank accounts. On the perusal of the documents which are on record it is crystal clear that the assessee was not having adequate infrastructure to handle such huge transactions in gold bars and had no experience to handle turnover in gold bars of such a huge magnitude, rather if the theory of assessee is accepted as to the sale and purchase of gold bars, then by not disclosing the names of ultimate buyers of gold who have allegedly bought gold through assessee, the assessee has in fact facilitated introduction of the undisclosed money of his buyers into the bank accounts of the assessee and its conversion into gold bars without disclosing their identity which also prevented end use of gold bars to be monitored. [Para 10]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor.

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material placed before it. The entire addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash payment for purchase of land rests on a very narrow foundation, namely the statement of Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications. If the statement of Rakesh Talati is examined closely, it is evident that the statement is general in nature and lacks all essential particulars which are necessary for treating it as evidence of actual expenditure. The statement does not identify the specific land parcel in respect of which cash was allegedly paid. It does not identify the survey number. It does not identify the seller who allegedly received cash. It does not mention the exact amount paid in cash. It does not mention the date of payment. It does not identify the source from which the cash was generated. It does not identify the person who physically delivered the cash to the seller in relation to any particular transaction. Such a statement, at the highest, may give rise to suspicion and may justify further enquiry, but it cannot by itself constitute proof of actual expenditure incurred by the assessee. [Para 96]

■

The evidentiary weakness becomes more pronounced because the statement of Rakesh Talati was subsequently retracted. It is true that a retraction by itself does not automatically wipe out an earlier statement; however, once a statement is retracted and the assessee contests the factual correctness of the alleged admission, the burden lies on the revenue to corroborate the original statement through independent material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

FACT: The assessee filed her return under VDIS, 1997, in which she declared sale proceeds of jewellery and diamonds received from two purchasers ‘G’ and ‘T’. The Commissioner accepted the return filed by the assessee and issued the certificate as envisaged under the VDIS. At a later stage, searches were conducted on those purchasers in which they conceded before the search party that no purchases were made by them and cheques had been issued after taking cash through the middlemen. Later on ‘T’ retracted from his statement and confirmed that he had purchased jewellery from the assessee. On the basis of statements of both the purchasers, the Assessing Officer reopened the assessment and added the sale proceeds of jewelleries to the income of the assessee under section 68, and he made further addition at the rate of 3 per cent of both those amounts towards commission payments under section 69C. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted both the additions made by the Assessing Officer under sections 68 and 69C.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: After perusing the orders of the lower authorities along with other materials placed on record, it was found that there was no infirmity in the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals). The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering the order of the Assessing Officer in the light of submissions made before him and other materials on record had found that there was lot of discrepancies and contradictions in the facts of the case and the statements recorded under section 132(4) in the case of ‘G’.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]

The assessee side has provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make the aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.25 crores even after announcement of demonetization. Therefore, the claim of cash sales of aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores is found to be acceptable. [Para E.2.1]

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. FACT: ■

Pursuant to the search on 23-12-2023, the AO treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on the basis of statements of Nisha Singh (Rs. 30,000 per month) and Ramesh Kundnani (Rs. 1 lakh per month). Treating the aggregate monthly cash salary at Rs. 1.30 lakhs (Rs. 15.60 lakhs annually), the AO extrapolated the addition uniformly from AY 2015-16 to AY 2023-24, relying on Nisha Singh's cash deposits and rejecting both retractions. No parallel payroll, cash salary records, vouchers or cash trail was found.

■

On appeal, the assessee submitted that the search yielded no evidence of cash salary payments; Nisha Singh's retraction explained that the Rs. 30,000 represented remuneration of her brother, Vishal Singh, under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani routed through her, which the AO never verified; and Kundnani's retraction remained unrefuted. The CIT(A) held that no contemporaneous evidence established cash salary payments, the explanation regarding Vishal Singh was not investigated, the foundational requirement of proving expenditure under section 69C was absent, and the uniform extrapolation across years lacked year-wise evidence. On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and examined the entire material available on record. At the outset, it would be appropriate to observe that the revenue's case, when reduced to its essential components, rests solely upon the statements of two employees recorded during the course of search proceedings. There is no dispute that no document evidencing payment of cash salary was found during the search. There is no dispute that no parallel payroll register was recovered. There is no dispute that no employeewise cash salary sheets were discovered. There is no dispute that no vouchers, approvals, authorisations, electronic communications, payroll records or cash disbursement statements were found. In other words, despite an extensive search operation conducted in the case of the assessee company, the revenue has not brought on record a single contemporaneous document indicating existence of a parallel salary structure. This factual background assumes considerable importance because the addition sought to be made is not in relation to an isolated cash payment but on the premise that the assessee was maintaining a recurring system of salary payments outside its books of account. [Para 78]

■

The Tribunal shall first deal with the statement of Nisha Singh. The revenue seeks to rely upon her original statement to establish that she received Rs.30,000 per month in cash. However, the matter does not end with the original statement. The record reveals that she subsequently filed a retraction affidavit furnishing a specific and verifiable explanation. According to her, the amount in question pertained to her brother Vishal Singh, who was working on a part-time basis under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani, and the amount was routed through her and deposited in her bank account. Once such a specific explanation came on record, it became incumbent upon the Assessing Officer to examine its correctness. The revenue could easily have verified the role of Vishal Singh. It could have examined Inder Jaisinghani. It could have brought material demonstrating that the amount actually emanated from the assessee company. None of these steps were taken. Instead, the explanation was rejected without investigation. In the Tribunal's considered view, rejection of a specific factual explanation without any enquiry cannot elevate the original statement into conclusive evidence against the assessee. [Para 79]

material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

■ The failure of the Assessing Officer to examine the land sellers is perhaps the most serious infirmity in the addition. Where the allegation is that the assessee paid cash consideration over and above the registered value, the most natural witness would be the seller of the land. If the allegation were correct, the seller would be the recipient of the alleged on-money. Yet, not a single seller has been examined. No seller has admitted receipt of cash. No statement of any vendor has been recorded. No enquiry has been conducted into the books, bank accounts, assets or conduct of the sellers. No document has been found from any seller indicating receipt of consideration outside the registered document. In the absence of examination of the alleged recipients of cash, the allegation remains one-sided and untested. [Para 98]

■

The registered sale documents and stamp duty valuation also assume great significance. The assessee has demonstrated that the lands at Halol were purchased at values equal to or higher than the stamp duty/circle rates. This factual position has not been rebutted by the Assessing Officer. The transactions were registered, the consideration was recorded in the books of account and payments were made through banking channels. When registered documents disclose consideration not below the statutory valuation adopted for stamp duty purposes, and no seller disputes the stated consideration, the revenue cannot presume payment of additional cash merely on the basis of a general statement. The normal suspicion of undervaluation itself becomes weak in such circumstances. If despite this, the Revenue alleges payment of on-money, the allegation must be supported by direct and cogent evidence. That is completely absent here. [Para 99]

■

The WhatsApp chats relied upon by the Assessing Officer also do not advance the revenue's case. The CIT(A) has examined these chats and found that they do not contain any reference to actual payment of cash in relation to Halol land transactions. They do not record any completed payment. They do not contain any admission by the assessee or acknowledgement by any seller. They do not identify any amount paid in cash. They do not establish movement of money. More importantly, the chats pertain to a proposed land transaction at Valsad, whereas the additions have been made in respect of land purchased at Halol. No addition has been made in respect of Valsad. Therefore, even if the chats are accepted at their highest, they are evidentiary neutral for the purpose of the Halol land additions. A communication relating to one proposed transaction cannot be used to estimate cash payment in entirely different registered transactions without any connecting material. [Para 100]

■

The search perspective also supports the assessee's case. The allegation concerns payment of cash consideration in land transactions. If such payment had actually been made, one would ordinarily expect some trace of it either from the assessee's premises, from the employee allegedly involved, from the recipient seller or from the person alleged to have arranged or delivered the cash. However, no cash ledger, no on-money sheet, no seller acknowledgement, no loose paper, no payment trail, no cash flow record and no documentary evidence of any nature has been found. The alleged roles of Shri Chirag Shah, Shri Inder Jaisinghani and Smt. Parul Patel also remain unsubstantiated by any independent material. In a search assessment, where the Department has the benefit of seized records and statements, addition cannot be made merely by estimating a percentage on registered transaction value without first establishing the factum of actual cash payment. [Para 101]

■

The methodology adopted by the Assessing Officer in estimating 20 percent of the agreement value as unexplained expenditure is also legally unsustainable. No basis has been given for adopting 20 percent uniformly. No comparable transaction has been cited. No seller-wise material exists. No land-wise evidence exists. No year-wise evidence exists. The statement itself, even as relied upon by the Assessing Officer, refers to a general range of 15 percent to 20 percent and not to actual payment in any specific case. Estimation may have a role where the foundational fact of expenditure is proved and only quantification remains uncertain. Here, however, the foundational fact itself is unproved. Therefore, estimation cannot substitute evidence. [Para 102]

■

Section 69C requires three foundational conditions. First, there must be material to show that an expenditure has actually been incurred. Second, such expenditure must be shown to have been incurred by the assessee. Third, the assessee must fail to explain the source of such expenditure. In the present case, the Revenue has not crossed the first threshold itself. Actual cash expenditure has not been proved. Incurrence by the assessee has not been proved. The alleged recipient has not been identified through evidence. Once the expenditure itself is not established, the question of explaining its source does not arise. Therefore, the invocation of section 69C fails at the very threshold. [Para 103]

■

headnotes.text: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh during demonetisation period - Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that there was abnormal increase in cash sales during October 2016 and some cash sales were made to unidentified persons - It was noted that no discrepancy was found in assessee's audited books of account, VAT returns, cash book, stock register, purchase register or sales register - It was further noted that assessee had established a direct nexus between cash sales, stock movement and cash deposits, and Assessing Officer had neither disturbed stock records nor rejected sales - Whether once AO had accepted sales and assessee had substantially established on basis of financials that there was a direct nexus of cash sales with closing stock, then addition under section 68 was not justified - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69A, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained Moneys (Demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery - During demonetization period, assessee deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers in its bank account - Assessing Officer observed that cash sales were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by assessee company merely to build an explanation for cash deposits in to bank account and made an addition of total cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE - Assessee furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for relevant period and cash sales made by assessee had been credited in books of account and, thus, assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences - Further, no defect had been pointed out in books of account of assessee - When sale had been offered to tax, adding same again would amount to double taxation - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving source of cash deposited in bank, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Sales during demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee was engaged in business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) - During demonetisation, assessee made cash sales of Rs. 10.28 crores on 08-11-2016 - Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to income of assessee under section 68 - It was noted that no specific transaction of sale, not even one, had been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue - Allegation of Revenue holding that cash sales of aforesaid amount claimed by assessee to be untrue, was without convincing materials - Aforesaid addition had been made by Revenue based merely on suspicion, doubt, conjecture and guess work - Assessee had provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.24 crores even after announcement of demonetisation - Moreover, assessee had shown sales in VAT returns, which had been accepted by VAT authorities - Whether, on facts, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Para E.2.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Cash deposits during demonetisation) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of about Rs. 6.34 crores in bank during demonetisation period, stated to be out of cash sales of jewellery recorded in books - AO doubted cash sales and treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 - CIT(A) confirmed addition - Assessee contended that cash deposits were out of recorded cash sales supported by bills, vouchers, bank extracts and VAT returns, and that books and trading results, including impugned cash sales, had not been rejected - Whether where trading results have been accepted and books not rejected, no addition is permissible - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

III. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash salary) - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on basis of statements of Nisha Singh and Ramesh Kundnani and extrapolated alleged cash salary uniformly across Assessment Years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - It was noted that no parallel payroll, cash sheets, vouchers, approvals or cash withdrawal trail was found and existence of expenditure was sought to be inferred solely from retracted statements - Whether since revenue failed to prove actual expenditure incurred by assessee, invocation of section 69C failed at threshold - Held, yes - Whether further, extrapolation of alleged cash salary payments across all assessment years, without any material showing similar payments in each year, was unsustainable - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash salary payments was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 82, 83 and 85] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 69C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 - Assessee filed her return under VDIS, 1997 and declared sale proceeds of jewellery and diamonds received from two purchasers - Commissioner accepted return filed by assessee and issued certificate as envisaged under VDIS - At a later stage, searches were conducted on those purchasers in which they conceded before search party that no purchases were made by them and cheques were issued after taking cash through middlemen - On basis of said information, Assessing Officer reopened assessment and added sale proceeds of jewelleries to income of assessee under section 68 and he made further addition at rate of 3 per cent of both those amounts towards commission payment under section 69C - Commissioner (Appeals) found that no material was brought on record regarding payment of commission; statements of purchasers were not supplied to assessee and one purchaser had retracted from his statement given during course of investigation and deleted both additions made by Assessing Officer - Whether since findings of Commissioner (Appeals) were not controverted by revenue, and no other material was brought on record so that it could be established otherwise, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes

IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-HUF filed its return of income for assessment year 1998-99 and declared long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds - Assessee submitted that said diamonds had been declared under voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced VDIS certificate issued by Commissioner - Assessee further submitted that sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts and was deposited in savings bank account of assessee and he also placed before Assessing Officer confirmation letters from buyers of diamonds; sale invoices; copy of extract of bank account and valuation report of diamonds - Assessing Officer, however, found that (i) main activity of purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries; (ii) demand drafts were purchased by depositing equivalent amounts of cash in bank account; (iii) assessee travelled to Surat alone in unreserved compartment carrying diamonds and stayed in dharamshala under a fictitious name; (iv) 'G' who was connected with purchasing parties in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between - In view of said details Assessing Officer concluded that assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold diamonds to Surat based parties and he, accordingly, rejected claim of capital gains of assessee and made addition under section 68 - Whether since diamonds were declared in VDIS which was supported through certificate issued by Commissioner and further, buyers had confirmed to have purchased diamonds and sale invoices; copy of bank account giving full description and details had been placed on record, which were not controverted by Assessing Officer, it could be said that there was a strong presumption in favour of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes

VII. Section  68,  read with sections  69A  and  153A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  102,  read with section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash credit (Unaccounted sales)  - Assessment years 2021-22 to 2023-24 - During search in Nathani Group, Assessing Officer, relying on statement of Shri Vinay Nathani, WhatsApp communications and allegation that certain orders were not routed through P-Connect, alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash sales to Nathani Group aggregating Rs. 42.54 crores and brought profit at 14.75 per cent to tax - Assessee contended that Nathani Group, by clarification and retraction affidavits, stated that impugned cash transactions related to third-party purchases and not assessee; orders received through WhatsApp or other modes were duly recorded through Oracle ERP and quantities appearing in chats were supported by invoices - It was noted that no parallel sales records, stock discrepancy, unaccounted production, dispatch, cash receipt or other incriminating material was found from assessee - Whether since revenue failed to establish by independent corroborative evidence that assessee made unaccounted sales or received any unaccounted cash consideration, addition was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 185 to 190] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash payments) - Assessment year  2021-22  - During search, forensic analysis of assessee’s Unit-III desktop and statements of officials revealed cash payments towards Good Work Reward/Overtime/Bonus without ERP/book entries across three units - An excel sheet and statements under section 132(4) detailed cash/cheque inflow from head office and cash disbursement - Overtime Muster Roll Register and emails corroborated cash-based payouts - Assessing Officer quantified cash expenditure at Rs.1.58 crores and added as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - Whether since ample clinching documentary evidences were found from all three units of assessee indicating incurrence of such cash expenditure and there was clear admission by concerned employees, addition of Rs.1.58 crores so made by Assessing Officer was to be confirmed - Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of revenue]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]
