Section  69A,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104,  read with section  195,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Cash sales)  - Assessment year  2022-23  - Pursuant to a search of lockers of two employees of assessee-company, cash of about Rs. 2.99 crores was found - Both employees admitted that cash belonged to assessee - Assessee explained that cash represented sale proceeds of leftover construction material from its project, duly recorded in books of account and GST returns, and was kept in employees' lockers for safekeeping - Assessing Officer treated entire cash as unexplained money under section 69A and invoked section 115BBE - It was noted that sales were duly recorded in books and GST returns, buyers had confirmed transactions and copies of their ITRs were furnished - Whether since entire transaction of sale of goods was duly backed by stock and recorded in books of account which had been accepted without raising any doubts, provisions of section 69A could not be invoked - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition made under section 69A was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  68,  read with sections  69A  and  153A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  102,  read with section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash credit (Unaccounted sales)  - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Assessing Officer, relying on parallel Tally data, WhatsApp chats and statements of Sunrise/SP Group personnel, alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash sales to SP Group aggregating Rs. 980.15 crores and brought profit at 14.75 per cent to tax - Assessee contended that entire case rested on third-party material; no incriminating evidence was found during search on assessee; and SP Group, by clarification and retraction affidavits, stated that cash transactions related to third parties and open-market purchases, not assessee - Whether since revenue failed to establish through cogent independent evidence that assessee was source of goods reflected in third-party records or recipient of alleged cash consideration, addition was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 68] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section  68,  read with section  69A,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102,  read with section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash Credit (Business receipts)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2014-15  - Assessee's case was reopened on basis of specific information received from Investigation Wing regarding large cash deposits in assessee's account with co-operative credit society - Assessing Officer treated entire deposits as unexplained under sections 68/69A - Assessee claimed that cash deposits in Society account were sourced from cash sales and redeposit of earlier withdrawals -  Commissioner  (Appeals) accepted cash sales as explained - It was noted that explanation regarding cash deposits was based entirely on internal documents such as cash book and bank statements - No primary evidence had been placed on record to prove that actual sales took place against which cash was received - Supporting invoices were VAT-free and no VAT returns or sales tax records were submitted either before Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) - Further, no stock register or inventory movement summary was filed to establish that there was actual movement of goods justifying such cash sales - Whether thus, claim of assessee that deposits were sourced from genuine cash sales and re-deposits of withdrawals was not conclusively established on basis of material available on record - Held, yes - Whether therefore, treatment of this amount as explained by Commissioner (Appeals), without requisite verification, was unsustainable - Held, yes - Whether thus, matter was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for de novo verification - Held, yes [Paras 37 and 38][Matter remanded]

III. Section  69C,  read with section  56,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105,  read with section  92  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash payment) - Assessment year  2021-22  - A search was conducted on assessee company and its group - During search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced - Statements of assessee’s executives recorded under section 132(4) acknowledged planning a cash component of Rs.25 crores and indicated that Rs.7 crores had been paid, alongside Rs.75 crores towards share capital and unsecured loans - A cash receipt for Rs.5 crores dated 11-10-2020 signed by counterparty was also found - Relying on seized note, cash receipt and statements, AO held that Rs.7 crores had been paid in cash in connection with transaction and treated it as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - It was noted that respective statements made under section 132(4) were not shown to have any valid retraction and therefore, these statements were important and valid piece of evidence which could certainly be used while framing assessment particularly when same stood corroborated with seized material (cash receipt) during search on assessee - Whether therefore, impugned addition was to be confirmed - Held, yes [Paras 22 and 24] [In favour of revenue]

Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained moneys (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-firm, engaged in wholesale trading of sugar, regularly received cash from buyers and deposited it into its bank account - Assessee filed its return along with audit report under section 44AB and audited financial statements, disclosing turnover of Rs. 2.14 crores - Assessing Officer received information of cash deposits of about Rs. 19.02 lakhs linked to an individual who stated that bank account belonged to assessee-firm - Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 and obtained bank statement which showed aggregate cash deposits of about Rs. 1.11 crores during year and noted that such deposits were not shown in return and added said amount under section 69A as unexplained money - Assessee submitted that deposits were out of recorded cash sales and business receipts and furnished cash book, sales register, and bank statement highlighting cash deposits - CIT(A) found cash deposits to be out of regular cash sales recorded in books and deleted addition - It was noted that assessee had filed its audit report along with all financial statements along with returns and these demonstrated that assessee-firm had sales/turnover amounting to Rs. 2.14 crores on account of sale of sugar i.e., much more than cash deposits - Whether since breakup and explanation for deposits, bank statement and financial statements would have demonstrated that credits were on account of cash sales and could only be regarded as unexplained money if that explanation and financial statements were found to be defective or if cash deposits were over and above quantum of sales already disclosed in return and since there was no finding in assessment order on either issue, addition could not have been made under section 69A - Held, yes - Whether, thus, decision of CIT(A) to delete addition was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Jewellery) - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee availed of benefit under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme (VDIS) and declared items, which were mostly of jewellery, namely, gold and diamonds - Subsequently, assessee sold away jewellery declared by them under VDIS - Assessing Officer doubted genuinity of sale of diamonds - He thus treated amount shown as sale proceeds of diamonds as unexplained cash credit - Tribunal, however, deleted said addition - It was noted that not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds was furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed - Moreover, bank accounts of purchasers were verified and demand drafts issued to assessee towards consideration corresponded to entries in bank accounts - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, mere fact that on certain occasions, assessee did not proceed to Surat, could not be a factor to disbelieve transactions in question - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Cash purchases)  - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee, engaged in diamond trading, filed return of income - Reassessment was initiated under section 148 - During a search at premises of M/s. REPL, software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found - Based on this, it was alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL - Assessee submitted that it purchased diamonds from REPL through banking channels, exported goods, and offered income to tax, supported by invoices and stock records - AO, relying solely on third-party software, treated cash purchases as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - Assessee sought copies of corroborative material and statement of authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided - Whether since addition rested solely on alleged recovery of software during search action on M/s. REPL, which according to AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales, and said material was not supplied to assessee and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted, impugned addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading in gold and jewellery - During demonetization, assessee had deposited substantial amount of cash in his bank accounts - Assessee claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers for gold scheme - Assessing Officer treated cash receipts as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to prove genuineness of credits found in his bank account - It was noted that assessee had filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there was no discrepancy in books of account - Further, assessee had reported sales made before date of demonetization to GST authorities - Whether since assessee received trade advances in cash and same had been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68 - Held, yes - Whether furthermore assessee had furnished name and address of customers from whom it had received cash for sale of jewellery and law did not mandate assessee to collect PAN details of persons, if sale value of jewellery did not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs, assessee had satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of persons and thus, additions under section 68 was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 13, 14 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee during demonetization deposited substantial amount of cash in banks and claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers which were subsequently converted into sales of jewellery, since said trade advances were subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68

VI. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Gifts) - Assessment year  2023-24  - During search at residence of assessee's employee, a loose sheet was found and, relying on said document and his initial statement that cash was spent at Daman on liaisoning and Diwali gifts on instructions of senior management, Assessing Officer treated Rs. 7.38 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - It was noted that Assessing Officer neither identified recipients or suppliers nor produced any vouchers, acknowledgements or other corroborative evidence, and loose sheet was neither recovered from assessee's premises nor linked to its records - Further, employee subsequently retracted his statement - Whether since addition was based solely on a loose sheet and a retracted statement, unsupported by any independent evidence of actual expenditure, essential conditions for invoking section 69C were not satisfied and addition was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 134, 138, 140 and 145] [In favour of assessee]

X. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Bullion)  - Assessment year  2023-24  - During search, a rough slip was found and confronted to assessee - In statement under section 132(4), assessee stated purchase of two gold coins of 100 grams each, admitted to have paid Rs.5 lakhs in cash to jewellers with balance of about Rs.11.50 lakhs pending - He explained source of Rs.5 lakhs as withdrawal from capital account in M/s Kalta Liquors and later furnished purchase bill and evidence that balance was paid through banking channels - Whether since assessee furnished ample evidences during course of assessment proceedings to substantiate its stand, this addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section  69A,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  104,  read with section  195,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Cash sales)  - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and sale of pan masala and tobacco products - A search under section 132 was conducted upon one, MEPL, a supplier of packaging material to assessee - Based on notepads seized during search from MEPL, Assessing Officer made addition of certain amount under section 69A as unexplained cash sales of assessee -  Commissioner  (Appeals) deleted gross-sale addition under section 69A but made addition under section 69C of gross profit element under head business income and further invoked section 115BBE - Whether section 69C requires a finding that expenditure was actually incurred and source is unexplained - Held, yes - Whether once income from alleged suppressed sales was subjected to a best-judgment profit estimation, a second independent addition under section 69C, again estimated on same stream amounts to duplication and an impermissible attempt to re-characterise a trading estimation into deemed income, thereby artificially invoking punitive regime of section 115BBE - Held, yes - Whether in instant case, Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in making addition under section 69C for unexplained expenditure for first unaccounted sales by applying stock-in-trade to turnover ratio of 0.68 per cent as on 31.03.2022 as per audit report in place of addition under section 69A - Held, yes - Whether where hypothesis of department that assessee, by alleged over-invoicing/excess receipt of packing material, manufactured alleged unaccounted finished goods effected alleged unaccounted/suppressed sales was deleted and addition made by AO under section 69A and amount estimated and confirmed by CIT(A) by applying GP rate @ 10.68 per cent on estimate basis was also deleted, consequently, corresponding entire enhancement made/confirmed under section 69C would be liable to be deleted and consequential direction to tax under section 115BBE would not survive - Held, yes [Paras 10.1, 10.1.1 and 10.1.2] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading in gold and jewellery - During demonetization, assessee had deposited substantial amount of cash in his bank accounts - Assessee claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers for gold scheme - Assessing Officer treated cash receipts as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to prove genuineness of credits found in his bank account - It was noted that assessee had filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there was no discrepancy in books of account - Further, assessee had reported sales made before date of demonetization to GST authorities - Whether since assessee received trade advances in cash and same had been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68 - Held, yes - Whether furthermore assessee had furnished name and address of customers from whom it had received cash for sale of jewellery and law did not mandate assessee to collect PAN details of persons, if sale value of jewellery did not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs, assessee had satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of persons and thus, additions under section 68 was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 13, 14 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section  69A,  read with sections  145  and  115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  104,  read with section  276  and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Cash sales)  - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessing Officer based on alleged over-invoicing/price-variance in packaging material deduced unaccounted/suppressed cash sales and taxed entire amount as unexplained money under section 69A - It was noted that department's allegation was of cash sales, yet assessment order did not anchor upon cash discovery, cash deposit, cash utilization patterns, unexplained assets, or a consistent cash-flow that could support alleged unaccounted cash sales - Further, defence of department of packaging material differed in technical specifications, as revenue failed to rebut it by testing it on parity of facts or like-to-like purchase comparison - Whether addition against assessee on charges of clandestine procurement of packaging material and clandestine supply of finished goods, consequential bogus unaccounted sales without any independent, positive and cogent evidence brought on record by department was not sustainable - Held, yes - Whether revenue's mere contention that alleged unaccounted sales was made out of exiting manufactured goods generating unaccounted income was not established with cogent evidence, applicability of section 69A was ruled out - Held, yes - Whether since department failed to prove or establish existence of alleged suppressed sales, by way of satisfying conditions for applicability of section 145(3) and estimation of GP rate, addition made by Assessing Officer under section 69A was to be deleted - Held, yes - Whether once addition was deleted, consequently applicability of section 115BBE did not survive - Held, yes [Paras 9.3, 9.3.5 and 9.3.6] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether provisions of section 68 are in pari materia with section 69 and, therefore, before making an addition under section 68, Assessing Officer has to exercise his discretion judiciously - Held, yes - Assessee sold gold and diamond separately and same was shown in its return - However, Assessing Officer did not accept sale of diamond as genuine and added it towards assessee’s income as unexplained credit - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving that sale transaction in diamonds was genuine and creditworthiness of purchasers had been proved beyond doubt, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating transaction as not being genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition under section 68 was to be deleted - Held, yes

I Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Sales) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was into business of trading and manufacturing of jewellery like gold and diamond, etc. - It had filed its return of income - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer formed a belief that there was an abnormal increase in percentage of cash sales during period 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - Further, sales did not have name of purchaser and PAN and that cash sales from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 amounting to Rs. 4.73 crores was added as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and accordingly, added to income of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to restrict addition to Rs. 3.25 crores - It was observed that assessee had furnished month-wise purchases, month-wise details, stock register, valuation of closing stock, month-wise details of cash sales, copies of VAT returns and not a single defect had been pointed out by Assessing Officer in these clinching evidences - Whether merely because there was a minor variation in cash sales during alleged period compared to previous year would not mean that assessee had inflated its sales to cover up demonetized currency - Held, yes - Whether since cash sales have already been offered as income, same could not be taxed in garb of inflation sales to cover up demonetization currency - Held, yes [Paras 22 to 27] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where cash sales were already offered as income, same could not be taxed in garb of inflation sales to cover up demonetization currency  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had claimed business promotion expenses, since all expenses were supported by bills and vouchers, duly recorded in books of account, addition by Assessing Officer in respect of said expenses was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals)  INCOME TAX : Where car running expenses were fully supported by bills and vouchers and were incurred towards petrol and regular repair and maintenance of cars, said expenses were rightly allowed by Commissioner (Appeals)

Section 68 of Income-tax Act - Cash credits
Where assessee had certain credit entry as sale of jewellery and had supported sale on basis of purchase voucher of purchaser, copy of account of assessee as appearing in books of account of purchaser, and evidence of having received payment from purchaser through banking channel, such credit entry could not be treated as unexplained cash credit in assessee’s hands.

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 40A (3)  of Income-tax Act, 1961
Bachubhai Alias Vithalbhai Thakershibhai Patel v. ITO [1992] 42 TTJ (Ahd.) 153
It cannot be argued that the section 40A (3) should not be applied merely because the practice in a section of the business community like diamond trade has been to make purchase and sale in cash.
The assessee had made cash purchases of diamonds exceeding Rs. 2,500. Its explanation was that the said purchase had not been made by the assessee from one person but from different persons during the whole day. The assess also contended that the goods being stolen goods, the assessee had no evidence about parties from which it had purchased. As the assessee had not produced any purchase bill or proof of identity of persons, all the cash purchases above the prescribed limit were disallowed under section 40A (3). The Commissioner (Appeals), upheld the addition.
Held that details regarding different items of purchases on each day, if at all there were different items of purchase each day, must be available with the assessee. In so far as no such details had been produced, it was to be presumed that in fact the purchases shown on the different dates did not break up into smaller amounts as alleged and that each purchases was of the amount stated in the cash book. Therefore, the disallowance under section 40A (3) was justified.

Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 104 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained moneys (Cash found during search) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and trading of wheat flour - A search under section 132 was conducted at its premises, where cash of about Rs. 79.81 lakhs was found against book cash of about Rs. 12.37 lakhs, resulting in excess cash of about Rs. 67.43 lakhs - Part of cash of Rs. 50 lakhs was found in a locker in Managing Director’s chamber and about Rs. 17.43 lakhs with company’s cashier - Assessee stated that cash belonged to Managing Director, allegedly refunded by one individual against advances for purchase of villas - However, cash withdrawal was recorded after dates of alleged advances and no evidence of refund was produced - Whether since explanation furnished by assessee was not genuine and credible, impugned addition was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 16.5] [In favour of revenue]

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102,  read with section  195  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Demonetization period) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company, engaged in trading of solar panels, deposited cash of about Rs. 33.55 lakhs in its bank account during demonetization period - AO treated same as unexplained cash credits and made addition under Section 68 read with Section 115BBE - Assessee contended that deposits were out of cash sales duly recorded in books - It was noted that assessee attempted to prove entire cash deposit as being out of sales and recorded in books of account - However, contentions to prove cash deposits during demonetization period hardly deserved to be accepted in entirety, especially when a satisfactory explanation for disproportionate increase in cash sales just before demonetization period was not given - On other hand, revenue’s endeavour to disbelieve contention that cash deposits were supported by stock register and purchase records could not be fully justified - Whether, in such circumstances, it was deemed appropriate, in larger interest of justice, that a lump-sum addition of Rs. 3.50 lakh only would be just and proper - Held, yes [Para 6] [Partly in favour of assessee]

II. Section  69A,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961/ Section  104,  read with section  195,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Unexplained asset (Cash sales) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and sale of pan masala and tobacco products - A search under section 132 was conducted upon one, MEPL, a supplier of packaging material to assessee - Based on notepads seized during search from MEPL, Assessing Officer made addition of certain amount under section 69A as unexplained cash sales of assessee - Whether recording of satisfaction is a sine qua non for assuming jurisdiction on basis of material found in course of search of another person - Held, yes - Whether under new regime such satisfaction must be recorded with prior approval of Principal Commissioner/Commissioner - Held, yes - Whether use of third-party material is subject to strict jurisdictional safeguards and cannot be resorted to in a casual or mechanical manner - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer made huge additions solely based on third-party information/material found and seized during a search action, without establishing any direct or indirect nexus with assessee and in absence of mandatory satisfaction and prior approval of competent authority, very assumption of jurisdiction by Assessing Officer was invalid and accordingly, additions made on such basis were liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 7.1.4, 7.2 and 7.4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposits post demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization - Assessee claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration - Assessing Officer made addition under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format, and thus, claim made by assessee remained unexplained - Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed order of Assessing Officer on ground that assessee made sale transaction below Rs. 2 lakhs and cash sales during demonetization was 90.59 per cent of cash sales for entire period of next financial year - It was noted that other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT - Also Assessing Officer without examining any parties to whom goods were sold by assessee concluded that sales were not genuine - Whether since Assessing Officer accepted books of account of assessee and entries in books of account were matched, there would be no case to make additions - Held, yes - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) committed error in upholding addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Sales transactions) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of sale of gold jewellery and ornaments - Assessing Officer completed assessment of assessee by making certain addition by holding that certain amount of cash deposited by assessee in his bank account during demonetization period was nothing but undisclosed income of assessee which was under garb of cash sales - He therefore, held that cash deposited was liable to be added under section 68 and taxable @60% under provision of section 115BBE - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition - It was found from records that assessee had maintained regular books of account, bills, vouchers and day-to-day stock register having complete quantitative details of cash sale transactions of jewellery and cash sales and receipts were duly supported by relevant bills which were produced in course of assessment proceedings and sales were made out of stock-in-trade - Whether thus, all such scenario indicated that assessee had duly substantiated its claim from documentary evidences and also with facts - Held, yes - Whether further, provisions of section 68 would not be applicable on sale transactions recorded in books of account as sales were already part of income which was already credited in PL account - Held, yes - Whether therefore, there was no occasion to consider same as income of assessee by invoking provisions of section 68 and addition was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes [Para 2.6] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-jeweller claimed that cash deposited in bank account during demonetization period pertained to cash sale transaction of gold jewellery, since assessee had maintained regular books of account, bills, vouchers and day-to-day stock register having complete quantitative details of cash sale transaction of jewellery, addition under section 68 could not be made

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Sales transactions) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of sale of gold jewellery and ornaments - Assessing Officer completed assessment of assessee by making certain addition by holding that certain amount of cash deposited by assessee in his bank account during demonetization period was nothing but undisclosed income of assessee which was under garb of cash sales - He therefore, held that cash deposited was liable to be added under section 68 and taxable @60% under provision of section 115BBE - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition - It was found from records that assessee had maintained regular books of account, bills, vouchers and day-to-day stock register having complete quantitative details of cash sale transactions of jewellery and cash sales and receipts were duly supported by relevant bills which were produced in course of assessment proceedings and sales were made out of stock-in-trade - Whether thus, all such scenario indicated that assessee had duly substantiated its claim from documentary evidences and also with facts - Held, yes - Whether further, provisions of section 68 would not be applicable on sale transactions recorded in books of account as sales were already part of income which was already credited in PL account - Held, yes - Whether therefore, there was no occasion to consider same as income of assessee by invoking provisions of section 68 and addition was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes [Para 2.6] [In favour of assessee]

Section  69C,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing, buying and selling of jewellery - During relevant assessment year, assessee had entered into transactions with five parties - Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in books of assessee - Assessing Officer further presumed that assessee had earned additional gross profit by procuring diamonds from grey market and accordingly made addition being 8 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases -  Commissioner  (Appeals) restricted profit estimation to 3 per cent - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating detailed evidences filed by assessee including quantitative details, purchase and sales registers, bank statements, confirmations, sales-tax registration, and income-tax returns of supplier parties, came to conclusion that sales and closing stock figures were duly accepted by Assessing Officer - Commissioner (Appeals) further observed that without corresponding purchases, assessee could not have affected sales - Thus, only profit element embedded in such alleged purchases could be brought to tax, not entire purchase value - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly restricted addition to 3 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases was fair, reasonable and in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69A of Income-tax Act, 1961
Others
Navinchandra M. Patel v. ITO [1992] 42 TTJ (Ahd.) 98 
In the course of raid conducted by custom authorities, the assessee was found in possession of certain diamonds to which the assessee explained that he took loans from two persons and out of the amount of loan he purchased those diamonds from several persons in the market whom he did not know and from whom he did not obtain any receipt. On enquiry by the custom officers those persons denied having lent any amount to the assessee. Then the assessee changed his version about the diamonds and stated that diamonds were received on approval basis under Jhangad receipts and he was not owner at the time of seizure. The ITO holding that there was no satisfactory explanation, assessed value of diamonds as income of the assessee.
Held that the source of the amount which was invested in acquiring diamonds was not proved by the assessee and as such addition was rightly made by the ITO.

III. Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 105 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Telescoping) – Assessment year 2023-24 – AO alleged that assessee had procured accommodation RTGS entries through traders and paid commission at rate of 4 per cent on RTGS amounts aggregating to about Rs. 1188 crores, and accordingly made addition of about Rs. 47.52 crores under section 69C – Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition by granting telescoping against estimated profits and treated RTGS-linked amounts as sales made through traders and recorded in books rather than accommodation entries – Tribunal observed that addition was based only on statement of an employee which was never reaffirmed by directors or principal officer of assessee-company – Tribunal further observed that once sales made to traders were treated as recorded sales, allegation regarding accommodation RTGS entries had no basis – Whether therefore, no addition could be sustained on account of alleged commission for obtaining such accommodation entries – Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Unexplained money) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account during period of demonetization - He contended that same were proceeds of cash sales - Assessing Officer observed that assessee failed to explain source of such huge cash deposit - He thereby invoked provision of section 145(3) and rejected book results - Further, he did not consider sales to tune of Rs. 37.96 lakhs out of cash deposited by assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016 and made addition under section 68 on account of same - It was noted that in support of sales so made, assessee submitted all invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of persons to whom cash sales were made - On this information Assessing Officer had not made any independent inquiry - He considered part of sales as genuine and on same set of records, part of sales were not considered as genuine - This pick  chose approach was not correct on same set of evidence - Assessee had maintained all records that sales were duly reflected in VAT return and also in books of accounts of assessee - Further, Assessing Officer had not given required notice before rejection of book results, as required under law - Also profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting books of account by invoking provisions of section 145(3) and further impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was also liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of gold and diamond jewellery deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs during demonetization period in his bank accounts and claimed that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales

II. Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 102 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Cash Credit (Unexplained cash deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading/export of dry fruits, spices and other exotic kirana goods - During year, cash deposits during year were examined and Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs. 37 lakhs under section 68 on account of unexplained cash deposits - It was noted that cash sales during festive season of Diwali in regard to product dealt by assessee certainly increases being a phenomenon but without pointing out any discrepancy in stocks, sales, and purchases cash sales were doubted and additions were made - Whether, on facts, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits -  Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2001-02 - Assessee showed long-term losses on account of sale of jewellery in its original returns of income filed for assessment years under consideration - Jewellery was shown to be sold to 'S' and 'JJ' - Said jewellery was earlier declared by assessee under VDIS - Subsequently, Assessing Officer by relying upon findings of Commissioner of Customs and Central Excise, doubted genuineness and existence of those two parties as they were not found at their given addresses and, accordingly, made additions on account of bogus cash credits - On further appeal, Tribunal found that assessee had produced all necessary information about these transactions and abovenamed parties supported with documents like their permanent account numbers, bank accounts, their trade-tax assessment orders, sale vouchers issued by them against claimed sales as well as their full addresses - Assessee had also produced buyers income-tax returns for relevant years in which profits on sale of jewellery shown in respective returns were accepted by department - Sale considerations were also paid by them to assessee through account payee cheques - It, therefore, held that assessee had furnished all necessary information supported with documents about transactions and parties which could have been expected from a prudent seller to establish genuineness of claimed sales and, accordingly, deleted said additions - Whether Tribunal had given cogent reasons for arriving at its factual conclusion and same needed no interference - Held, yes

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposits post demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Asseesse firm was engaged in business of jewellery trading - A survey under section 133A was conducted at business premises of assessee by Deputy Director (Investigation) in which he found that assessee deposited huge sum in high denominations of specified bank notes post demonetization - Assessee had explained source of cash deposits as cash sales and advances received against sales - However, Assessing Officer held that said amount was unexplained cash credits representing unaccounted money brought in to business in guise of jewellery sales, and, accordingly, made addition under section 68 on account of said cash deposit - It was noted that assessee had explained source of said amount in question as sales, produced sale bills and admitted same as revenue receipt as well as offered it to - There was no defect in purchases and sales and same were matching with inflow and outflow of stock - Audit report under section 44AB and financial statements clearly showed reduction of stock position matching with sales which clearly showed that cash generated represented sales - Assessing officer accepted sales and stocks - He had not disturbed closing stock which had direct nexus with sales - Both Assessing Officer and DDIT (Inv.) did not find any defects in books of account, trading account, PL account and financial statements of assessee - Whether, on facts, impugned addition made under section 68 was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 7, 7.2 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where AO made addition under section 68 on account of huge cash amount deposited by assessee-jeweller in its bank account post demonetization, since assessee had explained source of said cash deposits as sales of jewellery, produced sale bills and admitted same as revenue receipt as well as offered it to tax and assessee also represented outgo of stocks which was matching with sales, impugned addition was to be deleted

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified

II. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained moneys (Purchase of Jewellery)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - In course of search and seizure operation, a pair of diamond bangles purchased from FI was found during search in case of assessee - Departmental valuer valued one bangle at Rs. 7.76 lakhs and left out other - Assessee in a statement under section 132(4) stated that pair of bangles was purchased for a consideration of Rs. 8.72 lakhs and also furnished supporting evidence by way of purchase bill - He further stated that other bangle left out by Departmental valuer was valued by another registered valuer at Rs. 4.39 lakhs and, hence, value of two bangles would work out to Rs. 8.78 lakhs, which was more or less equal to invoice value - However, Assessing Officer relying upon statement of an employee of FI added back an amount of Rs. 8.62 lakhs, being amount allegedly paid in cash over and above invoice value - Whether addition made to income of assessee under section 69A solely relying upon statement of a third party was not sustainable, more so, when assessee denied of having paid any cash - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition so made was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]

Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained moneys (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company, engaged in trading of IT products, filed its return for A.Y. 2017-18 declaring NIL income - AO noted cash deposits of about Rs. 34.66 lakhs during demonetization period and treated same as unexplained money under section 69A -  Commissioner (Appeals) sustained addition on ground that assessee failed to establish nexus between prior cash withdrawals and cash deposits  - It was noted that assessee had made cash deposits during demonetization period and that there existed sufficient cash withdrawals preceding impugned deposits - However, neither AO nor Commissioner (Appeals) examined or correlated such earlier withdrawals while treating deposits made during demonetization period as unexplained money under section 69A - Whether once availability of cash from prior withdrawals stood demonstrated from bank records, cash deposits made during demonetization period could not be brought to tax merely on surmises without disproving nexus between withdrawals and redeposits - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition made under section 69A was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section  69C,  read with section  153C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (On-money)  - Assessment years  2017-18 to 2019-20  - During search conducted in case of real estate developer company, statements of its employees were recorded that cash component was received over and above registered consideration in respect of sale of shops - Further, data in form of excel sheets was also seized which contained details of shop sales, including names of buyers and alleged cash components - On basis of such material, Assessing Officer issued notice under section 153C to assessee who had purchased a shop - Subsequently, assessment was completed under section 153C wherein Assessing Officer treated alleged cash component as unexplained expenditure/investment - - It was noted that assessee specifically sought cross-examination of third party whose statement constituted fulcrum of addition but same was declined on premise that statement was not sole basis of addition - Further, no independent evidence had been brought on record to demonstrate actual payment of cash by assessee and there was no receipt, no diary, no acknowledgment, no corroborative evidence linking assessee to alleged cash payment, apart from third-party record - - Further, alleged electronic data was found from possession of a third party and, assessee was not provided copies of complete statements or electronic data, nor was cross-examination permitted - Whether therefore, impugned addition having been made solely on basis of uncorroborated third-party material and statements, without affording assessee an effective opportunity to confront or rebut same, and in violation of principles of natural justice, could not be sustained - Held, yes [Paras 8.23 to 8.26] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

The assessee was into the business of trading and manufacturing of jewellery like gold and diamond, etc. The return for the year was electronically filed declaring income.

During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer formed a belief that there was an abnormal increase in the percentage of cash sales during the period 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016. Further, sales did not have the name of the purchaser and PAN. Cash sales from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 amounting to Rs. 4.73 crores was added as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and accordingly, added to the income of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to restrict the addition to Rs. 3.25 crores.

On cross appeal:

■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of retail sales of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited certain amount in specified bank notes to the bank account. The case was selected for scrutiny to verify the source for cash deposited and certain details were called for.

■

The assessee submitted that it had deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers and had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period and demonstrated that the cash deposited in bank was out of sales proceeds of stock on hand.

■

The Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee and observed that cash sales entered in the cash book and sales register were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by the assessee company merely to build an explanation for the cash deposits in to the bank accounts and made addition of total of cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the assessee had explained the sources of cash deposits as cash sales received on 08-11-2016 against the sales and the assessee also produced the sale bills and books of accounts and that when there was sufficient stock to effect the sales and no defect had been found in the stock as well as the sales and purchases and since, the assessee has already admitted the sales as revenue receipt, there was no case for considering cash deposit as not explained and adding the same and deleted the addition.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

■

The assessee was a resident individual. A search action was undertaken in the case of Firestar International Pvt. Ltd.(FI), in the course of which a statement was recorded from one of its employees. In the statement recorded, the concerned employee stated that, in addition to the bill amount paid by cheque towards sale of jewellery, cash was also paid. In this context, the employee provided a list containing details of date of purchase, customer name and amounts allegedly paid in cash and by cheque.

■

As per the said list, it was alleged that assessee’s wife had paid ₹28.80 lakh in cash and ₹19.20 lakh by cheque, aggregating to ₹48 lakh, towards purchase of earrings and rings. On the basis thereof, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee had paid ₹28.80 lakh in cash over and above the amount paid by cheque towards purchase of jewellery and made an addition under section 69A.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2005-06 declaring certain income. In the meantime, the competent authority conducted a survey under section 133A at the Mumbai office of the assessee. He conducted the survey in consequence to the information received from the Economic Offence Wing, Crime Branch, Mumbai, where the assessee admitted that he was doing the business of bogus diamond billing on commission basis and he issued the bill and got commission at 0.25 per cent on the amount of bills.

The Assessing Officer having found that during the year the assessee had paid an amount of Rs. 18.22 crores in cash to six different parties asked the assessee to explain the said amount. The assessee in reply submitted that he had not made any single payment exceeding Rs. 20,000 to the aforesaid parties at a time. The Assessing Officer being not satisfied with the explanation of the assessee held that the assessee had violated the provisions of section 40A(3) in respect of the aggregate payment of Rs. 18.22 crores. He accordingly disallowed 20 per cent of such payment under section 40A(3).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the impugned disallowance made by the Assessing Officer. He further directed the Assessing Officer to compute the income of the assessee at 0.25 per cent on the total amount of bills.

On second appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal to High Court:

■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh in its bank account during the demonetisation period.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that there was an unusual increase in cash sales during October 2016 and held that the cash sales recorded immediately before demonetisation were non-genuine and represented unaccounted money introduced into the books.

■

After allowing credit for estimated cash-in-hand and estimated genuine cash sales, the Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and taxed the same under section 115BBE.

■

On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

■

In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the cash sales were duly recorded in regular books of account and supported by VAT returns, cash book, ledger accounts, stock register, purchase register, sales register and audited financial statements. It was further submitted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor disputed purchases or stock movement.

■

The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in the business of gold jewellery and ornaments, had deposited cash amounting to Rs. 1.03 crores in its bank account during the demonetisation period and filed its regular return declaring total income at Rs. 1.53 lakhs. Reassessment proceedings were initiated and in course of scrutiny, books of accounts (cash book, ledger, stock register) produced and examined, and the cash deposit in bank was explained by the assessee to have been deposited out of regular sale proceeds of gold jewelleries out of stock in trade available with the assessee (as per day to day stock register duly maintained).

■

The Assessing Officer observed that the closing cash balance as per cash book as on 31-10-2016 was Rs. 1.05 crores and the cash sales disclosed by the assessee for the month of October, 2016 was Rs. 95.15 lakhs, against average monthly sales of Rs. two lakhs per month during the period 1-4-2016 to 30-9-2016, which did not compare logically considering the fact that sales for the month of October 2016 alone is 47 times more than the assessee's regular sales in earlier months and the assessee was not able to substantiate the said sales with supporting sales and purchase bills, in spite of requisition for the same.There was failure on the part of the assessee to substantiate the sales with supporting evidence like sale invoices and the purchases with supporting purchase invoices, and to explain the cash deposited by the assessee in bank a/c which had arisen out of cash available with the assessee as on 31-10-2016 and subsequently deposited in bank during the period 10-11-2016 to 16-11-2016 totalling Rs. 1.03 crores. The assessment was completed on a total income of Rs. 1.05 crores (including an addition of Rs. 1.03 crores under section 69A) being the amount of cash deposited in bank during the demonetisation period and the same was charged to tax at rates prescribed under section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee for want of customer wise sales invoices, delivery challan payment acknowledgment, and in absence of details of parties to whom the alleged jewellery had been sold.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, filed its return of income.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that during the demonetization period, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 3.80 crores in three bank accounts. He further noted that the assessee had made total sales of Rs. 49.99 crores during the financial year 2016-17 and the total cash sales during the year amounted to Rs. 4.94 crores. However, of the total cash sales, the assessee had made cash sales of Rs. 3.68 crores in October, 2016 and of Rs. 37.25 lakhs uptil 8.11.2016 i.e. in the period between 1.10.2016 to 8.11.2016, the assessee had suddenly made cash sales to the tune of Rs. 4.05 crores to unidentifiable small customers.He held that the assessee had not satisfactorily explained the credit of Rs. 3.68 crores recorded as cash sales in his books during the period 1.10.2016 to 30.10.2016, he held the same to be unexplained under section 68

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had not established that the assessee had accumulated cash in its books which was deposited on 10-11-2016. The assumptions made on the basis of comparison of sales figures of earlier years were not foolproof, as similar or higher sales had been made by the assessee in following financial year and the refusal to accept the sales shown by the assessee was not on account of any independent enquiry but only on the basis of assumptions/interpretations made by the Assessing Officer while comparing results of earlier years.

■

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition of Rs. 2.98 crores on account of unexplained cash deposit.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, a retail jeweller, deposited cash of about Rs. 38.42 lakhs into her bank account on various dates during the demonetization period and explained the source as opening cash balance as on 8-11-2016 arising from recorded cash sales and receipts from debtors, furnishing cash book extracts.

■

The Assessing Officer added about Rs. 38.42 lakhs under section 69A, on the ground that the claimed cash balance as on 8-11-2016 was not substantiated; citing abnormal variation in sales from 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016 compared to earlier/subsequent periods; and alleging belated VAT returns were filed to cover backdated sales.

■

The Commissioner(Appeals) gave opportunities but, in absence of response, upheld the addition towards cash deposits during the demonetization period.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer did not accept the reply of the assessee and by taking view that the assessee had not provided the details of purchases and the names of the parties and had also not produced the persons to whom sales made with documents showing the colour and size of diamonds made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to the income of the assessee on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought the same for taxation at the rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer by holding that the assessee had to prove the nature and source of deposit with three conditions as per provisions of section 68 and the assessee could not explain the nature and source of aforesaid amount of Rs. 29.66 lakhs.

On appeal to Tribunal:

■

The assessee, engaged in the jewellery business, filed its return for A.Y. 2017-18 declaring income of about Rs. 29.98 lakhs. A survey under section 133A was conducted. During scrutiny, it was noted that cash of about Rs. 6.34 crores was deposited in bank during the demonetisation period, and in online enquiries the assessee stated that the deposits represented cash sales of jewellery recorded in the books.

■

The AO doubted the factum of cash sales and treated the bank cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68.

■

The CIT(A) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the cash deposits were out of recorded cash sales supported by bills, vouchers, bank extracts and VAT returns, and that the books and trading results, including the impugned cash sales, had not been rejected; the Department relied on the orders of the lower authorities.

The assessee was an Individual and deriving income from business of jewellery in his proprietorship concern and interest income from saving bank account, FDR and parties. The assessee's books of account were audited by chartered accountant. He filed his income tax return for relevant assessment year.

The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 1,03,00,000/- in its bank account during demonetization period viz. between 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 out of which cash of Rs. 91,00,000/- was in the demonetized currency notes (SBN i.e. Old Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes). The assessee explained it to be out of cash sales made by him. The Assessing Officer tried to analyze the cash sale vis-à-vis cash sales in the earlier years and had also observed that the cash sale so shown during the demonetization was exceptionally high vis-à-vis cash sale in financial year 2015-16 however, he also observed that the total sales for the entire year had decreased substantially in the current financial year when compared with the previous year. He further held that assessee had not provided name, address and PAN of customers to whom cash sales was made. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer observed that these cash sales were not real sales and the assessee had tried to introduce his own unaccounted money in the garb of cash sales and therefore, made addition of aforesaid amount of Rs. 1,03,00,000.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no abnormal rise in the cash sale made by the assessee. The sales were genuine and supported by the proper invoices and properly shown in the VAT return, which was also accepted by the VAT authorities, therefore, the same could not be considered as fabricated or manipulated transactions. He held further, that assessee was having only source of income from business of Jewellery and except to that the assessee was not having any other business and the Assessing Officer also could not prove the source of generation of undisclosed income. Therefore, merely on the basis of presumption and assumption no such addition could be made in total income of the assessee. Thus, addition under section 68 was completely wrong, unjustified, perverse and not according to the settled principal of law, therefore the same deserves to be deleted.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee was engaged in the business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) and other items of gold, silver and diamond. The assessee made a total deposit of Rs. 10.28 crores in the bank out of cash sales made on 08-11-2016. The aforesaid cash deposits in bank were made out of Specified Bank Notes (SBN) in the denomination of 1000 and 500, which were demonetized with effect from 09-11-2016.

■

The Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to the income of the assessee under section 68.

■

The assessee's appeal was dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during the demonetization and claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration.

The Assessing Officer issued show cause notice to assessee with respect to cash deposited in bank during demonetization. The Assessing Officer after verifying the details opined that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format. He thus, held that claim made by assessee remained unexplained and accordingly, made addition treating same as undisclosed income under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition made by Assessing Officer on ground that the assessee failed to discharge its onus of providing item-wise sale for each invoice especially for the month of November, 2016 and the fact that average per day sale in 39 days from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 was Rs. 20.87 lakhs as compared to Rs. 53,514/- only in financial year 2017-18 points to the fact that claim of cash sales was an afterthought to justify huge cash deposits in bank account during the demonetization period.

On appeal to the Tribunal.

■

A search and seizure action under section 132 was carried out in the case of the ''Rubberwala Group'', including RHIL, its promoters and directors TS and key employee of the group, IA. During the course of the search, statements on oath were recorded from IA, a key employee handling sale and registration of shops in the ''Platinum Mall'' project, and TS, Director and Promoter of RHIL. IA stated that cash components were received over and above the registered consideration in respect of sale of shops, which statement was stated to have been affirmed by TS. A pen drive was also seized from IA containing Excel sheets allegedly recording details of shop sales, including names of buyers and alleged cash components.

■

It was noticed from the said Excel sheets that a shop had been booked in the name of the assessee and an aggregate cash payment of Rs. 12.88 lakhs was recorded as having been received over three financial years. On the basis of such material, notice under section 153C was issued to the assessee. In response, the assessee filed a return declaring Nil income. The assessment was completed under section 153C read with section 153A, wherein the Assessing Officer treated the alleged cash component as unexplained expenditure/investment. For the assessment year 2017-18, an addition of Rs. 1 lakh was made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the assessee primarily challenged the addition on the ground that the addition was based solely on third-party statements and documents, the incriminating material was never supplied to the assessee, and no opportunity of cross-examination of IA was granted. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected the contentions of the assessee, holding that the right of cross-examination was not absolute, that adequate opportunity had been granted, and that the material relied upon constituted corroborated digital evidence supported by sworn statements and disclosure by the developer group.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading in bullion and jewellery. During demonetization, the assessee had deposited a significant amount of cash in its bank accounts. The assessee explained that the cash deposits were out of cash advances received from customers against cash sales of jewellery/bullion.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and treated the amount of cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68, read with section 115BBE, and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

During the search conducted in the case of the assessee, a pair of diamond bangles purchased from FI was found.

■

The Departmental Valuer valued one bangle at about ₹7.77 lakh and left out the other. Relying upon the statement of an employee of FI, who alleged that the bangles were purchased for ₹17.25 lakh and that ₹8.62 lakh was paid in cash over and above invoice value, the Assessing Officer made an addition under section 69A.

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■
