Following the search on 23-12-2023, the AO alleged that the assessee paid cash on-money for Halol land purchases and made additions under section 69C of Rs. 78.82 lakhs (AY 2016-17), Rs. 87.97 lakhs (AY 2018-19) and Rs. 30.20 lakhs (AY 2023-24), aggregating about Rs. 1.97 crores, by estimating cash payment at 20 per cent of the agreement value. The AO principally relied on the statement of Rakesh Talati, alleging a customary 15-20 per cent cash component and cash delivery through an employee, and certain WhatsApp chats with Dharendra Pathak.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that Talati's statement was general, devoid of transaction-specific details and later retracted; no seller was examined; no cash trail or seized material evidenced cash payment; and all purchases were registered, made through banking channels and at or above stamp duty values. It was further shown that the WhatsApp chats related to a proposed Valsad transaction, whereas the additions concerned Halol lands. The CIT(A) found no corroborative evidence of cash payment, noted the absence of enquiry from sellers, accepted that the registered values were not below stamp duty values, held the chats unrelated to Halol and found the uniform 20 per cent estimation to be without factual basis. The additions were deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

■

The assessee-firm was engaged in business of trading in bullion, jewellery, etc.

■

Based on information/material found during the search and seizure/ survey operations in case of partners of assessee-firm the departmental authorities observed that large amount of cash was deposited in various bank accounts of different entities, which, after layering were transferred to the assessee. The Assessing Officer found that as per the investigation carried out by the Investigation Wing, the assessee had purportedly sold gold and bullions to 44 entities controlled and managed by an entry operator, namely, Sonu Punjabi, which were sham transactions carried out during the demonetization period. It was alleged by the Assessing Officer that though notices under section 133(6) as well as summons under section 131 were issued, no information came from such entities as most of the summons returned back unserved. The Assessing Officer finally concluded that sales of gold/bullion to 44 entities allegedly controlled by Sonu Punjabi, were bogus sales and made for the purpose of introducing own money routed through bogus firms to its accounts. Thus, he treated the amount credited to the books of account as receipts from sale of gold/bullion, as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

The Assessing Officer further observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of gold/bullion worth Rs. 20.87 crore to RBPL and that in course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of M of RBPL statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he allegedly stated that cash amounting to Rs. 32.81 crore given to him by a firm, namely, DL Jewellers was deposited in the bank account of RBPL, for the purpose of transferring the fund to specific accounts on commission basis. The Assessing Officer ultimately concluded that the purported sales of gold/bullion to RBPL was bogus. Accordingly, he treated the receipt from sale of gold/bullion to RBPL as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee.

■

Further, the Assessing Officer observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of Rs. 19.30 lakhs to Olivia, towards sale of gold/ bullion. He observed that in course of survey conducted in the case of Olivia, it was found that the said company was incorporated in January 2015 and in assessment year 2015-16 it had filed the return of income offering NIL income without any turnover whereas, huge amount of cash was found to have been deposited in the bank account of Olivia, which suggested that the entity was an entry provider. Accordingly, he treated the amount in dispute as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee. Similarly, he treated receipts from S.S Overseas as bogus sales and held it as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member, having found that the assessee was able to establish the identity and creditworthiness of the entities purchasing gold/bullion from the assessee as well as the genuineness of the transactions, held that not only the sales were genuine but none of the conditions of section 68 were applicable to the subject transactions. Accordingly, he deleted the entire addition. Whereas, the Judicial Member did not agree with the view expressed by the Accountant Member. He was of the view that not only the sales were bogus but the amount representing bogus sales was required to be added to the business income by treating them as unexplained investment under section 69. Thus, the Judicial Member directed the Assessing Officer to convert the disputed addition from section 68 to section 69.

■

On reference to Third Member :

The assessee was engaged in the business of sale of farm fresh milk of cows.

During search, it was found that the assessee had made cash payments aggregating to Rs. 30 lakhs in three equal instalments of Rs. 10 lakhs each to one Deepak in October, November and December, 2019.

The Assessing Officer confronted the assessee and recorded his statement under section 132(4) in which the assessee deposed that Deepak had provided knowledge to him regarding his farm and cash transaction was made through Deepak for the purchase of cows. Regarding source he deposed that details will be declared later.

During the course of assessment proceedings, the assessee explained that cash was actually Rs. 10 lakhs which was given and received back from Deepak thrice, the final time through one Rahish Pal Singh.

The Assessing Officer considering the explanation given by the assessee on afterthought held that the source of cash remained unexplained. Accordingly, he made an addition of Rs. 30 lakhs to the income of the assessee under section 69C.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned addition.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

For the 2.12-acre sale, based on seized material and statements, the AO concluded total consideration at about Rs.8.91 crores (about Rs.1.91 crores by banking channels and about Rs.6.99 crores in cash) and made a corresponding addition to long-term capital gains.

On appeal, the CIT(A), for the 1.41-acre sale, relied on Evernote entries identifying the assessee and quantifying cash at about Rs.4.72 crores, the aggregator’s statements explaining contemporaneous recording and cash flows, and the assessee’s section 132(4) statement and subsequent admission letter; treating the later claim of only Rs.84.60 lakhs as a belated, unsupported retraction, the CIT(A) confirmed inclusion of about Rs.4.72 crores as on-money. ■

In instant appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that search statements were made under stress and later retracted. Evernote data were unilateral third-party records without proof of actual cash movement. It further contended that cross-examination clarified that only Rs.84.60 lakhs was received in the first sale and that no assets/investments/expenditure traceable to the larger sums were found despite investigation.

During the search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced. Statements of the assessee’s executives recorded under section 132(4) acknowledged planning a cash component of Rs.25 crores and indicated that Rs.7 crores had been paid, alongside Rs.75 crores towards share capital and unsecured loans. Relying on the seized note, the cash receipt and statements, the AO held that Rs.7 crores had been paid in cash in connection with the transaction and treated it as unexplained expenditure under section 69C. The assessee’s denial of cash exchange was not accepted, and the addition of Rs.7 crores was made. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition under section 69C.

held.text: During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer called upon the assessee to file details of name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. The assessee has filed a list of persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Out of list submitted by the assessee, the Assessing Officer has issued summons under section 131(1) to 50 persons to verify the genuineness of the assessee claim of receipt of cash from them. Out the above 50, summons issued to 40 persons returned by the Postal Authorities citing 'addressee cannot be located' or 'no such person' or 'no such address' or 'insufficient address' or 'no such address at the above place'. In response to summons, three persons were responded and out of three, two persons denied having any kind of transactions with the assessee. Further, one person confirmed having paid advance to the assessee company and also purchased jewellery from them. The Assessing Officer, on the basis of enquiry conducted under section 131(1), came to the conclusion that the assessee could not substantiate cash receipts received from various persons towards sale of jewellery before the date of demonetization. Therefore, vide letter called upon the assessee to file confirmation from all the parties and also called upon the assessee to show cause 'as to why' the credits should not be considered as unexplained cash credit under section 68. In response, the assessee submitted that as per law, it is not required to collect complete address and PAN from the persons to whom it has sold jewellery. Further, as per rules 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, if sale value of jewellery is in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs to a single person, then, it is required to collect PAN. Since, there is no requirement of collecting PAN, the assessee does not having details of PAN and correct postal address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Therefore, assessee submitted that the question of filing confirmation letter from the parties, from whom, it has collected advance for sale of jewellery does not arise, and consequently, cash receipts cannot be assessed under section 68. The assessee had also explained the Assessing Officer that it has sufficient cash balance as on 8-11-2016 as per books of account maintained for that assessment year and argued that the total cash deposits into bank account is explained out of cash in hand. The assessee has also made an alternative submission that it has sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12]

[Para 12] In light of above factual matrix, if one examines the issue, the Assessing Officer has rejected the contention of the assessee on two grounds. The first and foremost reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject the explanation of the assessee is that persons from whom assessee claims to have been received advance are not responded to summons issued under section 131(1) and in few cases, they have denied any kind of transactions with the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not discharge its onus cast upon as per the provisions of section 68, in respect of cash receipts, and thus, opined that cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee from various persons is unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has committed a fundamental mistake in examining the cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee towards sale of jewellery in light of provisions of section 68. [Para 13]

Be that as it may. The fact remains that, the assessee has furnished name and address of the customers from whom it has received cash for sale of jewellery. The assessee need not obtain confirmation and submit to the Assessing Officer, because, the law does not mandate collecting PAN details of the persons, if sale value of jewellery does not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs as per rule 114B of Income-tax Rules, 1962. In so far as compliance of KYC norms, it is mandatory under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with effect from 4-5-2023 onwards and not applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14]

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. Thus, revenue succeeds on this ground while the assessee fails on this issue in their respective appeals. [Para 10]

Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

[Para 10]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. It is stated by the assessee that there is no onus on the assessee under any law to reveal the identity of buyers who allegedly bought gold bars from the assessee, this argument is fallacious as the amount of cash allegedly received from unknown buyers of gold bars stood deposited in the bank account of the assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor.

The onus was on the assessee to prove genuineness of the business of gold bars conducted by the assessee. Provisions of section 68 is a special provisions and is a deeming provision which cast obligation on the assessee to satisfactorily explain the cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee by revealing identity, creditworthiness of the creditor and genuineness of the transaction which has not been fulfilled by the assessee and burden cast on the assessee is not fulfilled by the assessee in the instant case as detailed above.

The assessee failed to satisfactorily explain the sources of these cash deposits in bank accounts of the assessee which are in the nature of cash credits in the books of account /bank accounts of the assessee, which is stated to be from cash sales of gold bar wherein identity of the buyers is not revealed by the assessee and is a devise used to convert undisclosed income/money into gold bars without disclosure of the identity of depositor of cash in bank accounts, and thus burden cast on the assessee under section 68 did not stood discharged and the said cash credit will be deemed to be income of the assessee from the undisclosed income chargeable to tax within deeming fiction of section 68, which in the instant case it is held this issue against the assessee and in favour of revenue based on factual matrix of the case detailed above.

On both the counts, the Pr. Commissioner is totally incorrect. A bare perusal of the assessment order reveals that this aspect of cash deposit during the demonetization was thoroughly inquired into by the Assessing Officer and the assessee had repeatedly maintained that the cash deposited was on account of cash sales made by it. The assessment order reveals that the assessee had submitted comparative figures of sales made by it in the preceding and succeeding years and demonstrated huge turnover averaging Rs. 20-30 crores. He had also submitted comparative details of cash component of total sales reflecting the fact that the cash component was approx. more than 90 per cent of the turnover. The assessee had further demonstrated the fact of increase in sales in the impugned year by showing that its business had shown an increasing trend from year to year right from assessment year 2014-15 to assessment year 2018-19 including the year of demonetization i.e. financial year 2016-17. The assessee had shown its sales had continuously increased in the pre-demonetization period at the rate of 32.5 per cent and 39.01 per cent while during the demonetization period and post demonetization, the sales had shown a decline in the percentage of increase, increasing at the rate of 13.90 per cent and 17.22 per cent in the subsequent year i.e. financial years 2017-18 and 2018-19. He had explained the increase in turnover as compared to the preceding year in the year of demonetization, which is the impugned year in the present case. And had also explained the reason for turnover not increasing in the same proportion in the succeeding year. However, it is noted that the Assessing Officer was not completely satisfied with this reply of the assessee, noting that during the period of demonetization, i.e. 1st to 8-11-2016, there was abnormal increase in turnover, and therefore, he went to treat 20 per cent of the cash deposit as unexplained credits. Taking note of the fact the assessee had established that majority of its sales were made in cash which was deposited in bank, but noting the fact that during demonetization period, the assessee had shown substantially larger increase in turnover, he therefore, considering it fit, to treat only 20 per cent of the total cash deposits as unexplained. The entire addition of Rs.9.60 crores pertains to cash found deposited in the bank account of the assessee during demonetization period which the Assessing Officer held to have remained unexplained. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) reveals that he has noted some factual findings in relation to this issue leading to his conclusion that the source of cash deposit in the bank account of the assessee during demonetization period stood duly explained. The pertinent finding in this regard are with respect to the fact that the assessee had furnished all evidences proving the genuineness of sales made during this period duly supported with purchases made which were further evidenced by the copy of VAT returns filed by the assessee and also the stock records of the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that notices issued by the Assessing Officer to all parties from whom purchases were made by the assessee under section 133(6) were duly responded and the parties confirmed the sales made to the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has further noted that there is no abnormality in the quantum of sales made by the assessee in the impugned year as compared to the preceding year noting the fact that the component of cash sales had decreased by almost 87.96 per cent in the entire year; in the period preceding demonetization it was noted to have decreased by 88.54 per cent and during the demonetization period to have decreased by 65.56 per cent. The Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that neither the Auditor has pointed out any discrepancy in the accounts of the assessee nor has the Assessing Officer rejected the books of the assessee under section 145(3). He has noted the stock position depicted in the books of the assessee to have been accepted by the Assessing Officer. [Para 5]

■

All these facts noted by the Commissioner (Appeals), establish the genuineness of the cash deposited in the bank account of the assessee to have come out of cash sales made by the assessee during the course of business. The above facts have not been controverted by the revenue also. [Para 6]

■

In view of the detailed reasoning of the Commissioner (Appeals) based on uncontroverted facts, holding the source of cash deposited in the bank account to be out of cash sales, there is no reason to interfere in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) deleting the addition made of Rs.9.60 crores. [Para 7]

■

The Assessing Officer proceeded to make the total cash deposit made by the assessee during demonetization period since assessee could not submit the relevant cash deposit made by the assessee during the impugned year as well as previous year during the assessment proceeding. Since there was no information available with him, he proceeded to make the whole cash deposits as addition. In appeal, assessee filed additional evidences before the first appellate authority. In remand proceedings, after considering the additional evidences and other details submitted before the Assessing Officer, the Assessing Officer observed that assessee has achieved cash sales of Rs.36.54 crores and cash deposit of Rs.35.83 crores and the difference of Rs.71.40 lakhs with the assessee. He observed that assessee may have meet out the same in running the business. Accordingly, he assumed that cash balance was utilised for business expenses as dairy business being cash intensified enterprise. After observing the above, he further observed that during demonetization, assessee has deposited Rs.4.79 crores whereas achieved the total cash sales during the period of Rs.4.25 crores, therefore there is a difference of Rs.53.51 lakhs. Therefore, the assessee failed to furnish any explanation. The Commissioner (Appeals) also proceeded to sustain the above addition without considering the actual facts on record. Before demonetization i.e. on 7-11-2016, the assessee had closing cash balance which was not considered by the lower authorities and also they themselves observed that there is a difference of Rs.71.39 lakhs pre-demonetization period from the total cash sales and cash deposited by the assessee. They presumed that the abovesaid difference must have been utilised by the assessee for business purpose without duly verifying the cash book maintained by the assessee. Since they proceeded to sustain the addition arbitrarily without actually verifying the cash book maintained by the assessee. When the total cash sales and total cash deposit made by the assessee during the year is looked at, it clearly shows that assessee has made total cash sales of Rs.48.03 crores and made the cash deposit of Rs.47.45 crores. Therefore, there is absolutely no justification for making the abovesaid addition under section 68. Considering the above facts on record, the grounds raised by the assessee are to be allowed. [Para 9]

The limited controversy that arises for consideration is whether, on the facts of the present case, the addition of alleged cash payment in relation to purchase of shop at "Platinum Mall" can be sustained solely on the basis of third-party digital records and statements, without providing the assessee an effective opportunity to confront such material.

■

It is undisputed that the entire foundation of the impugned addition consists of: (i) Excel sheets found in a pen drive seized from IA, a third party containing name, shop number and amount of the cash, and (ii) his statement admitting receipt of cash on behalf of the Rubberwala Group and that cash was being handed over to director of the company TS. [Para 8.1]

■

On the basis of the said material and the statements of key person from their premises, the said company has accepted the fact of the on-money received in cash and declared 8 per cent of the net profit for undisclosed income. No independent evidence has been brought on record to demonstrate actual payment of cash by the assessee. There is no receipt, no diary, no acknowledgment, no contemporaneous document, and no corroborative evidence linking the assessee to the alleged cash payment, apart from the third-party record. [Para 8.2]

■

But the issue arises is whether the material found in possession of the third party, statement of the third party and the disclosure made by them, bind the assessee for the addition without providing opportunity of confronting the material to the assessee. [Para 8.3]

■

In the case assessment has been initiated under section 153C and under the provisions of section 153C material pertaining to the assessee which is basis of the recording of satisfaction under section 153C must have been forwarded to the Assessing Officer of the assessee. But despite specific request by the assessee no such material was provided to the assessee. The assessee also sought for the opportunity to cross-examine IA but both the Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) has declined on the ground that it was not the sole basis for making addition. But it is found that no other evidence has been brought on record by the lower authorities to substantiate that the cash on-money was actually paid by the assessee to IA except confession of IA. [Para 8.4]

■

The assessee submitted that said Rubberwala Group has credited 100 per cent cash in its books of accounts against offering 8 per cent of income on such declaration. In other words, they have generated huge amount of income in their hands at 33 per cent of tax on the 8 per cent income of the cash declared. For example, if the assessee get credited Rs.100 in its books of account against cash received then it has paid taxes at the rate of 33 per cent on Rs.8 which work out to Rs.2.6. The assessee submitted that this was one of the beneficial declaration and therefore, they have admitted and paid the taxes. The assessee submitted that the assessee has never paid such cash on-money and it might be their own money which they had brought into books in garb of cash on-money for tax benefit. [Para 8.5]

■

It is opined that though the Rubberwala Group has admitted receipt of unaccounted cash and offered a percentage thereof to tax, such admission by the seller cannot, by itself, fasten liability upon the purchaser unless there is cogent evidence establishing that the purchaser actually made such payment. The disclosure by the developer may explain the source of its own funds, but it does not dispense with the burden on the revenue to prove the assessee's investment or expenditure. [Para 8.6]

■

The assessee specifically brought to attention that IA in his answer to question No. 13 of the statement dated 17-3-2021 stated that after receipt of alleged cash from the customers a small diary was being used to provide containing cash details received from the customers. The assessee submitted that no such diary has been recovered from the assessee nor any kind of receipt issued by Rubberwala Group having signature of the assessee has been found from the premises of the Rubberwala group or from the assessee. The assessee submitted that in the case of one of the customer Rajesh Jain search was conducted by the Department but no such document in the form of diary was found which could corroborate statement of IA. According to him, IA cooked up a story of cash on-money in his statement for benefiting interest of their company. [Para 8.7]

There is no dispute with regard to the amount of cash deposits into her bank account during the demonetization period and the explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of opening cash balance available as on 8-11-2016 as per the cash book maintained for the relevant financial year. In fact, the Assessing Officer never disputed the fact that the assessee has explained the cash deposit into the bank account out of cash balance available as per books of account. The Assessing Officer disbelieved the arguments of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of sales declared from 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016 and claimed that, there is abnormal deviation in the sales declared by the assessee for the above period when compared to the earlier months and subsequent months. The Assessing Officer further noted that, the assessee has furnished VAT returns belatedly to cover up the backdated sale bills issued to the customers to show sufficient cash balance in the books of account to explain cash deposits into the bank account. Therefore, he disbelieved the evidences filed by the assessee and assessed the cash deposits as unexplained money under section 69A. [Para 19]

■

There is no dispute with regard to the fact that, the cash balance shown in the books of account as on 8-11-2016 is supported by necessary sales bills issued towards sale of jewellery from 1-11-2016 to 7-11-2016. It is also not in dispute that, the assessee was having sufficient stock-in-hand to explain the sale bills issued to the customers between 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016. The sales declared by the assessee are recorded in the books of account and also part of the turnover declared for the year under consideration which suffered taxation. Once the assessee has recorded sales in the books of account, which is supported by necessary sales bills with a corresponding stock-in-hand, the Assessing Officer ought not to have made additions towards cash deposits as unexplained money only on the ground that, there is abnormal variation in cash sales during the demonetization period when compared to earlier or subsequent periods. It was a well-known fact during the demonetization period that, there was a mad rush in jewellery shops for purchasing gold jewellery out of demonetized currency when the demonetization was announced on 8-11-2016. In the instant case, going by the facts available on record, the assessee has reported major sales on 7-11-2016, which is the previous day of the demonetization was announced, and from the details furnished by the assessee, it is very clear that, the assessee has made sales of gold jewellery in cash which is the source for cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period on 14-11-2016. Since the cash deposited into the bank account is supported by necessary cash balance available as per books of account maintained by the assessee which was further supported by necessary sales bills, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards cash deposits under section 69A as unexplained money cannot be sustained. Although the Assessing Officer has disbelieved the sales on the basis of VAT returns submitted by the assessee for the month of November, 2016 and claimed that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover backdated sales, but going by the history of the assessee in filing the VAT returns, it is evident that, for all the months in the financial year 2016-17, the assessee has filed VAT returns belatedly and from the above, it is very clear that, the argument of the Assessing Officer that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover up backdated sales, is contrary to the evidence available on record and cannot be accepted. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A. Thus, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made under section 69A. [Para 20]

The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

On examination of the assessee’s submissions, it is observed that the assessee had set up its business in the financial year 2015-16 and made sales of Rs.13.52 crores during the year. This had increased to Rs.49.49 crores in the financial year relevant to the assessment year in question and further increased to Rs.73.71 crores in the subsequent financial year. Thus, it is evident that the business of the assessee was an expanding business and the sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over the years. It is also observed that the assessee had an opening stock of jewellery worth Rs.4.69 crores on the 1-4- 2016. The assessee has furnished before the Assessing Officer the month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and the movement in the stock position. From the same, it is seen that on the 1-10-2016, the assessee had stock worth Rs.13.08 crores in its possession and that when viewed against the closing stock of Rs.9.54 crores as on 31-10-2016, had depleted a substantial amount of that stock by way of sales. The details of stock, purchases and sales that have been submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer have not been questioned or doubted in any manner by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, only because the month of October, 2016 saw a spurt in cash sales below the limit of Rs.2 lakhs, for which the assessee was not in a position to furnish details of purchasers, the sales made by the assessee cannot be doubted unless the purchases, sales and stock depletion are also cast into doubt. With regard to the argument that the assessee had not submitted the sales invoices to the Assessing Officer, it is observed that unless there is a finding that the stocks were not available or were diverted elsewhere, sales claimed out of those stocks cannot be doubted. The Assessing Officer has based his additions on the belief that there exists a possibility of manipulating the exact date of sale on account of the requirement of filing of VAT return for October, 2016 on 20-11-2016, but it is observed that first of all, in this case, all the cash from sales was deposited on 10-11-2016 leaving lesser scope for manipulation but even if that were so, it would not take the credits on account of those sales in his books outside the purview of sales receipts, unless it could be shown that the sales had not occurred or that the assessee did not have the stock to sell that which he claimed to have sold. It is observed that the assessee presented the cash book before the Assessing Officer and the Assessing Officer could not find any discrepancy in the same. Therefore, the credits made in the said cash book on account of cash sales, remain uncontroverted. In the circumstances, considering that the assessee has presented evidence of available stock and depletion of the said stock on account of sales and the Assessing Officer has not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of the receipts on account of the sale of that stock are unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 is made out. Therefore, the decision to delete the addition of Rs.2.99 crores on this account is upheld. [Para 10]

The main issue in instant appeal is addition made under section 69. [Para 15]

■

It is clear from decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that he has adopted theory of peak credit to sustain addition of Rs.4 crore and allowed relief of Rs.32.17 crores. Peak credit theory applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) is not acceptable since the Commissioner (Appeals) has not brought on record peculiar facts of case which compelled him to apply peak credit theory in picture. The Commissioner (Appeals) has simply taken amount of highest balance in the bank account and has treated it as ''''peak credit'''', which is not correct. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to take note that from 17 date-wise transactions, it can be observed that the cash deposits were made and then cheques were issued. It is not the case that cash was first deposited from which cash was withdrawn and same remained unutilized for subsequent deposit. The determination of the peak credit cannot be applied in case of appellant because of following reasons: (i) where there are cash deposits but withdrawals are through the cheques then benefit of the peak credit cannot be allowed for the cash deposit so made in bank account. In the assessee''''s case, against the cash deposits cheques were issued to some other entities. (ii) As amount of the cash credits were standing in the names of different persons which all along assessee had been claiming as genuine deposit, withdrawal/payment of amount to different set of persons would not at all entitle applicant to claim benefit of peak credits. [Para 15.1]

■

While determining the peak credit, the withdrawal of cash, if not utilized elsewhere, is considered as available for making the deposits. The highest unexplained cash deposit is considered as the peak credit. determination of the peak credit reduces taxable income. However, where withdrawal are through cheques, the benefits of those withdrawals will not be available to explain deposits. Therefore, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) to allow the peak credit to the assessee was not correct. [Para 15.2]

■

The appellant claimed to have sold gold bullion during demonetization period and demonetized currency was deposited in bank account of ''''N''''. The Commissioner (Appeals) has formed a hypothesis to decide case on the peak credit principle and restrict the addition to Rs.4 crore and delete the addition of Rs.32.17 crores. However, on facts of the case nowhere the assessee had been able to conclusively establish that he had made genuine sales during demonetization period from 10-11-2016 till date of survey on 23-12-2016 nor names have been furnished by the assessee before the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals)/CBI/ED. Significantly, neither revenue nor the appellant have requested to apply principle of the peak credit inthe instant case. In fact, the assessee itself has raised a ground to delete addition of Rs.4 crore based on peak credit principle. [Para 15.3]

■

The revenue took plea that survey by Department has established that the falsification of accounts had happened because the sale invoices were booked in the name of NC which was proved to be a bogus entity during survey proceedings and in subsequent proceedings before department. Further, mere payments made by cheques or RTGS does not establish that said gold was received immediately and same was serially and genuinely sold to unknown 2200 purchasers against demonetized currency notes. Even survey could not find evidence of such series of sale by the assessee or commensurate stock of gold and silver at known business premises. The net effect of cash deposited in the bank account of NC and subsequent cheques/RTGS payment is nothing but attempt to convert hoarded undisclosed income of the assessee into the stock of gold for future sales. Under these circumstances, granting benefit of peak credit to the assessee is not warranted. [Para 15.4]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) has considered that the transaction in the bank account of NC relates to the assessee and has accordingly, given benefit to the assessee by restricting the addition in the case. The assessee has not been able to explain as to how almost all cash deposited in bank account of NC were immediately transferred to bank account of assessee. [Para 15.5]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals), whose powers are co-terminus with that of the Assessing Officer should have examined the facts of case, which he failed to do. Considering totality of facts and circumstances of the case and once it is established that the assessee cannot be allowed benefit of the peak credit, the cash deposited in bank account of the assessee remains unexplained as the assessee has not been able to explain nature and source of such cash deposits along with the documentary evidence either before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 15.6]

It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer has accepted the transactions about purchase and sale of jewellery in gold and silver without raising any doubt regarding books of account, purchase and sale stock registers and the bills produced by the assessee. The cash transaction before the demonetisation period was also revealed by the assessee as the period before the demonetisation was also the period of Diwali and that itself shows that why the cash transaction took place in that particular period. The assessee is an individual and deriving income from business of jewellery. The books of account of the assessee are audited by the independent chartered accountant and copy of audit report and statement of profit and loss account is filed by the assessee. It is noted from the record that the case of the assessee was taken up for scrutiny for assessment under section 143(3) and desired information by the Assessing Officer were submitted by the assessee from time-to-time. The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee has deposited cash amounting to Rs. 91,00,000/- in its two bank accounts No. 50200017462772 account No. 02892020002124 with HDFC Bank Limited in Specified Bank Notes (SBN) during the demonetization period 12-11-2016 and 13-11-2016, and Rs. 12,00,000/- in non-demonetized currency on 28-03-2017 and this Rs. 12,00,000/- was offered for Income under "Pradhanmantri Garib Kalyan Yojna-2016" and the assessee has filed copy of Form 1 and Form 2. However, the Assessing Officer made the addition of Rs. 91,00,000+12,00,000 totalling to Rs. 1,03,00,000/- and he treated the sales as unexplained cash credit of the assessee under section 68 and added the same to the income of the assessee and thus taxed it as per the provisions of section 115BBE and vide her order dated 30-12-2019 assessed the income of the assessee at Rs. 1,43,11,520/- as against return income of Rs. 40,11,520/-. The Commissioner(Appeals) has deleted the addition.

■

The assessee had deposited the cash out of cash sales recorded during the period October, November and December 2016. The reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer to reject the reasons for such cash deposits are out of cash sales by observing that the cash is nothing but undisclosed funds of the assessee and it has manipulated the cash sales to make such cash deposits. From the records it is observed that the Assessing Officer neither rejected the book results or method of account adopted by the assessee. The Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) has not found any discrepancies in the method of accounting, margin declared by the assessee which are in consonance with the previous periods. The Assessing Officer did not have any material against the assessee but made the addition merely on the basis his perception that the same is only out of assessee’s undisclosed income. [Para 13]

On the other hand, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also sustained the addition made by the Assessing Officer by observing that the stock register is not maintained and purchase/sales are not substantiated with sales bills or names and address of the customers or not provided confirmations from the customers. Further, he has proceeded to sustain the addition under section 69A against the additions made by the Assessing Officer under section 68. As regards the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee has not maintained the stock register, it is observed that the assessee is engaged in trading of general purpose machinery parts/bearings. The method of maintenance of stock registers and other related records depends upon the nature of business, particularly in the line of business the assessee is into, it is dealing with the spare parts and bearings, which the assessee is purchasing from the industries and selling the same in the retail market. The value of each bills may be less than Rs. 20,000/-. What is important and relevant, is the stock reconciliation of each item and whether the same is certified by the statutory auditor before finalizing the accounts. In this case, it is observed that the same was submitted before the authorities below. The Commissioner (Appeals) has not found anything suspicious in the method of accounting in the recording of sales nor stock keeping but merely expressed his view on the contrary but failed to appreciate the nature of business and how difficult to maintain the several stock keeping units(sku) involved in this industry. The cash sales made by the assessee have been credited in the books of account and the same form part of the assessee’s cash book. On these facts, it could be very well said that the assessee claim was backed up by relevant evidences. Thus, the assessee has discharged the burden of proving the source of the cash/SBN deposited in the bank and the Assessing Officer failed to rebut the same. The partner of the assessee firm. 'M', in his statements made before the investigation wing, had stated that the sales had been made in cash and the persons, through whom sales were made, were unverifiable. In fact, he said that he knew the names of the customers to whom sales had been made, personally but he did not disclose the names due to professional/trade secret. It was in clear contradiction to his first statement recorded on 6-5-1999, when he stated that he did not know any such person and the buyers approached him directly. It was, thus, a case where the partner in the assessee-firm had been changing his stand as regards the particulars of sales. No evidence worth any credence had been led either in the course of the assessment proceedings or appellate proceedings to establish that the sales had been made and the cash deposited in the bank account was in lieu of the sales made of jewellery. In fact, unverifiability of the sales had been accepted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, when he had enhanced the income returned and the assessee, in the impugned proceedings, had not challenged that finding. Mere furnishing of cash memos could not by any stretch of imagination, be made a sole basis to conclude that any sales had been made by the assessee. Thus, the sales made by the assessee were unverifiable and unacceptable. Moreover, the entire transaction of purchase and sale of jewellery had been carried out by the assessee in a particular manner and abnormal circumstances, which irrefutably led to a conclusion that there was no business per se of the assessee of purchase and sale of jewellery. The assessee-firm did not even had the necessary infrastructure, i.e., dharam kanta to carry on the business of purchase and sale of diamond jewellery, which is the most essential infrastructure. Even otherwise, no particulars had been placed on record to show that such jewellery was allegedly purchased and sold by the assessee with a weighing scale of a third party. In fact, the evidence furnished by the assessee in the shape of purchase bills and sales bills did not include the weighment slips, which, as per the admission of the assessee, were the fundamental requirements for any transaction of purchase/sale of jewellery. There were no employees of the firm other than one 'G', who had not been produced in the course of the assessment proceedings and even his particulars had not been made available at any stage. Even as regards to his purported duties, there was a contradiction. In the initial statement, 'M' stated that said employee's duty was to assist him in carrying the cash to the bank, whereas subsequently even the same was contradicted by stating that when he went to deposit the cash, he stayed back at the premises. Thus, it was not possible to accept that the assessee had employed any such person. Even otherwise, it was not possible to carry on business of such a huge magnitude with only one employee and that too, having no formal qualifications. It had been stated by 'M' before the investigation wing and the Assessing Officer that the business was carried on with minimum furniture of one table, two chairs and a half size almirah, which was also used as a safe. However, it appeared that even the infrastructure as contended by the assessee in the shape of almirah, one table and two chairs was not available with the assessee to carry on the business of the projected magnitude. Further, there was no past track record of the assessee-firm. It had allegedly carried on the operations of business only for a short period of time and even within that short period of time, the entire alleged purchases of jewellery were from the persons, who had furnished declarations under the VDIS, 1997, and for all such purchases the sales were only in cash. In fact, even independently, the purchases had not been proved by the assessee-firm. Mere issue of purchase bills could not be regarded as sufficient basis to hold that the jewellery had been purchased by the assessee-firm. In that connection, the statements of four persons had been recorded by the investigation wing, wherein all of them had confirmed that they had not sold any jewellery to the assessee. Though in the assessment proceedings, they had retracted from their original statements, yet such retraction was not supported by any adequate reason. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act. That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further

Admittedly, the assessee has received advances from six customers towards sale of gold jewellery, and on subsequent dates, the assessee has issued sales invoices with particulars of jewellery sold to them and also adjusted the advances received from the parties in the final sales bills, which is evident from the relevant tabular statement submitted by the assessee. It is further noted that, from the tabular statement submitted by the assessee, except in two cases, in all the remaining cases, the assessee has received the advances through bank by RTGS or cheque, and against advances, had issued sales invoices either immediately after receipt of advances or within a reasonable time of one or two months and from the above, it is clear that, the assessee has received advances from customers for sale of gold jewellery, and the same has been adjusted against the sales recorded in the books of account. Since the assessee has filed relevant evidences to prove the sales advances received from customers and also made sales in subsequent periods, it is viewed that the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards sale advances from customers as loan creditors under section 68, on the ground that, the creditworthiness of the parties is not proved. It is viewed that once it is proved that, the credits relates to trade advances, then the question of examination of creditworthiness of the advance received from customers does not arise, and also additions cannot be made towards sale advances under section 68, as unexplained cash credit. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards advances from customers as loan creditors under section 68. Thus, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside and the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the additions made towards advances received from customers and made additions under section 68. The reasons given by the assessee that NK (HUF) holding sufficient funds is not supported by any documents or Income Tax Returns filed by the assessee for relevant assessment year. Although, the assessee claims that NK (HUF) does not have any taxable income for relevant assessment years, since the loan between the assessee and NK (HUF) is in cash, Income Tax Returns filed by the creditor is one of the pointer to creditworthiness of a person. Since, the assessee failed to file necessary evidences to prove the creditworthiness of the creditor, there is no error in the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject source for cash deposits claimed to have been received from NK (HUF). Thus, the arguments of the assessee are rejected and the findings of the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) in making additions towards cash deposits into bank account under section 68 are upheld. [Para 8.4]

In view of the ratio of the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Jamnaprasad Kanhaiyalal v. CIT [1981] 130 ITR 244, it was clear that in the absence of any satisfactory proof, the taxing authorities were perfectly justified in holding that the impugned cash credits represented the assessee's own income from undisclosed sources.

■

It is not disputed that the assessee has maintained proper books of account consisting of cash book, ledger, stock register and sale bills, purchase bills and vouchers. The books of account of the assessee have been audited and tax audit report has been filed with the Income-tax department. The assessee contended that cash deposited in the bank account stands explained as being made out of cash available in the books of account on account of cash sales and realization of debtors. It further argued that the purchases recorded in books of account have been accepted by the Assessing Officer and profit on sales declared by it was a normal profit and not exorbitant profit. Again the sales made by the assessee have been declared in VAT returns and payment VAT to State Government, where the sales declared in the VAT returns have been accepted by Punjab State Sales Tax Department. Since the cash sales during the demonetization period constitute the basic foundation of the cash deposit in bank credited as per profit and loss account and such cash sales have already been offered to tax as income of the assessee, further inference under section 69A was unwarranted based on assumptions and presumptions, surmises and conjectures by the authorities below to treat the cash sales as unaccounted income amounting to Rs. 57.32 lakhs. [Para 8]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) has neither appreciated the facts on record and the documentary evidence produced nor rebutted the contention of the assessee. The finding and decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) ignoring the submission based on facts and merits and reinforces the findings of the Assessing Officer in mechanical manner is not justified. Merely stating that the assessee’s reply has been considered and examined but the same has not been found satisfactory cannot be approved because the Commissioner (Appeals) has neither controverted nor disproved the contention with valid reasons and corroborative documentary evidence. [Para 9]

■

In the instant case, sales made by the assessee and shown in the regular books of account have been accepted as such by VAT authorities while framing the VAT assessment, the assessee was having sufficient stock-in-hand for making the impugned sales during the demonetization period and it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has shown bogus purchases to show bogus sales to cover up cash deposited during the demonetization period. [Para 11]

■

In view of the factual matrix, the Commissioner (Appeals)’s decision is infirm and perverse to the facts on record in confirming the addition under section 69A. Accordingly the addition amounting to Rs. 57.32 lakhs made by invoking provisions of section 69A is illegal and bad in law and as such same is deleted. [Para 12]

■

Since the addition of Rs. 57.32 lakhs made by invoking provisions of section 69A is deleted being held to be illegal, the issue of invoking of section 69A treating the deposits as income from undisclosed sources and applicability of tax rate as per provisions of section 115BBE stands rejected. [Para 13]

■

The revenue was unable to controvert the fact that the assessee had explained the source of cash deposits as being out of cash sales made by it and had duly substantiated the same by producing all books of account which were duly accepted by the revenue authorities and no infirmity found in the same. The assessee had also evidenced the genuineness of sales by demonstrating to have declared the same in his VAT returns which were accepted. The revenue was also unable to controvert the fact pointed out by the assessee that all abnormalities and inconsistencies noted by the revenue authorities in the case sales, cash deposits etc., were duly explained by the assessee and the explanation duly substantiated with the books of account, which were all accepted by the authorities below. The revenue also fairly agreed that no infirmity was found by the revenue authorities in the explanation of the assessee. [Para 19]

■

In the light of the above, noting the fact that the assessee had explained the source of cash deposit in bank during demonetization period as being out of its cash sales and had substantiated the same by producing its books of account and VAT returns declaring the said sales, in which no infirmity was found by the revenue authorities and which was not rejected also, it is to be held that the assessee had duly discharged its onus of proving the source of cash so deposited in the bank account during demonetization period. Noting the assessee to have duly explained the alleged inconsistencies noted by the revenue authorities in the figure of cash sales, cash deposit, cash balances in the impugned year as compared to their corresponding figures in the preceding year, and the assessee substantiating the said explanation by producing its entire records before the revenue authorities, who admittedly found no infirmity either in the explanation of the assessee or the books of account of the assessee, the entire addition made of cash deposit in the bank account of the assessee during the demonetization period was without any valid basis and was merely based on assumptions and presumptions. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) order confirming the addition made by the Assessing Officer on account of cash deposited in the bank account during demonetization under section 69A is not sustainable. The Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made to the income of the assessee. [Para 20]

As regards the first and second statements of VDT, the same having been recorded not during the proceedings pertaining to the assessee, but during survey in the case of VDT, the copies of the same having not been supplied to the assessee prior to assessment and supplied only as attached with the assessment order and opportunity for cross-examining VDT in respect of those statements having not been accorded to the assessee, the same could not be read/used against the assessee. The question of the assessee's self asking for cross examination of VDT in respect of those two statements, dated 30/31-3-2000 did not arise when the copies of the same had not been supplied to the assessee before making assessment. Besides, it is the basic principle of law that without affording opportunity of cross-examination, a statement recorded at the back of the assessee will not partake of the nature of evidence against the assessee and cannot be read/used against the assessee. Even apart, the said statements had been retracted by VDT vide his letter dated 4-4-2000. In the said retraction VDT had mentioned that those statements were given by him as directed by the department and he was under a state of total confusion. He had also mentioned in the said retraction letter that he had made the purchases, correctly issued bills, accounted for in his books and also furnished to the Sales-tax Department. He had supported the purchase of 71 carats of diamonds from the assessee by his affidavit and statement dated 25-10-2002 recorded by the Assessing Officer when he made his attendance before the Assessing Officer in response to the summons issued to him by the Assessing Officer during assessment proceedings pertaining to the present assessee. The sale of diamonds by the present assessee to VDT was also supported by VDT's purchase bill; the payments had been made by VDT to the assessee by account payee cheques and the same was corroborated by bank statement. That transaction of sale of 71 carats of loose diamonds by the assessee to VDT had already been accepted in the assessee's original assessment under section 143(3). There was no evidence on record that any cash amount was paid back by the assessee to VDT. The possession of loose diamonds by the assessee was proved by the assessee's declaration under VDIS. As such, there was no justification for holding the sale of loose diamonds by the assessee to 'DD' as bogus sale or as a mere paper transaction and not genuine, and in turn for making/sustaining addition. The addition of Rs. 11,18,250 made in the income of the assessee was, therefore, liable to be deleted.
