Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

Following the search on 23-12-2023, the AO alleged that the assessee paid cash on-money for Halol land purchases and made additions under section 69C of Rs. 78.82 lakhs (AY 2016-17), Rs. 87.97 lakhs (AY 2018-19) and Rs. 30.20 lakhs (AY 2023-24), aggregating about Rs. 1.97 crores, by estimating cash payment at 20 per cent of the agreement value. The AO principally relied on the statement of Rakesh Talati, alleging a customary 15-20 per cent cash component and cash delivery through an employee, and certain WhatsApp chats with Dharendra Pathak.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that Talati's statement was general, devoid of transaction-specific details and later retracted; no seller was examined; no cash trail or seized material evidenced cash payment; and all purchases were registered, made through banking channels and at or above stamp duty values. It was further shown that the WhatsApp chats related to a proposed Valsad transaction, whereas the additions concerned Halol lands. The CIT(A) found no corroborative evidence of cash payment, noted the absence of enquiry from sellers, accepted that the registered values were not below stamp duty values, held the chats unrelated to Halol and found the uniform 20 per cent estimation to be without factual basis. The additions were deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material placed before it. The entire addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash payment for purchase of land rests on a very narrow foundation, namely the statement of Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications. If the statement of Rakesh Talati is examined closely, it is evident that the statement is general in nature and lacks all essential particulars which are necessary for treating it as evidence of actual expenditure. The statement does not identify the specific land parcel in respect of which cash was allegedly paid. It does not identify the survey number. It does not identify the seller who allegedly received cash. It does not mention the exact amount paid in cash. It does not mention the date of payment. It does not identify the source from which the cash was generated. It does not identify the person who physically delivered the cash to the seller in relation to any particular transaction. Such a statement, at the highest, may give rise to suspicion and may justify further enquiry, but it cannot by itself constitute proof of actual expenditure incurred by the assessee. [Para 96]

■

The evidentiary weakness becomes more pronounced because the statement of Rakesh Talati was subsequently retracted. It is true that a retraction by itself does not automatically wipe out an earlier statement; however, once a statement is retracted and the assessee contests the factual correctness of the alleged admission, the burden lies on the revenue to corroborate the original statement through independent material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

Section 68 of Income-tax Act - Cash credits
Where assessee had certain credit entry as sale of jewellery and had supported sale on basis of purchase voucher of purchaser, copy of account of assessee as appearing in books of account of purchaser, and evidence of having received payment from purchaser through banking channel, such credit entry could not be treated as unexplained cash credit in assessee’s hands.

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 40A (3)  of Income-tax Act, 1961
Bachubhai Alias Vithalbhai Thakershibhai Patel v. ITO [1992] 42 TTJ (Ahd.) 153
It cannot be argued that the section 40A (3) should not be applied merely because the practice in a section of the business community like diamond trade has been to make purchase and sale in cash.
The assessee had made cash purchases of diamonds exceeding Rs. 2,500. Its explanation was that the said purchase had not been made by the assessee from one person but from different persons during the whole day. The assess also contended that the goods being stolen goods, the assessee had no evidence about parties from which it had purchased. As the assessee had not produced any purchase bill or proof of identity of persons, all the cash purchases above the prescribed limit were disallowed under section 40A (3). The Commissioner (Appeals), upheld the addition.
Held that details regarding different items of purchases on each day, if at all there were different items of purchase each day, must be available with the assessee. In so far as no such details had been produced, it was to be presumed that in fact the purchases shown on the different dates did not break up into smaller amounts as alleged and that each purchases was of the amount stated in the cash book. Therefore, the disallowance under section 40A (3) was justified.

Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 104 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained moneys (Cash found during search) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and trading of wheat flour - A search under section 132 was conducted at its premises, where cash of about Rs. 79.81 lakhs was found against book cash of about Rs. 12.37 lakhs, resulting in excess cash of about Rs. 67.43 lakhs - Part of cash of Rs. 50 lakhs was found in a locker in Managing Director’s chamber and about Rs. 17.43 lakhs with company’s cashier - Assessee stated that cash belonged to Managing Director, allegedly refunded by one individual against advances for purchase of villas - However, cash withdrawal was recorded after dates of alleged advances and no evidence of refund was produced - Whether since explanation furnished by assessee was not genuine and credible, impugned addition was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 16.5] [In favour of revenue]

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102,  read with section  195  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Demonetization period) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company, engaged in trading of solar panels, deposited cash of about Rs. 33.55 lakhs in its bank account during demonetization period - AO treated same as unexplained cash credits and made addition under Section 68 read with Section 115BBE - Assessee contended that deposits were out of cash sales duly recorded in books - It was noted that assessee attempted to prove entire cash deposit as being out of sales and recorded in books of account - However, contentions to prove cash deposits during demonetization period hardly deserved to be accepted in entirety, especially when a satisfactory explanation for disproportionate increase in cash sales just before demonetization period was not given - On other hand, revenue’s endeavour to disbelieve contention that cash deposits were supported by stock register and purchase records could not be fully justified - Whether, in such circumstances, it was deemed appropriate, in larger interest of justice, that a lump-sum addition of Rs. 3.50 lakh only would be just and proper - Held, yes [Para 6] [Partly in favour of assessee]

II. Section  69A,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961/ Section  104,  read with section  195,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Unexplained asset (Cash sales) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and sale of pan masala and tobacco products - A search under section 132 was conducted upon one, MEPL, a supplier of packaging material to assessee - Based on notepads seized during search from MEPL, Assessing Officer made addition of certain amount under section 69A as unexplained cash sales of assessee - Whether recording of satisfaction is a sine qua non for assuming jurisdiction on basis of material found in course of search of another person - Held, yes - Whether under new regime such satisfaction must be recorded with prior approval of Principal Commissioner/Commissioner - Held, yes - Whether use of third-party material is subject to strict jurisdictional safeguards and cannot be resorted to in a casual or mechanical manner - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer made huge additions solely based on third-party information/material found and seized during a search action, without establishing any direct or indirect nexus with assessee and in absence of mandatory satisfaction and prior approval of competent authority, very assumption of jurisdiction by Assessing Officer was invalid and accordingly, additions made on such basis were liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 7.1.4, 7.2 and 7.4] [In favour of assessee]

As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998, the assessee had stated in response to a question that he was at Surat on most of the dates and not necessarily on all the dates. In view of the fact that preceding the date of 15-3-1998, there was sales of diamonds on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 24-1-1998 of other family members of the assessee, sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998 was to be accepted as genuine. [Para 33]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 25-3-1998 after perusal of statement and rejoinder of the assessee, it was found that Rs. 5,00,000 was not drawn on 25-3-1998 but was credited to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and it was a transfer entry on 25-3-1998 from the bank account of ‘H’ in State Bank of India to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and, therefore, the contention of the revenue that the assessee was at Hyderabad on 25-3-1998 was not correct. [Para 34]

of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: A search and survey action under section 133A was carried out on the premises of assessee-company, engaged in the business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery and bullion. It was noticed that the assessee had deposited huge amounts in its bank account after demonetization was announced.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the additions made under section 68 to the extent of Rs. 28.37 crores on various ground; firstly, that the statement of third party given before police/E.D. was not contradicted by the AO; secondly, no inquiry was made from the parties whose details had been given by third party and thirdly, the deposit of cash by the third party in the account of the assessee has not been disputed by the Assessing Officer.

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposits post demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization - Assessee claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration - Assessing Officer made addition under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format, and thus, claim made by assessee remained unexplained - Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed order of Assessing Officer on ground that assessee made sale transaction below Rs. 2 lakhs and cash sales during demonetization was 90.59 per cent of cash sales for entire period of next financial year - It was noted that other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT - Also Assessing Officer without examining any parties to whom goods were sold by assessee concluded that sales were not genuine - Whether since Assessing Officer accepted books of account of assessee and entries in books of account were matched, there would be no case to make additions - Held, yes - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) committed error in upholding addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

The assessee, engaged in the jewellery business, filed its return for A.Y. 2017-18 declaring income of about Rs. 29.98 lakhs. A survey under section 133A was conducted. During scrutiny, it was noted that cash of about Rs. 6.34 crores was deposited in bank during the demonetisation period, and in online enquiries the assessee stated that the deposits represented cash sales of jewellery recorded in the books.

■

The AO doubted the factum of cash sales and treated the bank cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68.

■

The CIT(A) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the cash deposits were out of recorded cash sales supported by bills, vouchers, bank extracts and VAT returns, and that the books and trading results, including the impugned cash sales, had not been rejected; the Department relied on the orders of the lower authorities.

HELD: ■

Tribunal has noted that this Tribunal has been consistently holding that where the trading result of the assessee have been accepted by the Revenue and books of accounts have not been rejected, no addition is permissible. [Para 6]

■

The facts of the present case are akin to those deliberated in the judicial precedents above. In respectful compliance to the decisions of Co-ordinate Benches of this Tribunal in DCIT v. Adarsh Kanch Udyog (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No.4741 (Del) of 2024, dated 21.03.2025], ITO v. Mobi Tradelink [IT Appeal No.3520 (Del) of 2024, dated 6-12 2024] and HKT Retail Ventures Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO [IT Appeal No.1337 (Del) of 2024, dated 7-5-2025], and for consistency, no case for any addition is made out in the hands of the assessee. The order of the CIT(A) is set aside and the AO is directed to delete the addition of Rs.6.35 crore under Section 68 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The appellant succeeds on this issue. [Para 9]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. The case of assessee was selected for scrutiny to examine the issue of abnormal increase in cash deposits during demonetization period as compared to average rate of cash deposited during pre-demonetization period. The assessee claimed that deposits made in bank account was with respect to cash sales made during the period of 1-1-2016 to 8-11-2016. The Assessing Officer examined submissions made by assessee in response to show cause notice and observed on verification of bills that all bills were of value less than Rs. 2 lakhs and assessee was not able to provide details of purchasers. He, thus, held that genuineness of sale bills could not be verified and the huge cash deposited in the bank was from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale. Accordingly, Assessing Officer invoked section 68 and cash deposited was added in income of assessee as undisclosed income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the additions made by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: The nature of business of the assessee is not disputed that he is engaged in the wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. It is also not in dispute that in this line of business sale of jewellery in cash is normal trade practice. The books of assessee are audited by the independent Chartered Accountant and copy of audit report and statement of profit and loss account is filed by the assessee. It is noted from the record that the case of the assessee was taken up for scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) on the basis of CASS and desired information by the Assessing Officer were submitted by the assessee from time-to-time. After completion of assessment the Assessing Officer vide his order assessed the income of the assessee by making a single addition of Rs. 80 lakh out of the total cash deposited being the demonetized currency for an amount of Rs. 84 lakh. The assessee is selling the jewellery in cash in past year also and the assessee in his submission explained that in fact in the year under consideration the overall sales as per cent to total sales has reduced. [Para 9]

The said sum is picked as unexplained as the assessee has deposited a sum of Rs. 84 lakhs being the demonetized currency in the bank account considering the sales shown by the assessee as not genuine. Out of total sales of Rs. 1.86 crores made in the year under consideration only a sum of Rs. 80 lakh not considered as genuine. The only reasons that was advanced that the details of the buyers showing complete name, address and phone were not verifiable. The sales shown by the assessee is supported by the following documents which were not doubted by Assessing Officer :

(a)

Bill wise detail in respect of cash sales during the period from 03-11-2016 to 8-11-2016, along with the sales sills. (b) Copy of the monthly summary of stock register. (c) Copy of sales register from the books of account of assessee for the relevant previous year. (d) Copy of cash book for the relevant previous year. (e) Copies of VAT return filed by the assessee, for the year under consideration. (f) Tax Audit Report Audited Financial Statements. [Para 9.1]

If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17] Assuming the revenue was right in its contention that the sale did not involve actual delivery of diamond jewellery, then unless it was established that the assessee had passed on his undisclosed income to T, it could not be said that the amount received by the assessee from T represented the undisclosed income of the assessee. Neither T in his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 had stated that the assessee had given the cash amount to T nor in the reassessment proceedings the Assessing Officer had gathered any evidence to that effect. Perusal of the reassessment order showed that the Assessing Officer had not made any efforts to link that the cash received and deposited by T in his bank account was, in fact, paid by the assessee. In those circumstances, in the absence of any cogent evidence brought on record, the decision of the Tribunal in holding that the Assessing Officer had failed to establish the nexus between the cash amount deposited in the bank account of T was attributable to the cheque issued by T in favour of the assessee could not be faulted. [Para 18]

In the instant case, cash credits were not introduced in the accounts of the assessee. From the fact that the cash credits were introduced in the accounts of T, it could not be inferred that the said cash belonged to the assessee. The assessee was not under any obligation to prove the cash credits in the accounts of 'T'. The assessee had proved that he was in possession of the diamond jewellery which was duly declared and certified under the VDIS, 1997. He had proved the identity of the person to whom the said diamond jewellery was sold, his creditworthiness and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from the sale of the diamond jewellery. [Para 19]

The sale transaction of diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 between the assessee and T had been accepted by the Sales Tax Authorities and the assessments made them had attained finality. In any event, in the facts of the instant case, the view taken by the Tribunal that the retracted statement of T was corroborated by the pay-in-slips/cash deposits in the bank account of T and the non-availability of the jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee to T was a reasonable and possible view. [Para 20]

Therefore, the appeal filed by the revenue was without any merit and was liable to be dismissed. [Para 21]

FACT: ■

During the search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced. HELD: ■

HEADNOTE: Section 68, read with section 69C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 - Assessee filed her return under VDIS, 1997 and declared sale proceeds of jewellery and diamonds received from two purchasers - Commissioner accepted return filed by assessee and issued certificate as envisaged under VDIS - At a later stage, searches were conducted on those purchasers in which they conceded before search party that no purchases were made by them and cheques were issued after taking cash through middlemen - On basis of said information, Assessing Officer reopened assessment and added sale proceeds of jewelleries to income of assessee under section 68 and he made further addition at rate of 3 per cent of both those amounts towards commission payment under section 69C - Commissioner (Appeals) found that no material was brought on record regarding payment of commission; statements of purchasers were not supplied to assessee and one purchaser had retracted from his statement given during course of investigation and deleted both additions made by Assessing Officer - Whether since findings of Commissioner (Appeals) were not controverted by revenue, and no other material was brought on record so that it could be established otherwise, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee filed her return under VDIS, 1997, in which she declared sale proceeds of jewellery and diamonds received from two purchasers ‘G’ and ‘T’. The Commissioner accepted the return filed by the assessee and issued the certificate as envisaged under the VDIS. At a later stage, searches were conducted on those purchasers in which they conceded before the search party that no purchases were made by them and cheques had been issued after taking cash through the middlemen. Later on ‘T’ retracted from his statement and confirmed that he had purchased jewellery from the assessee. On the basis of statements of both the purchasers, the Assessing Officer reopened the assessment and added the sale proceeds of jewelleries to the income of the assessee under section 68, and he made further addition at the rate of 3 per cent of both those amounts towards commission payments under section 69C. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted both the additions made by the Assessing Officer under sections 68 and 69C.

On revenue’s appeal :

The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering the order of the Assessing Officer in the light of submissions made before him and other materials on record had found that there was lot of discrepancies and contradictions in the facts of the case and the statements recorded under section 132(4) in the case of ‘G’.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]

However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified

Even those persons who responded to notice under section 133(6) could not substantiate the source of funds. Therefore, he rejected cash sales made during demonetisation period and taxed cash deposits under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

The nature of business of the assessee is not disputed that he is engaged in the wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. It is also not in dispute that in this line of business sale of jewellery in cash is normal trade practice. The books of assessee are audited by the independent Chartered Accountant and copy of audit report and statement of profit and loss account is filed by the assessee. It is noted from the record that the case of the assessee was taken up for scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) on the basis of CASS and desired information by the Assessing Officer were submitted by the assessee from time-to-time. After completion of assessment the Assessing Officer vide his order assessed the income of the assessee by making a single addition of Rs. 80 lakh out of the total cash deposited being the demonetized currency for an amount of Rs. 84 lakh. The assessee is selling the jewellery in cash in past year also and the assessee in his submission explained that in fact in the year under consideration the overall sales as per cent to total sales has reduced. [Para 9]

The said sum is picked as unexplained as the assessee has deposited a sum of Rs. 84 lakhs being the demonetized currency in the bank account considering the sales shown by the assessee as not genuine. Out of total sales of Rs. 1.86 crores made in the year under consideration only a sum of Rs. 80 lakh not considered as genuine. The only reasons that was advanced that the details of the buyers showing complete name, address and phone were not verifiable. The sales shown by the assessee is supported by the following documents which were not doubted by Assessing Officer :

(a)

Bill wise detail in respect of cash sales during the period from 03-11-2016 to 8-11-2016, along with the sales sills. (b) Copy of the monthly summary of stock register. (c) Copy of sales register from the books of account of assessee for the relevant previous year. (d) Copy of cash book for the relevant previous year. (e) Copies of VAT return filed by the assessee, for the year under consideration. (f) Tax Audit Report Audited Financial Statements. [Para 9.1]

The assessee by selling the goods in cash did not violate any provision of the Income-tax Act and even the. Assessing Officer has not mentioned any of the law provision to disbelieve the sales so made by the assessee. All the sales made by the assessee is supported by a commercial invoice duly complied with the value added tax (VAT) provision and the related VAT is also paid by the assessee. The invoices issued is also reported in VAT return filed and the sales has been accepted by the VAT authority without any adverse remark and in fact even the Assessing Officer has not made any adverse remark on the sales register and cash book submitted by the assessee to support the contentions of having been sold the goods/jewellery in cash. [Para 9.2]

The Assessing Officer accepted the opening stock, purchase, as well as the closing stock at the year-end to be genuine and correct. It is also worthwhile to mention that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and even there is no whisper in the order about any defects in the books of account. The Assessing Officer has not brought any material on record to establish that the sale bills were bogus or any evidences indicating that sales were bogus. The Assessing Officer is wrong in not accepting the declared cash sales as not verifiable which are recorded in books of account which were found to be correct and complete. It was also noted that the assessee has undertaken cash sales of Rs. 1.86 crores. Out of the total cash sales, cash sales amounting to Rs. 80 lakhs has been found to be non-genuine and added under section 68. Explanation offered to substantiate the cash sales has been arbitrarily rejected without holding that the sales is duly recorded in the books and is also supported by the various records produced in the assessment proceedings. [Para 9.5]

Respectfully following the consistent view and after considering the factual matrix of the cash on hand the addition made cannot be sustained and therefore, the addition of Rs. 80 lakhs made under section 68 is vacated as the same cannot be made without rejecting the books of account of the assessee regularly maintained by the assessee and the said cash deposited is duly supported by the entries passed in the books of account and part of the sale accepted by the Assessing Officer. [Para 9.8]

Insofar as purchases of old ornaments effected from its own customers, explanation of the assessee was that such purchases were effected on a condition that they purchased new jewellery from the assessee.

• As per the assessee, though such purchases were treated as cash purchases in its cash book, there was no payment in cash ever made, but, these were adjusted against sales effected to such parties by the assessee. In other words, according to assessee, it was only an exchange of new jewellery for old jewellery and differential amount alone was paid by the customers. The assessee also pointed out that in certain cases, the sale of new jewellery would happen on a day later to the purchase of old jewellery since new jewellery would be delivered to customers only after making changes suggested by the customers.

• The Assessing Officer opined that the payments effected in cash through its cash book against a number of purchases exceeded Rs. 20,000 and therefore, section 40A(3) was attracted while making said disallowance, explanation of the assessee that rule 6DD(d) saved it from rigours of section 40A(3), since purchase of old gold and diamonds and sale of new jewellery were from and to the same parties was rejected.

• According to Assessing Officer, argument of the assessee could be accepted only for purchases and sales effected on the same day, but, where such purchases were effected on one day and sale was effected on subsequent day and payments for such purchases were shown in the cash book as cash payments, section 40A(3) was to be applied.

• The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that at no point of time there were any cash payments effected by the assessee. The transactions were reflected in the cash book and ledger account for the purchases and sales as contras.

• He, thus, held that there was no outflow of cash and there was no justification for invoking section 40A(3).

On second appeal :

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

HEADNOTE: III. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash salary) - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on basis of statements of Nisha Singh and Ramesh Kundnani and extrapolated alleged cash salary uniformly across Assessment Years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - It was noted that no parallel payroll, cash sheets, vouchers, approvals or cash withdrawal trail was found and existence of expenditure was sought to be inferred solely from retracted statements - Whether since revenue failed to prove actual expenditure incurred by assessee, invocation of section 69C failed at threshold - Held, yes - Whether further, extrapolation of alleged cash salary payments across all assessment years, without any material showing similar payments in each year, was unsustainable - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash salary payments was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 82, 83 and 85] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

Pursuant to the search on 23-12-2023, the AO treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on the basis of statements of Nisha Singh (Rs. 30,000 per month) and Ramesh Kundnani (Rs. 1 lakh per month). Treating the aggregate monthly cash salary at Rs. 1.30 lakhs (Rs. 15.60 lakhs annually), the AO extrapolated the addition uniformly from AY 2015-16 to AY 2023-24, relying on Nisha Singh's cash deposits and rejecting both retractions. No parallel payroll, cash salary records, vouchers or cash trail was found.

■

On appeal, the assessee submitted that the search yielded no evidence of cash salary payments; Nisha Singh's retraction explained that the Rs. 30,000 represented remuneration of her brother, Vishal Singh, under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani routed through her, which the AO never verified; and Kundnani's retraction remained unrefuted. The CIT(A) held that no contemporaneous evidence established cash salary payments, the explanation regarding Vishal Singh was not investigated, the foundational requirement of proving expenditure under section 69C was absent, and the uniform extrapolation across years lacked year-wise evidence. The addition was deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and examined the entire material available on record. At the outset, it would be appropriate to observe that the revenue's case, when reduced to its essential components, rests solely upon the statements of two employees recorded during the course of search proceedings. There is no dispute that no document evidencing payment of cash salary was found during the search. There is no dispute that no parallel payroll register was recovered. There is no dispute that no employeewise cash salary sheets were discovered. There is no dispute that no vouchers, approvals, authorisations, electronic communications, payroll records or cash disbursement statements were found. In other words, despite an extensive search operation conducted in the case of the assessee company, the revenue has not brought on record a single contemporaneous document indicating existence of a parallel salary structure. This factual background assumes considerable importance because the addition sought to be made is not in relation to an isolated cash payment but on the premise that the assessee was maintaining a recurring system of salary payments outside its books of account. [Para 78]

■

The Tribunal shall first deal with the statement of Nisha Singh. The revenue seeks to rely upon her original statement to establish that she received Rs.30,000 per month in cash. However, the matter does not end with the original statement. The record reveals that she subsequently filed a retraction affidavit furnishing a specific and verifiable explanation. According to her, the amount in question pertained to her brother Vishal Singh, who was working on a part-time basis under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani, and the amount was routed through her and deposited in her bank account. Once such a specific explanation came on record, it became incumbent upon the Assessing Officer to examine its correctness. The revenue could easily have verified the role of Vishal Singh. It could have examined Inder Jaisinghani. It could have brought material demonstrating that the amount actually emanated from the assessee company. None of these steps were taken. Instead, the explanation was rejected without investigation. In the Tribunal's considered view, rejection of a specific factual explanation without any enquiry cannot elevate the original statement into conclusive evidence against the assessee. [Para 79]

[Para 11]

As per section 69A, if the assessee cash, bullion, jewellery or any valuable article etc. is found in possession of the assessee and failed to explain the source thereof. The same could be held as unexplained in the hands of the assessee. As it could be seen from the order of Assessing Officer, the cash in hand of Rs. 87.25 lakhs was duly recorded in the books of account as cash in hand of 18 group companies of the ACE Group and therefore, the source of the same is duly explained and cannot be held as unexplained. [Para 12]

■

It is further observed that the Commissioner (Appeals) has appreciated this fact and deleted the addition made which observations were not controverted by the revenue. [Para 13]

■

In view of these facts, there is no error in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in deleting the addition so made. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is upheld on this issue. [Para 14]

The source of cash of Rs. 2.69 crores found in the Lockers of Ankit Verma and Mohit Singh belonged to the assessee which was categorically admitted by both of them since beginning of the proceedings. With respect to the immediate source of the said cash, both the employees during the course of search and in post search proceedings, before the Investigation Wing has admitted that the immediate sources of this cash was from the sales of left over construction material comprising of bricks, sand etc. left at the work site of project Gardenia Grace, sector-61, Noida which were sold during the period of July, 2021 to October, 2021. Further in order to secure the payments, cash was preferred by the assessee. It is further observed that the cash received from the sales have duly been recorded in the books of accounts maintained in regular course and duly reported in GST returns filed by the assessee. The assessee further filed the details with respect to the sales made to the parties who had confirmed the transactions with the assessee in their replies directly filed before the AO. The copy of their ITRs and other particulars of buyers are placed at pages 182 to 191 of PB. It is further observed that the sales declared, has been accepted by the revenue and profits declared were assessed without raising any doubts. [Para 8]

■

The revenue has failed to controvert the findings given by the CIT(A) by placing any contrary material or evidence through which the observations of the CIT(A) could be rebutted. It is observed that the CIT(A) has very categorically observed that goods were sold and was duly recorded in the books of accounts and further GST collected on the said payments was also deposited in due course as per law. When the entire transactions of sales of goods is duly backed by the stock and was recorded in the books of accounts which have been accepted without raising any doubts, section 69A could not be invoked. [Para 9]

■

In view of the above discussion and by respectfully following the judgement of the Delhi High Court in the case of Pr. CIT v. Akshit Kumar [2021] 124 taxmann.com 123/277 Taxman 423 (Delhi), it is viewed that the CIT(A) has rightly deleted the additions made by the AO and this cannot be interfered in the order of the CIT(A) deleting the additions made and therefore the order of the CIT(A) is hereby, confirmed. All the Grounds of appeal raised by the revenue are thus, dismissed. [Para 10]

In the result, appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 11]

On both the counts, the Pr. Commissioner is totally incorrect. A bare perusal of the assessment order reveals that this aspect of cash deposit during the demonetization was thoroughly inquired into by the Assessing Officer and the assessee had repeatedly maintained that the cash deposited was on account of cash sales made by it. The assessment order reveals that the assessee had submitted comparative figures of sales made by it in the preceding and succeeding years and demonstrated huge turnover averaging Rs. 20-30 crores. He had also submitted comparative details of cash component of total sales reflecting the fact that the cash component was approx. more than 90 per cent of the turnover. The assessee had further demonstrated the fact of increase in sales in the impugned year by showing that its business had shown an increasing trend from year to year right from assessment year 2014-15 to assessment year 2018-19 including the year of demonetization i.e. financial year 2016-17. A search was conducted at the business and residential premises of the assessee-firm wherein cash of Rs. 1,56,380 was found from rooms of different family members and Rs. 26,910 from business premises. The Assessing Officer considered the entire cash found as unexplained by holding that the assessee did not produce any evidence either at the time of search or in post search proceedings or at the time of assessment proceedings. He, considered Rs. 26,910 found at the business premises and Rs. 16,460 found from the room of children aggregating to Rs. 43,370 as unexplained in the hands of the assessee and the remaining amount in the hands of the different family members. He further held that as per statement of VK, the son of the assessee Rs. 2.75 lakhs was given on the previous day to one ‘S’ for purchase of material, source of which also remained unexplained. He, therefore, treated cash of Rs. 3,18,370 (26,910+16,460+2,75,000) as unexplained in the hands of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that from the cash flow statement it was seen that no withdrawals for the household expenses had been shown by the assessee in the current year and expenditure shown by rest of family members were insufficient and if the appropriate amount of cash outgoing was taken for the purpose of household expenses then remaining cash balance with the assessee and other family members would be very small. He, therefore, confirmed the addition for Rs. 26,910. The amount with the children was accepted in view of their petty savings. As regards the source of Rs. 2.75 lakhs given to ‘S’, he held that sufficient cash was available in the books of account of the assessee to make the payment of Rs. 2.75 lakhs to ‘S’. On cross appeal :

■

The entire addition of Rs.9.60 crores pertains to cash found deposited in the bank account of the assessee during demonetization period which the Assessing Officer held to have remained unexplained. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) reveals that he has noted some factual findings in relation to this issue leading to his conclusion that the source of cash deposit in the bank account of the assessee during demonetization period stood duly explained. The pertinent finding in this regard are with respect to the fact that the assessee had furnished all evidences proving the genuineness of sales made during this period duly supported with purchases made which were further evidenced by the copy of VAT returns filed by the assessee and also the stock records of the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that notices issued by the Assessing Officer to all parties from whom purchases were made by the assessee under section 133(6) were duly responded and the parties confirmed the sales made to the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has further noted that there is no abnormality in the quantum of sales made by the assessee in the impugned year as compared to the preceding year noting the fact that the component of cash sales had decreased by almost 87.96 per cent in the entire year; in the period preceding demonetization it was noted to have decreased by 88.54 per cent and during the demonetization period to have decreased by 65.56 per cent. The Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that neither the Auditor has pointed out any discrepancy in the accounts of the assessee nor has the Assessing Officer rejected the books of the assessee under section 145(3). He has noted the stock position depicted in the books of the assessee to have been accepted by the Assessing Officer. [Para 5]

■

All these facts noted by the Commissioner (Appeals), establish the genuineness of the cash deposited in the bank account of the assessee to have come out of cash sales made by the assessee during the course of business. The above facts have not been controverted by the revenue also. [Para 6]

■

In view of the detailed reasoning of the Commissioner (Appeals) based on uncontroverted facts, holding the source of cash deposited in the bank account to be out of cash sales, there is no reason to interfere in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) deleting the addition made of Rs.9.60 crores. FACT: Assessee company was engaged in jewellery business, selling jewellery items to its retail customers.

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer required the assessee to justify the deposits of cash in the bank accounts during the period of demonetization.

In response, the assessee filed detailed explanation along with all the books of account, sale and purchase vouchers, stock statement, etc., and also had given the reasons for the cash deposits along with cash book.

The Assessing Officer noted that immediately after the demonetization, the assessee had shown inflated cash sales and also made deposits in the bank account which was completely abnormal as compared to the earlier year and also subsequent year. Apart from that, the assessee could not substantiate cash sales made to different parties and some of them could not be identified. Even those persons who responded to notice under section 133(6) could not substantiate the source of funds. Therefore, he rejected cash sales made during demonetisation period and taxed cash deposits under section 68.

On revenue's appeal :

■

The Assessing Officer proceeded to make the total cash deposit made by the assessee during demonetization period since assessee could not submit the relevant cash deposit made by the assessee during the impugned year as well as previous year during the assessment proceeding. Since there was no information available with him, he proceeded to make the whole cash deposits as addition. In appeal, assessee filed additional evidences before the first appellate authority. In remand proceedings, after considering the additional evidences and other details submitted before the Assessing Officer, the Assessing Officer observed that assessee has achieved cash sales of Rs.36.54 crores and cash deposit of Rs.35.83 crores and the difference of Rs.71.40 lakhs with the assessee. He observed that assessee may have meet out the same in running the business. Accordingly, he assumed that cash balance was utilised for business expenses as dairy business being cash intensified enterprise. After observing the above, he further observed that during demonetization, assessee has deposited Rs.4.79 crores whereas achieved the total cash sales during the period of Rs.4.25 crores, therefore there is a difference of Rs.53.51 lakhs. Therefore, the assessee failed to furnish any explanation. The Commissioner (Appeals) also proceeded to sustain the above addition without considering the actual facts on record. Before demonetization i.e. on 7-11-2016, the assessee had closing cash balance which was not considered by the lower authorities and also they themselves observed that there is a difference of Rs.71.39 lakhs pre-demonetization period from the total cash sales and cash deposited by the assessee. They presumed that the abovesaid difference must have been utilised by the assessee for business purpose without duly verifying the cash book maintained by the assessee. Since they proceeded to sustain the addition arbitrarily without actually verifying the cash book maintained by the assessee. When the total cash sales and total cash deposit made by the assessee during the year is looked at, it clearly shows that assessee has made total cash sales of Rs.48.03 crores and made the cash deposit of Rs.47.45 crores. Therefore, there is absolutely no justification for making the abovesaid addition under section 68. Considering the above facts on record, the grounds raised by the assessee are to be allowed. [Para 9]

In the result, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed.

■

The limited controversy that arises for consideration is whether, on the facts of the present case, the addition of alleged cash payment in relation to purchase of shop at "Platinum Mall" can be sustained solely on the basis of third-party digital records and statements, without providing the assessee an effective opportunity to confront such material.

■

It is undisputed that the entire foundation of the impugned addition consists of: (i) Excel sheets found in a pen drive seized from IA, a third party containing name, shop number and amount of the cash, and (ii) his statement admitting receipt of cash on behalf of the Rubberwala Group and that cash was being handed over to director of the company TS. [Para 8.1]

■

On the basis of the said material and the statements of key person from their premises, the said company has accepted the fact of the on-money received in cash and declared 8 per cent of the net profit for undisclosed income. No independent evidence has been brought on record to demonstrate actual payment of cash by the assessee. There is no receipt, no diary, no acknowledgment, no contemporaneous document, and no corroborative evidence linking the assessee to the alleged cash payment, apart from the third-party record. [Para 8.2]

■

But the issue arises is whether the material found in possession of the third party, statement of the third party and the disclosure made by them, bind the assessee for the addition without providing opportunity of confronting the material to the assessee. [Para 8.3]

■

In the case assessment has been initiated under section 153C and under the provisions of section 153C material pertaining to the assessee which is basis of the recording of satisfaction under section 153C must have been forwarded to the Assessing Officer of the assessee. But despite specific request by the assessee no such material was provided to the assessee. The assessee also sought for the opportunity to cross-examine IA but both the Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) has declined on the ground that it was not the sole basis for making addition. But it is found that no other evidence has been brought on record by the lower authorities to substantiate that the cash on-money was actually paid by the assessee to IA except confession of IA. [Para 8.4]

■

The assessee submitted that said Rubberwala Group has credited 100 per cent cash in its books of accounts against offering 8 per cent of income on such declaration. In other words, they have generated huge amount of income in their hands at 33 per cent of tax on the 8 per cent income of the cash declared. For example, if the assessee get credited Rs.100 in its books of account against cash received then it has paid taxes at the rate of 33 per cent on Rs.8 which work out to Rs.2.6. The assessee submitted that this was one of the beneficial declaration and therefore, they have admitted and paid the taxes. The assessee submitted that the assessee has never paid such cash on-money and it might be their own money which they had brought into books in garb of cash on-money for tax benefit. [Para 8.5]

■

It is opined that though the Rubberwala Group has admitted receipt of unaccounted cash and offered a percentage thereof to tax, such admission by the seller cannot, by itself, fasten liability upon the purchaser unless there is cogent evidence establishing that the purchaser actually made such payment. The disclosure by the developer may explain the source of its own funds, but it does not dispense with the burden on the revenue to prove the assessee's investment or expenditure. [Para 8.6]

■

The assessee specifically brought to attention that IA in his answer to question No. 13 of the statement dated 17-3-2021 stated that after receipt of alleged cash from the customers a small diary was being used to provide containing cash details received from the customers. The assessee submitted that no such diary has been recovered from the assessee nor any kind of receipt issued by Rubberwala Group having signature of the assessee has been found from the premises of the Rubberwala group or from the assessee. The assessee submitted that in the case of one of the customer Rajesh Jain search was conducted by the Department but no such document in the form of diary was found which could corroborate statement of IA. According to him, IA cooked up a story of cash on-money in his statement for benefiting interest of their company. [Para 8.7]

INCOME TAX : Where assessee during demonetization deposited substantial amount of cash in banks and claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers which were subsequently converted into sales of jewellery, since said trade advances were subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills,

The assessee was a limited liability partnership engaged in the business of resale of jewellery, diamond and other related items. A search operation was conducted in the K group of cases. Notice under section 153A was issued to the assessee and in response to the notice, the assessee filed its return declaring an income of Rs. 22.53 lakhs.

During the course of assessment proceedings the Assessing Officer observed that the assessee had deposited Rs. 2.90 crores post-demonetisation in its account and that during the course of search, books of account and sales bill books relating to the demonetisation period and pre-demonetisation period were verified which revealed that the assessee was maintaining its books of account in the computer of its accountant. The Assessing Officer further observed that on examination of the digital data it was noticed that there were two sets of books of account, i.e., one in the computer of the accountant and another in the pen drive of the accountant. On comparison of the two accounts it was found that there was a difference in the sale figures for the month of October, 2016 as cash sales were increased in one set of books of account. On appeal to the Tribunal :

■

Investigations following a search on a land aggregator (LCPL) led to seizure of electronic Evernote records and statements indicating cash payments to landowners at Madambakkam. A search at the assessee’s premises followed. In relation to the 1.41-acre sale registered at about Rs.1.27 crores, the assessee’s statement under section 132(4) acknowledged total consideration of about Rs.5.99 crores including about Rs.4.72 crores in cash; during cross-examination on 10.08.2021 of the aggregator’s director, he maintained cash payment of Rs.4.72 crores, while the assessee disputed the quantum and, in a revised computation, admitted only Rs.84.60 lakhs as cash. In another Madambakkam sale of about 2.12 acres registered at about Rs.1.91 crores, the assessee’s statement recorded cash receipt of about Rs.6.78 crores.

■

For the 1.41-acre sale, the AO issued a show-cause to tax about Rs.4.72 crores cash and, relying on the assessee’s section 132(4) admission, corroborative seized materials and the cross-examined witness’s confirmation, added the full Rs.4.72 crores to the consideration. For the 2.12-acre sale, based on seized material and statements, the AO concluded total consideration at about Rs.8.91 crores (about Rs.1.91 crores by banking channels and about Rs.6.99 crores in cash) and made a corresponding addition to long-term capital gains.

On appeal, the CIT(A), for the 1.41-acre sale, relied on Evernote entries identifying the assessee and quantifying cash at about Rs.4.72 crores, the aggregator’s statements explaining contemporaneous recording and cash flows, and the assessee’s section 132(4) statement and subsequent admission letter; treating the later claim of only Rs.84.60 lakhs as a belated, unsupported retraction, the CIT(A) confirmed inclusion of about Rs.4.72 crores as on-money. Evernote data were unilateral third-party records without proof of actual cash movement.
