INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order passed by High Court that where assessee made purchase of Jewellery worth Rs. 34.48 crores in cash by submitting that a group of bidders formed a syndicate and participated in auction and after successful bidding, money from prospective purchasers were collected and same was remitted to 'M' Ltd., since assessee could not demonstrate that he was representing any syndicate and, moreover, he also failed to demonstrate a situation

■

During the search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced. Statements of the assessee’s executives recorded under section 132(4) acknowledged planning a cash component of Rs.25 crores and indicated that Rs.7 crores had been paid, alongside Rs.75 crores towards share capital and unsecured loans. A cash receipt for Rs.5 crores dated 11-10-2020 signed by the counterparty was also found.

■

Relying on the seized note, the cash receipt and statements, the AO held that Rs.7 crores had been paid in cash in connection with the transaction and treated it as unexplained expenditure under section 69C. The assessee’s denial of cash exchange was not accepted, and the addition of Rs.7 crores was made. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition under section 69C.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

■

There is no dispute with regard to the amount of cash deposits into her bank account during the demonetization period and the explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of opening cash balance available as on 8-11-2016 as per the cash book maintained for the relevant financial year. In fact, the Assessing Officer never disputed the fact that the assessee has explained the cash deposit into the bank account out of cash balance available as per books of account. The Assessing Officer disbelieved the arguments of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of sales declared from 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016 and claimed that, there is abnormal deviation in the sales declared by the assessee for the above period when compared to the earlier months and subsequent months. The Assessing Officer further noted that, the assessee has furnished VAT returns belatedly to cover up the backdated sale bills issued to the customers to show sufficient cash balance in the books of account to explain cash deposits into the bank account. Therefore, he disbelieved the evidences filed by the assessee and assessed the cash deposits as unexplained money under section 69A. [Para 19]

■

There is no dispute with regard to the fact that, the cash balance shown in the books of account as on 8-11-2016 is supported by necessary sales bills issued towards sale of jewellery from 1-11-2016 to 7-11-2016. It is also not in dispute that, the assessee was having sufficient stock-in-hand to explain the sale bills issued to the customers between 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016. The sales declared by the assessee are recorded in the books of account and also part of the turnover declared for the year under consideration which suffered taxation. Once the assessee has recorded sales in the books of account, which is supported by necessary sales bills with a corresponding stock-in-hand, the Assessing Officer ought not to have made additions towards cash deposits as unexplained money only on the ground that, there is abnormal variation in cash sales during the demonetization period when compared to earlier or subsequent periods. It was a well-known fact during the demonetization period that, there was a mad rush in jewellery shops for purchasing gold jewellery out of demonetized currency when the demonetization was announced on 8-11-2016. In the instant case, going by the facts available on record, the assessee has reported major sales on 7-11-2016, which is the previous day of the demonetization was announced, and from the details furnished by the assessee, it is very clear that, the assessee has made sales of gold jewellery in cash which is the source for cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period on 14-11-2016. Since the cash deposited into the bank account is supported by necessary cash balance available as per books of account maintained by the assessee which was further supported by necessary sales bills, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards cash deposits under section 69A as unexplained money cannot be sustained. Although the Assessing Officer has disbelieved the sales on the basis of VAT returns submitted by the assessee for the month of November, 2016 and claimed that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover backdated sales, but going by the history of the assessee in filing the VAT returns, it is evident that, for all the months in the financial year 2016-17, the assessee has filed VAT returns belatedly and from the above, it is very clear that, the argument of the Assessing Officer that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover up backdated sales, is contrary to the evidence available on record and cannot be accepted. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A. Thus, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made under section 69A. [Para 20]

The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

HEADNOTE: II. Section  68,  read with sections  69A  and  153A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/Section  102,  read with section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash credit (Unaccounted sales)  - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Assessing Officer, relying on parallel Tally data, WhatsApp chats and statements of Sunrise/SP Group personnel, alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash sales to SP Group aggregating Rs. 980.15 crores and brought profit at 14.75 per cent to tax - Assessee contended that entire case rested on third-party material; no incriminating evidence was found during search on assessee; and SP Group, by clarification and retraction affidavits, stated that cash transactions related to third parties and open-market purchases, not assessee - Whether since revenue failed to establish through cogent independent evidence that assessee was source of goods reflected in third-party records or recipient of alleged cash consideration, addition was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 68] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

A search was conducted on 23-12-2023 in the case of the assessee-company and connected persons. Separately, search in the Sunrise/SP Group yielded parallel Tally data ('Ka', 'Km' and 'CN'), coded ledgers, WhatsApp chats and statements. Relying solely on this third-party material, the AO alleged unaccounted cash sales by the assessee to the SP Group aggregating about Rs. 980.15 crores, applied an average profit margin of 14.75 per cent and taxed the profit element. The AO further alleged that Rs. 432.27 crores was routed to the assessee through Rashmikant Amin and Rs. 547.88 crores was paid towards the assessee's expenses, relying on coded ledger references such as 'Shankarbhai' and 'CKP'.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that the entire case rested on third-party material; no incriminating evidence was found during its search; the coded ledgers did not name the assessee; and the SP Group, by clarification dated 17-4-2024 and retraction affidavits, stated that the cash transactions related to third parties and open-market purchases, not the assessee. The AO neither examined the named third parties nor established any cash trail to the assessee. The CIT(A), noting absence of discrepancies in stock, production, dispatches or books, no undisclosed assets, and no beneficiary linkage between the 'Rashmi Amin' ledger and the assessee, deleted the profit addition.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

■

On examination of the assessee’s submissions, it is observed that the assessee had set up its business in the financial year 2015-16 and made sales of Rs.13.52 crores during the year. This had increased to Rs.49.49 crores in the financial year relevant to the assessment year in question and further increased to Rs.73.71 crores in the subsequent financial year. Thus, it is evident that the business of the assessee was an expanding business and the sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over the years. It is also observed that the assessee had an opening stock of jewellery worth Rs.4.69 crores on the 1-4- 2016. The assessee has furnished before the Assessing Officer the month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and the movement in the stock position. From the same, it is seen that on the 1-10-2016, the assessee had stock worth Rs.13.08 crores in its possession and that when viewed against the closing stock of Rs.9.54 crores as on 31-10-2016, had depleted a substantial amount of that stock by way of sales. The details of stock, purchases and sales that have been submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer have not been questioned or doubted in any manner by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, only because the month of October, 2016 saw a spurt in cash sales below the limit of Rs.2 lakhs, for which the assessee was not in a position to furnish details of purchasers, the sales made by the assessee cannot be doubted unless the purchases, sales and stock depletion are also cast into doubt. With regard to the argument that the assessee had not submitted the sales invoices to the Assessing Officer, it is observed that unless there is a finding that the stocks were not available or were diverted elsewhere, sales claimed out of those stocks cannot be doubted. The Assessing Officer has based his additions on the belief that there exists a possibility of manipulating the exact date of sale on account of the requirement of filing of VAT return for October, 2016 on 20-11-2016, but it is observed that first of all, in this case, all the cash from sales was deposited on 10-11-2016 leaving lesser scope for manipulation but even if that were so, it would not take the credits on account of those sales in his books outside the purview of sales receipts, unless it could be shown that the sales had not occurred or that the assessee did not have the stock to sell that which he claimed to have sold. It is observed that the assessee presented the cash book before the Assessing Officer and the Assessing Officer could not find any discrepancy in the same. Therefore, the credits made in the said cash book on account of cash sales, remain uncontroverted. In the circumstances, considering that the assessee has presented evidence of available stock and depletion of the said stock on account of sales and the Assessing Officer has not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of the receipts on account of the sale of that stock are unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 is made out. Therefore, the decision to delete the addition of Rs.2.99 crores on this account is upheld. [Para 10]

one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

The main issue in instant appeal is addition made under section 69. [Para 15]

■

It is clear from decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that he has adopted theory of peak credit to sustain addition of Rs.4 crore and allowed relief of Rs.32.17 crores. Peak credit theory applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) is not acceptable since the Commissioner (Appeals) has not brought on record peculiar facts of case which compelled him to apply peak credit theory in picture. The Commissioner (Appeals) has simply taken amount of highest balance in the bank account and has treated it as ''''peak credit'''', which is not correct. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to take note that from 17 date-wise transactions, it can be observed that the cash deposits were made and then cheques were issued. It is not the case that cash was first deposited from which cash was withdrawn and same remained unutilized for subsequent deposit. The determination of the peak credit cannot be applied in case of appellant because of following reasons: (i) where there are cash deposits but withdrawals are through the cheques then benefit of the peak credit cannot be allowed for the cash deposit so made in bank account. In the assessee''''s case, against the cash deposits cheques were issued to some other entities. (ii) As amount of the cash credits were standing in the names of different persons which all along assessee had been claiming as genuine deposit, withdrawal/payment of amount to different set of persons would not at all entitle applicant to claim benefit of peak credits. [Para 15.1]

■

While determining the peak credit, the withdrawal of cash, if not utilized elsewhere, is considered as available for making the deposits. The highest unexplained cash deposit is considered as the peak credit. determination of the peak credit reduces taxable income. However, where withdrawal are through cheques, the benefits of those withdrawals will not be available to explain deposits. Therefore, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) to allow the peak credit to the assessee was not correct. [Para 15.2]

■

The appellant claimed to have sold gold bullion during demonetization period and demonetized currency was deposited in bank account of ''''N''''. The Commissioner (Appeals) has formed a hypothesis to decide case on the peak credit principle and restrict the addition to Rs.4 crore and delete the addition of Rs.32.17 crores. However, on facts of the case nowhere the assessee had been able to conclusively establish that he had made genuine sales during demonetization period from 10-11-2016 till date of survey on 23-12-2016 nor names have been furnished by the assessee before the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals)/CBI/ED. Significantly, neither revenue nor the appellant have requested to apply principle of the peak credit inthe instant case. In fact, the assessee itself has raised a ground to delete addition of Rs.4 crore based on peak credit principle. [Para 15.3]

■

The revenue took plea that survey by Department has established that the falsification of accounts had happened because the sale invoices were booked in the name of NC which was proved to be a bogus entity during survey proceedings and in subsequent proceedings before department. Further, mere payments made by cheques or RTGS does not establish that said gold was received immediately and same was serially and genuinely sold to unknown 2200 purchasers against demonetized currency notes. Even survey could not find evidence of such series of sale by the assessee or commensurate stock of gold and silver at known business premises. The net effect of cash deposited in the bank account of NC and subsequent cheques/RTGS payment is nothing but attempt to convert hoarded undisclosed income of the assessee into the stock of gold for future sales. Under these circumstances, granting benefit of peak credit to the assessee is not warranted. [Para 15.4]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) has considered that the transaction in the bank account of NC relates to the assessee and has accordingly, given benefit to the assessee by restricting the addition in the case. The assessee has not been able to explain as to how almost all cash deposited in bank account of NC were immediately transferred to bank account of assessee. [Para 15.5]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals), whose powers are co-terminus with that of the Assessing Officer should have examined the facts of case, which he failed to do. Considering totality of facts and circumstances of the case and once it is established that the assessee cannot be allowed benefit of the peak credit, the cash deposited in bank account of the assessee remains unexplained as the assessee has not been able to explain nature and source of such cash deposits along with the documentary evidence either before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 15.6]

, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes FACT: The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. HELD: ■

■

It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer has accepted the transactions about purchase and sale of jewellery in gold and silver without raising any doubt regarding books of account, purchase and sale stock registers and the bills produced by the assessee. The cash transaction before the demonetisation period was also revealed by the assessee as the period before the demonetisation was also the period of Diwali and that itself shows that why the cash transaction took place in that particular period. Addition for unexplained cash payment on jewellery purchase unsustainable as no incriminating evidence found in search: ITAT

material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

■ The failure of the Assessing Officer to examine the land sellers is perhaps the most serious infirmity in the addition. Where the allegation is that the assessee paid cash consideration over and above the registered value, the most natural witness would be the seller of the land. If the allegation were correct, the seller would be the recipient of the alleged on-money. Yet, not a single seller has been examined. No seller has admitted receipt of cash. No statement of any vendor has been recorded. No enquiry has been conducted into the books, bank accounts, assets or conduct of the sellers. No document has been found from any seller indicating receipt of consideration outside the registered document. In the absence of examination of the alleged recipients of cash, the allegation remains one-sided and untested. [Para 98]

■

The registered sale documents and stamp duty valuation also assume great significance. The assessee has demonstrated that the lands at Halol were purchased at values equal to or higher than the stamp duty/circle rates. This factual position has not been rebutted by the Assessing Officer. The transactions were registered, the consideration was recorded in the books of account and payments were made through banking channels. When registered documents disclose consideration not below the statutory valuation adopted for stamp duty purposes, and no seller disputes the stated consideration, the revenue cannot presume payment of additional cash merely on the basis of a general statement. The normal suspicion of undervaluation itself becomes weak in such circumstances. If despite this, the Revenue alleges payment of on-money, the allegation must be supported by direct and cogent evidence. That is completely absent here. [Para 99]

■

The WhatsApp chats relied upon by the Assessing Officer also do not advance the revenue's case. The CIT(A) has examined these chats and found that they do not contain any reference to actual payment of cash in relation to Halol land transactions. They do not record any completed payment. They do not contain any admission by the assessee or acknowledgement by any seller. They do not identify any amount paid in cash. They do not establish movement of money. More importantly, the chats pertain to a proposed land transaction at Valsad, whereas the additions have been made in respect of land purchased at Halol. No addition has been made in respect of Valsad. Therefore, even if the chats are accepted at their highest, they are evidentiary neutral for the purpose of the Halol land additions. A communication relating to one proposed transaction cannot be used to estimate cash payment in entirely different registered transactions without any connecting material. [Para 100]

■

The search perspective also supports the assessee's case. The allegation concerns payment of cash consideration in land transactions. If such payment had actually been made, one would ordinarily expect some trace of it either from the assessee's premises, from the employee allegedly involved, from the recipient seller or from the person alleged to have arranged or delivered the cash. However, no cash ledger, no on-money sheet, no seller acknowledgement, no loose paper, no payment trail, no cash flow record and no documentary evidence of any nature has been found. The alleged roles of Shri Chirag Shah, Shri Inder Jaisinghani and Smt. Parul Patel also remain unsubstantiated by any independent material. In a search assessment, where the Department has the benefit of seized records and statements, addition cannot be made merely by estimating a percentage on registered transaction value without first establishing the factum of actual cash payment. [Para 101]

■

The methodology adopted by the Assessing Officer in estimating 20 percent of the agreement value as unexplained expenditure is also legally unsustainable. No basis has been given for adopting 20 percent uniformly. No comparable transaction has been cited. No seller-wise material exists. No land-wise evidence exists. No year-wise evidence exists. The statement itself, even as relied upon by the Assessing Officer, refers to a general range of 15 percent to 20 percent and not to actual payment in any specific case. Estimation may have a role where the foundational fact of expenditure is proved and only quantification remains uncertain. Here, however, the foundational fact itself is unproved. Therefore, estimation cannot substitute evidence. [Para 102]

■

Section 69C requires three foundational conditions. First, there must be material to show that an expenditure has actually been incurred. Second, such expenditure must be shown to have been incurred by the assessee. Third, the assessee must fail to explain the source of such expenditure. In the present case, the Revenue has not crossed the first threshold itself. Actual cash expenditure has not been proved. Incurrence by the assessee has not been proved. The alleged recipient has not been identified through evidence. Once the expenditure itself is not established, the question of explaining its source does not arise. Therefore, the invocation of section 69C fails at the very threshold. [Para 103]

The assessee had deposited the cash out of cash sales recorded during the period October, November and December 2016. The reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer to reject the reasons for such cash deposits are out of cash sales by observing that the cash is nothing but undisclosed funds of the assessee and it has manipulated the cash sales to make such cash deposits. From the records it is observed that the Assessing Officer neither rejected the book results or method of account adopted by the assessee. The Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) has not found any discrepancies in the method of accounting, margin declared by the assessee which are in consonance with the previous periods. The Assessing Officer did not have any material against the assessee but made the addition merely on the basis his perception that the same is only out of assessee’s undisclosed income. [Para 13]

■

On the other hand, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also sustained the addition made by the Assessing Officer by observing that the stock register is not maintained and purchase/sales are not substantiated with sales bills or names and address of the customers or not provided confirmations from the customers. Further, he has proceeded to sustain the addition under section 69A against the additions made by the Assessing Officer under section 68. As regards the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee has not maintained the stock register, it is observed that the assessee is engaged in trading of general purpose machinery parts/bearings. The method of maintenance of stock registers and other related records depends upon the nature of business, particularly in the line of business the assessee is into, it is dealing with the spare parts and bearings, which the assessee is purchasing from the industries and selling the same in the retail market. The value of each bills may be less than Rs. 20,000/-. It is difficult to maintain the stock register item wise and considering the frequent movement of stocks, it may not be practical for the assessee to maintain the same. As submitted by the assessee that it reconciles the stock movement at the end of each month with the physical quantity. It cannot be denied based on the nature of industry it is into. What is important and relevant, is the stock reconciliation of each item and whether the same is certified by the statutory auditor before finalizing the accounts. In this case, it is observed that the same was submitted before the authorities below. The Commissioner (Appeals) has not found anything suspicious in the method of accounting in the recording of sales nor stock keeping but merely expressed his view on the contrary but failed to appreciate the nature of business and how difficult to maintain the several stock keeping units(sku) involved in this industry. Therefore, the observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) is impractical. [Para 14]

■

Coming to the other issue of non-substantiation of sale bills with the names and address of the customers, it is observed from the sale bills and cash register submitted by the assessee that each cash bill is with the value which varies from Rs. 5000 to 18000. When the value is less than Rs. 20,000/- there is no requirement for any assessee to maintain such details like name of the customer and address. This requirement raised by the Commissioner (Appeals) is also not practical, mere his opinion. [Para 15]

■

The actual issues raised by the Assessing Officer are that the assessee has recorded sales only during the demonetization period and there is no history of such cash sales in the earlier period. Based on the above observation, he was of the view that the assessee has introduced its own undisclosed cash into the system and booked the cash sales without there being any cash sales. This can be traced if at all the assessee has introduced such unaccounted money into the system, it will show from the financial results or parameters where it can be deducted with: Abnormal profit, No stock movement and Recording of excess sales. From the information submitted, all the purchase and sales are properly recorded in the books and also substantiated by the information submitted before the GST officials and relevant quarterly reports. There is absolutely no discrepancies found by the lower authorities either in the stock registers submitted or quarterly reports submission before the GST authorities. [Para 16]

■

From the financial results declared by the assessee in the last three years: Assessment year 2015-16 GP Ratio 7.10% NP Ratio 0.35% Assessment year 2016-17 7.14% 0.40% Assessment year 2017-18 7.27% 0.31%, it is clear that the results declared by the assessee is within the range of book results. The lower authorities has not made any adverse comments nor found any deviations in the book results. [Para 17]

Any additions made by the Assessing Officer under sections 69A or 69C would be justified only if it is established that certain amounts, such as funds mobilized through 'B' of Rs. 39.22 lakhs under section 69A, interest payments on these funds of Rs. 42.30 lakhs under section 69C, and unexplained money of Rs. 81,230 under section 69A are not reflected in the cash flow statement. [Para 136]

■

Under the law, the Assessing Officer cannot simultaneously rely on the peak credit balance method and make independent additions for the same amounts. If income has already been offered and accounted for based on the peak credit balance, independent additions for the same amounts in the relevant assessment year are not permissible. [Para 137]

■

The computation of additional income by determining the peak credit balances in the cash flow statement is a widely accepted and reliable method of recognizing revenue. [Para 138]

■

Furthermore, the additions made under sections 69A and 69C are already reflected in the income offered under the concept of 'Peak Credit Balance'— Rs. 6.35 crores for all assessment years from assessment year 2014-15 to assessment year 2022-23, together with Rs. 4.82 crores offered on account of the land sale totalling Rs. 11.18 crores. Therefore, separate additions under these sections for the year under consideration would result in double taxation of the same income, which is not permissible under law. [Para 141]

■

The fact with regard to the impugned dispute are that the assessee has deposited a sum in specified bank notes during demonetization period to the bank account. In response to notice under section 142(1), the assessee had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period. The stock moved out of the books on account of sales made by the assessee has been established from stock registers. The VAT returns and annual audit report under TNVAT Act for the relevant period reflected such sales which have been accepted by the VAT authorities. The assessee has maintained proper books of account which are subjected to tax audit under section 44AB. The assessee also maintained quantitative details of the stock of Gems, Gold and Diamond separately and furnished before the lower authorities, which have not been rejected. The books of account of the assessee have been accepted by the lower authorities while framing the assessment and not rejected by pointing out any defects. [Para 8]

■

On perusal of the records and facts and circumstances of the case, it is opined that when the sale has been reflected in the books of account and offered to tax, adding the same again would amount to double taxation, which is impermissible in law. The cash sales made by the assessee have been credited in the books of account and the same form part of the assessee’s cash book. On these facts, it could be very well said that the assessee claim was backed up by relevant evidences. Thus, the assessee has discharged the burden of proving the source of the cash/SBN deposited in the bank and the Assessing Officer failed to rebut the same. Further, it is also noted that the assessee has sold only 17.50 per cent on 8-11-2016 out of the stock held before the demonetisation day. The allegations/statistics relied upon by Assessing Officer to take an adverse view is not backed up by relevant evidence/material and therefore the action of Assessing Officer, which has been rightly set aside by the Commissioner (Appeals) and hence cannot be interfered. The finding of the Assessing Officer that such abnormal sales could not be achieved immediately upon announcement of demonetization by the Government are bereft of any concrete evidence to prove otherwise on record. It is trite law that no addition could be made merely on the basis of suspicion, conjectures and surmises. Moreover, since cash generated out of sales has been credited in the books of account, the provisions of section 69A could not be invoked in the present case. [Para 9]

■

Therefore, on the given facts, the impugned additions are not sustainable in the eyes of law and hence, the action of the Commissioner (Appeals) in deleting the addition need not be interfered and hence the grounds raised by the revenue are dismissed. [Para 10]

■

Undisputedly, in the year under consideration, the assessee has declared total sales turnover of Rs. 163.98 crores out of which, as alleged by the Department, sales worth Rs. 109.07 crores were made during the month of November 2016, after declaration of demonetization of Rs. 1000 and Rs. 500 currency notes. It is interesting to note that out of the total sales made of Rs. 163.98 crores the Departmental Authority have disputed/doubted sales worth Rs. 72.15 crore. Even, sales worth Rs. 37 crores made during the demonetization period have been accepted by the Departmental Authorities. [Para 12]

■

As far as the sales alleged to have been made to bogus entities controlled by entry operator Sonu Punjabi is concerned it is observed that in course of assessment proceeding as well as before the first appellate authority the assessee has furnished various documentary evidences, such as, party-wise details of purchase and sale for the entire year, VAT returns and VAT assessment orders, item-wise stock register and purchase invoices, confirmation from the suppliers, audited books of account, quantitative tally of purchase and sale, etc. It is also a fact that the suppliers from whom the assessee purchases gold/bullion confirmed the transactions in response to notices issued under section 133(6). Pertinently, no deficiency or discrepancy was found either in the books of account maintained by the assessee or the documentary evidences furnished. This is so because, neither the Assessing Officer nor the first appellate authority have returned any adverse inference, either in relation to the books of account maintained by the assessee or the documentary evidences furnished. Merely because the notices issued under section 133(6) and summons issued under section 131 returned unserved or remained unanswered, cannot lead to the conclusion that sales are bogus, when there are overwhelming documentary evidences brought on record in the form of audited books of account, stock register, item-wise purchase and sales, VAT return, VAT assessment order accepting the sale transactions to demonstrate that the assessee indeed has effected the sales. [Para 13]

■

Similarly, in respect of sales made to RBPL the addition was made purely on conjectures and surmises. The Assessing Officer has attempted to treat the sales made by the assessee as non-genuine only because of statement recorded on oath from M stating that cash amounting to Rs. 32 crores was given to him by DL Jewellers for depositing in the bank account of RBPL. The purported cash deposit in the bank account of RBPL, even assuming it to be correct, cannot prove that the sales effected by the assessee to RBPL is non-genuine. On the contrary, it proves availability of fund with RBPL to effect the purchases from the assessee. Even in respect of the sales made to RBPL the assessee has furnished all documentary evidences including audited books of account, item-wise purchase and sales, VAT return, VAT assessment orders, stock register, etc, to prove the genuineness of sales. Admittedly, the Assessing Officer has not found any discrepancy or deficiency in the books of account and stock register maintained by the assessee. Thus, when the assessee has maintained item wise purchase and sale details as well as stock register and, moreover neither in course of survey any stock discrepancy was found nor any unaccounted cash was found, certain sales cannot be treated as bogus. More so, when one of the directors of RBPL has stated before the Assessing Officer that he had taken delivery of gold/bullion purchased from assessee. [Para 14]

■

Similar is the factual position qua the sales effected to Olivia and S.S Overseas, as the assessee has furnished all documentary evidences to prove the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of transaction. Thus, the assessee has sufficiently discharged the initial burden cast upon it to prove the credit entries appearing in the books of account. In fact, the first appellate authority has accepted the fact that the assessee has discharged the initial burden cast upon it. Once it is established that the initial burden cast upon the assessee has been discharged, the burden shifts to the Assessing Officer to conclusively prove that the credit entries appearing in the books of account are unexplained in terms with section 68. In the facts of the instant appeal, the Assessing Officer has failed to do so. Therefore, the amount in dispute cannot be treated as unexplained cash credit under section 68. [Para 15]

INCOME TAX : Where cash deposited post-demonetization by assessee was out of cash sales which had been accepted by Sales Tax/VAT Department and not doubted by Assessing Officer and there was sufficient stock available with assessee to make cash sales, sales made by assessee out of existing stock were sufficient to explain deposit of cash (obtained from realization of sales) in bank account and, thus, cash deposits could not have been treated as undisclosed income of assessee

The partner of the assessee firm. 'M', in his statements made before the investigation wing, had stated that the sales had been made in cash and the persons, through whom sales were made, were unverifiable. In fact, he said that he knew the names of the customers to whom sales had been made, personally but he did not disclose the names due to professional/trade secret. It was in clear contradiction to his first statement recorded on 6-5-1999, when he stated that he did not know any such person and the buyers approached him directly. It was, thus, a case where the partner in the assessee-firm had been changing his stand as regards the particulars of sales. No evidence worth any credence had been led either in the course of the assessment proceedings or appellate proceedings to establish that the sales had been made and the cash deposited in the bank account was in lieu of the sales made of jewellery. In fact, unverifiability of the sales had been accepted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, when he had enhanced the income returned and the assessee, in the impugned proceedings, had not challenged that finding. Mere furnishing of cash memos could not by any stretch of imagination, be made a sole basis to conclude that any sales had been made by the assessee. Thus, the sales made by the assessee were unverifiable and unacceptable. Moreover, the entire transaction of purchase and sale of jewellery had been carried out by the assessee in a particular manner and abnormal circumstances, which irrefutably led to a conclusion that there was no business per se of the assessee of purchase and sale of jewellery. The assessee-firm did not even had the necessary infrastructure, i.e., dharam kanta to carry on the business of purchase and sale of diamond jewellery, which is the most essential infrastructure. Even otherwise, no particulars had been placed on record to show that such jewellery was allegedly purchased and sold by the assessee with a weighing scale of a third party. In fact, the evidence furnished by the assessee in the shape of purchase bills and sales bills did not include the weighment slips, which, as per the admission of the assessee, were the fundamental requirements for any transaction of purchase/sale of jewellery. There were no employees of the firm other than one 'G', who had not been produced in the course of the assessment proceedings and even his particulars had not been made available at any stage. Even as regards to his purported duties, there was a contradiction. In the initial statement, 'M' stated that said employee's duty was to assist him in carrying the cash to the bank, whereas subsequently even the same was contradicted by stating that when he went to deposit the cash, he stayed back at the premises. Thus, it was not possible to accept that the assessee had employed any such person. Even otherwise, it was not possible to carry on business of such a huge magnitude with only one employee and that too, having no formal qualifications. It had been stated by 'M' before the investigation wing and the Assessing Officer that the business was carried on with minimum furniture of one table, two chairs and a half size almirah, which was also used as a safe. However, it appeared that even the infrastructure as contended by the assessee in the shape of almirah, one table and two chairs was not available with the assessee to carry on the business of the projected magnitude. Further, there was no past track record of the assessee-firm. It had allegedly carried on the operations of business only for a short period of time and even within that short period of time, the entire alleged purchases of jewellery were from the persons, who had furnished declarations under the VDIS, 1997, and for all such purchases the sales were only in cash. In fact, even independently, the purchases had not been proved by the assessee-firm. Mere issue of purchase bills could not be regarded as sufficient basis to hold that the jewellery had been purchased by the assessee-firm. In that connection, the statements of four persons had been recorded by the investigation wing, wherein all of them had confirmed that they had not sold any jewellery to the assessee. Though in the assessment proceedings, they had retracted from their original statements, yet such retraction was not supported by any adequate reason. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act. That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further

Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

12.12-1 Evidence for ascertaining the value of investments

During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee. Assessee submitted a bill in respect of purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges. However, AO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee. Held once the identity of the diamond jewellery found during the course of search had been accepted as explainable from the purchase voucher and labour charges bill produced by the assessee at the time of search as well as during the course of regular assessment proceedings, the addition of the difference could be made by the AO only by establishing the fact that the value stated in the purchase invoice was fictitious. The burden clearly lay upon the department to prove that the value shown in the purchase invoice was not the real value. The department had not brought any material whatever on records to prove that the value of such diamonds embedded in the diamond jewellery at the time of its purchase in the month of July 1981 was understated in the purchase invoices. Such a burden was required to be discharged by the department by bringing clinching and conclusive evidence on record. The AO had not even examined the jeweller from whom these diamonds were purchased. The assessee had successfully discharged the initial burden of proving the source of acquisition of aforesaid diamond jewellery by producing the aforesaid bills at the time of search. The AO had completely failed to bring any evidence on record to show that the cost of ornaments shown by the assessee did not represent the real cost. Therefore, the addition on account of the difference in value of diamond ornaments in question is not justified and deserves to be deleted. - Gautam Laljibhai Gajjar v. ITO [1991] 37 ITD 514 (Ahd.)

CIT [IT Appeal Nos. 3841 and 3842, dated 26/11/2024] primarily on the ground that the assessee therein was subjected to search, whereas the present assessee was not. This distinction is wholly irrelevant to the core issue of evidentiary reliance on third-party material without cross-examination. Considerable reliance has been placed on the alleged admission by the Rubberwala Group that it received on-money and offered the same to tax. This, however, cannot be determinative of the assessee's liability. The ratio of Rajesh Jain rests squarely on two pillars: absence of corroborative material against the assessee, and denial of cross-examination despite specific request. [Para 8.14]

■

Both these features are present in the instant case. Judicial discipline mandates that a co-ordinate Bench decision on identical facts be followed unless shown to be per incuriam, which is not the case here. [Para 8.15]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) relied on various decisions to contend that providing cross examination of IA was not required. These authorities do not lay down a blanket proposition dispensing with cross-examination. On the contrary, they consistently hold that the requirement depends on the nature of evidence, its role in the adjudication, and the prejudice caused. In the present case: the assessee has categorically denied having made any cash payment; no cash, diary, or corroborative document was found from the assessee; the alleged diary, though repeatedly referred to in statements, was never recovered; and the entire edifice of the addition rests on third-party statements and electronic data interpreted by those very persons. [Para 8.16]

■

In such circumstances, denial of cross-examination causes manifest prejudice and cannot be brushed aside as a mere procedural irregularity. [Para 8.17]

■

It is found that, in identical factual circumstances relating to alleged cash ''on-money'' payments for purchase of shops in Platinum Mall from the Rubberwala Group, the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Praveen Khetaramm Purohit v. DCIT (ITA Nos. 4742 to 4744/Mum/2025) has deleted similar additions. The Bench also placed reliance upon another decision of the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Akhraj Pukhraaj Chopra v. DCIT and Lilaram v. DCIT in ITAs No.5553 and 5554/Mum/2025, vide order dated 12-11-2025, wherein similar addition was made on the basis of search and seizure action on Rubberwala Group. [Para 8.18]

■

The consistent factual matrix emerging from above decisions is that the additions were made solely on the basis of (i) statements of IA, an employee of the Rubberwala Group, recorded during the course of search, and (ii) data contained in an Excel sheet retrieved from a pen drive found from his possession. No incriminating material was found from the assessee. The assessee, from the inception, categorically denied having paid any cash over and above the documented consideration. [Para 8.19]

■

The Co-ordinate Bench, after an exhaustive examination of the facts, has held that such third-party statements and electronic records, uncorroborated by any independent evidence and not directly linking the assessee to the alleged cash payment, do not constitute credible evidence for sustaining an addition under section 69. The Bench further noted that, despite specific requests, the assessee was neither confronted with the complete adverse material nor afforded an opportunity to cross-examine IA or any other person whose statements were relied upon. [Para 8.20]

■

It is well settled that while the rigours of the Evidence Act do not strictly apply to income-tax proceedings, additions must nevertheless be founded on material which is reliable, cogent, and has a direct nexus with the assessee. Third-party statements, cannot be treated as conclusive unless supported by independent corroborative evidence. At best, such material may give rise to suspicion, but suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of proof. [Para 8.21]

Finance Act, 2013

13.3 Tax Collected at Source - Section 206C

13.3-1 Existing Provisions

In order to reduce the quantum of cash transaction in bullion and jewellery sector and for curbing the flow of unaccounted money in the trading system of bullion and jewellery, the Finance Act, 2012 inserted new sub-section (1D) in section 206C with effect from 1-7-2012 to provide for TCS on cash sale of jewellery and bullion to be collected by the seller.

According to new sub-section (1D), every person, being a seller, who receives any amount in cash as consideration for sale of bullion (excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less) or jewellery, shall, at the time of receipt of such amount in cash, collect from the buyer, a sum equal to 1% of sale consideration as income-tax, if such consideration,—

(i)

for bullion, exceeds two hundred thousand rupees; or

(ii)

for jewellery, exceeds five hundred thousand rupees.

13.3-2 Amendments

The Finance Act, 2013 has omitted the words "(excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less)" with effect from 1-6-2013.

13.3-3 Impact

So cash sale of gold coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less will also attract TCS with effect from 1-6-2013 if consideration exceeds Rs. 2,00,000.

To put in other words, with effect from June 1, 2013, consideration of "any coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less" shall not be excluded while calculating the monetary limit of Rs. 2,00,000.

Press release dated 1-5-2013 read as under :—

Currently, sale in cash of bullion (excluding coin or any other article weighing 10 grams or less) in excess of Rs. 2 lakh or jewellery in excess of Rs. 5 lakh is subject to Tax Collection at Source (TCS) @ 1%. As coins were neither included in bullion nor in jewellery, therefore, coins, even when amounting to more than Rs. 2 lakh in value, were being sold in cash without TCS.

The Finance Bill, 2013 proposes to delete exclusion of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less from bullion. Hence, the sale of bullion (including coins/articles) in cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%. Similarly, sale of jewellery in cash in excess of Rs. 5 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%.

It is not a new levy of tax but continuation of old levy except withdrawal of exemption in the case of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less.

Assessing Authorities' Stand in OCM/Demonetisation Assessment Cases concerning Assesses' Claims of Cash deposits being made out of Cash Sales in Business

5. In the cases of persons engaged in business and maintaining books of accounts, the most common and natural explanation and justification for the cash deposits being made by them in the post demonetisation period has been cash sales being made by them in their businesses.

The assessing authorities, in majority of the OCM assessment cases, have declined to accept the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made out of cash sales of business in post demonetisation period and have made huge income-tax demands under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in the regular assessment orders in such OCM/demonetisation cases. The most common arguments and contentions being made by the assessing authorities in rejecting the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made by the assessees out of their cash sales in business post demonetisation period are discussed as under:

i.

Since w.e.f. 8.11.2016 midnight, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes (SBNs) were declared invalid and were not to be considered as legal tender, therefore, for the assesses carrying on business, booking of cash sales and accepting such SBNs for transacting business transactions, during post demonetisation period, was prohibited.

ii.

The money measurement concept of accounting underlines the fact that in accounting and economics generally, every recorded event or transaction is measured in terms of money, i.e., the local currency monetary unit of measure. Since the SBNs were just a piece of papers and they bear no value on 9th November 2016 or after, as Central Government, the guarantor, had withdrawn its guarantee and hence, the receipt of these SBNs can't be journalized in books of account. Therefore, the transactions made in SBNs on or after 9th November 2016 cannot be entered into cash books.

iii.

Therefore, if the assessee has received any SBN notes after 09.11.2016 on account of any monetary transactions and utilizes the same for making cash deposits into the bank account, then the credit of the same into the books of accounts is not to be considered as valid and has to be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act and brought to tax.

In some other cases, where the cash deposits have been explained by the assessees as pertaining to cash sales being made by them prior to the demonetisation period, the assessing authorities have again rejected the genuineness and authenticity of such claims believing that the assessees might have backdated the cash sales just before the demonetisation period so as to reflect cash in hand as on 8.11.2016 consisting of banned notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000, which they have deposited in their bank accounts post demonetisation.

Mere filing of PAN, acknowledgement of ITRs of the entry providers and bank account statement is not sufficient to discharge the onus on the assessee [CIT v. Nova Promoters & Finlease (P.) Ltd. [2012] 18 taxmann.com 217/206 Taxman 207 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. N. Tarika Properties Investment (P.) Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 525/[2014] 221 Taxman 14 (Delhi), SLP dismissed inN. Tarika Property Investment (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 51 taxmann.com 387/227 Taxman 373 (SC).

Where assessee had sold a new product launched by it on test market basis over and above its counter sale but failed to explain as to how and why such cash sales of huge amount effected only in one month of a year, AO was justified in making additions in respect of such unexplained sales [J. M. J. Essential Oil Co. v. CIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 181/259 Taxman 546 (HP), SLP dismissed inJ. M. J. Essential Oil Co. v. CIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 463/269 Taxman 202 (SC)].

Department need not to locate source of receipt - Where the assessee has failed to prove satisfactorily the source and nature of a credit entry in his books, and it is held that the relevant amount is the income of the assessee, it is not necessary for the department to locate its exact source [A. Govindarajulu Mudaliar v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 807 (SC); CIT v. M. Ganapathi Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 623 (SC)].

The above principle applies alike to cases in which an entry is found in the books of account of the assessee and to cases in which no such entry is found. If the amount represented the income of the assessee of the previous year, it was liable to be included in the total income and an enquiry whether for the purpose of bringing the amount to tax it was from a business activity or from some other source was not relevant [CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1969] 72 ITR 807 (SC)].

Mere unsatisfactory explanation does not result in treating cash credits as income - In the absence of a satisfactory explanation, the unexplained cash credit may be charged to income-tax, therefore, the unsatisfactoriness of the explanation would not automatically result in deeming the amount credited in the books as income of the assessee [CIT v. Smt. P. K. Noorjahan [1999] 103 Taxman 382 (SC)]. The word 'may' indicate that the intention of the Legislature is to confer a discretion on the AO in the matter of treating the source of investment or credit which had not been satisfactorily explained as income of an assessee, but it is not obligatory to treat such source as income in every case where the explanation offered was found to be not satisfactory [CIT v. Pragati Co-operative Bank Ltd. [2005] 149 Taxman 149 (Guj.)].

Even after rejecting the explanation given by the assessees if found unacceptable, the crucial aspect, whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, it should be inferred the sums credited in the books of the assessees constituted income of the PY must receive the consideration of the authorities provided the assessees rebut the evidence and the inference drawn to reject the explanation offered as unsatisfactory [CIT v. P. Mohanakala [2007] 161 Taxman 169 (SC)].

Alternative explanations - The provision does not debar the assessee from offering alternative explanation and if either of them is accepted, the cash credit cannot be charged as the income of the assessee [Addl. CIT v. Ghai Lime Stone Co. [1982] 11 Taxman 58 (MP)]. Also see, Dhansiram Agarwalla v. CIT [1995] 81 Taxman 1 (Gauh.).

In K.Gomathi v. DCIT, Central Circle-2(3), Chennai ; ITAT order, dated 19-10-2022, it was held that addition u/s 69A & tax u/s 115BBE are justified w.r.t. unexplained cash equal to cash seized introduced by assessee in the books on the date of the search. The Tribunal held as follows:

Where cash seized of Rs. 1,73,40,790 seized during the search was explained by assessee as repayments by borrowers in his financing business and same was shown in P& L account as amounts accepted as income during search with corresponding entry in balance sheet of cash seized but assessee continued with same cash balance as on date of search with reducing cash seized from cash in hand, it amounts to introduction of cash in books of an amount equal to cash seized on date of search for which source is to be explained satisfactorily.

Where assessee failed to explain satisfactorily the source of the cash, addition of the amount under section 69A and tax on the addition under section 155BBE by AO were justified and such action did not amount to treating the seized cash as unexplained income as action was with reference to fresh cash introduced in the books as on date of search. The explanation of cash so introduced was business income was rightly not accepted by AO and CIT(A) as business income was subsumed in the cash seized duly accounted in Profit and loss account with corresponding entry as cash seized in the balance sheet.

| SALIENT FEATURES/ACTION POINTS |
| --- |
| Introducing own black money in books as credits in the names of fictitious creditors or persons of inadequate means is no longer advisable in view of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act,1988. Better show it as own money by crediting capital account and bringing on books the relevant assets and pay 78% tax and disclose in ITR under section 115BBE(1)(a). If own black money introduced in books in names of fictitious persons/persons of low means, it will attract additions u/s 68, tax of 78% and penalty as also confiscation under the Benami Act. If assessee of limited means acts as benamidar and shows huge black money credited in books of someone else as his own, he can't get away paying 78% tax under section 115BBE(1)(a) with voluntary disclosure in ITR. It will be liable for confiscation under Benami Act. Credit of any sum in the books of the assessee in order to be cash credit u/s 68 should be capable of being treated as his income-Ali Hussain Abdeali Lokhandwala v. ITO [1991] 36 ITD 247 (Indore) Although section 68 heading is 'Cash Credits', it is not limited to cash receipts. The expression 'any sum' in section 68 is wide and would cover all credits including loans, receipts, trade credits, credits in capital account or in the name of third party. Assessee bound to offer satisfactory explanation as to the nature and source of credit in his books of account. There is no bar on assessee offering an alternative explanation. If either of them is accepted by AO, then, no additions can be made by AO. Explanation as to source does not mean assessee has to explain source of the source. However, to this rule, there is an exception. . . . credits in respect of share application money or share capital or share premium in the books of closely-held company. If assessee fails to offer any explanation or the explanation offered is unsatisfactory, then the amount of credit shall be assessable u/s 68 read with section 115BBE. Explanation must be a factual explanation and not merely a legal argument. It is one thing to say that credits are out of intangible additions in past periods. This is a factual explanation and must be proved. It is quite another thing for the assessee to say that intangible additions were made in the past and these be deemed to be/treated as source of cash credits. This is not an explanation as to source and is merely a legal argument and doesn't discharge the onus of explanation which section casts on the assessee. If assessee's explanation is not satisfactory, AO can make additions. AO is not bound to prove that unexplained credit is from a particular source. |

Prohibition of Receipts of Cash in excess of Rs. Two Lakhs (Section 269ST of the Income Tax Act, 1961)

3. A new Section 269ST has been inserted by the Finance Act, 2017, w.e.f. 1.4.2017, for the AY 2017-18 and onwards, which provides as under:

No person shall receive an amount of two lakh rupees or more—

(a)

in aggregate from a person in a day; or

(b)

in respect of a single transaction; or

(c)

in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account.

Therefore, w.e.f. AY 2017-18 and onwards, any person who receives cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs, in aggregate from a person in a day or in respect of a single transaction or in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person shall be liable to a penalty of an amount equivalent to the amount of such cash transaction.

Certain entities/transactions have been kept outside the purview of the above provisions of section 269ST as under:

The provisions of the section 269ST shall not apply to—

(i)

any receipt by—

(a)

Government;

any banking company, post office savings bank or co-operative bank;

(ii)

transactions of the nature referred to in section 269SS;

(iii)

such other persons or class of persons or receipts, which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify.

Assessments in OCM/ Demonetisation Cases

4. The demonetisation period i.e. period from 9.11.2016 till 30.12.2016, fell in the FY 2016-17 corresponding to the AY 2017-18. So, in the regular assessments for the AY 2017-18, a large number of scrutiny cases were pertaining to the issue of huge and abnormal cash deposits during the demonetisation period.

The earlier deadline for completing regular assessments for OCM/demonetisation cases was 30.9.2019. However, due to the paucity of time, the CBDT has extended the deadline for assessing officers to complete and conclude the assessments of such OCM/demonetisation cases by December 31, 2019, which in any case was the time barring deadline for completion of regular assessment cases for the AY 2017-18, other than transfer pricing cases.

The assessing authorities have segregated such OCM cases separately for business cases and non-business cases and have analysed these in terms of various criterion.

Further, cash deposits made in a financial year have been segmented into three parts, i.e. pre demonetisation period (1.04.2016 till 8.11.2016), post demonetisation period (9.11.2016 till 31.12.2016) and total in the financial year 016-17 and corresponding period in FY 2015-16. The assessing authorities have subjected these data to analytics and have worked out the percentage increase in cash deposits against all the three combinations to derive the meaningful inferences. The analysis of month wise cash sales and deposits for demonetisation period and also the corresponding period in the FY 2015-16 have also been undertaken.

Strengthening the Provisions One more method can be used to bring these exchanges in the ambit of regulation i.e. by bringing these exchanges under section 285BA and treating them as reportable entities (REs). By this, the obligation of disclosing the transaction lies with the exchange. For the time being, in the absence of the change in section 285BA, a special pilot project by Intelligence and Criminal Investigation (I&CI) can be launched to gather the information for such Specified Financial Transactions (SFT). There is no information available in the organized form that how many exchanges are dealing with crypto currencies. Similarly, only the exchanges located in a country can be brought to the scheme. The exchanges located outside are not obliged to comply either with the provisions of the Act or with any notices issued under Section 133(6) of the Act. At first, for the domestic exchanges, a master list is required to be prepared by collecting information from Google etc.Then these REs may be asked to furnish the SFT, which should contain data of all persons who have made these transactions. The entries during the gain period should be specifically checked. The collected information can be disseminated to the Assessing Officers for further verification or scrutiny. Similarly, Section 194S provides for a deduction of tax, even if the VDA is sold for another VDA. In case the sale is made in any recognised currency, the sale value is determined as per the realised value, but in case, the sale is made in another VDA, the issue of the valuation may arise. The fair market value has not been defined, which is another challenge.

Cash Transaction

The above mechanism is useful for transactions made through banking channels, but for cash transactions, it is near to impossible to catch them as the cash system works in the same fashion as 'hawala' works. The word 'hawala' is a local version of the English word 'reference'; this system works only on a reference basis. An anonymous person cannot go directly to the 'hawala' dealer for transfer of money between cities or countries. A reference from some known person is required. These dealers are not maintaining any written record; once a transaction is completed, the record is erased. Even if any record is found during the course of the survey or search, nothing can be made out of these jotted entries. Generally, these transactions are very smooth. Trust and risk are primary conditions. So dealing with cash crypto is almost like dealing with 'hawala' transactions. No separate provisions of the law are applicable, and no special expertise is required to crack these transactions. Traditional hawala methods were mainly operating through two methods. Firstly, the quantum of money of the sender and receiver should be the same. The second method is 'under-invoicing or over-invoicing' of import and export bills as required. But transfer through crypto is not based on any such conditions, the money can be sent unilaterally. So the emphasis is required only on those transactions which are done through banking channels.

Major Challenge

The main danger of cryptocurrencies is the convenience of transferring money to offshore places. A person can buy crypto in cash in India and transfer it to some person living abroad. That person would sell it and receive money in the local currency. Same as in the case of international debit or credit cards, where the deposits are made in one country in local currency, but ATM withdrawals can be made in any country. But these transactions contain heavy transaction fees, which is not there in the case of crypto. The central banks are honouring the transactions of debit and credit cards, as in the case of crypts also. The central bank has to honour at least in those countries that have given legal status to some cryptocurrencies. So why have some countries, like China, completely banned any transaction in these currencies. Section 194S comes into the picture when the amount is credited to a resident. Hence the money sent outside of the countries is out of the purview of these provisions. The first-time buyers of the crypto are also required to bring under these provisions.

Thus, to compute the 5% threshold, only cash receipts should be considered, and any receipts by way of journal entry should not be considered in the 5% threshold. Similarly, sales made on a credit basis, even if funds are not realised, should not form part of the 5% threshold. The term "receive" or "received" has been judicially explained as follows:

(a)

"To come into possession of, get, acquire, or the like, from any source outside of oneself." [In re McCullough's Estate, 193 Wash. 145, 74 P.2d 877 (1928)]

(b)

"To receive means to get by a transfer, as, to receive a gift, to receive a letter, or to receive money and involves an actual receipt." [The Major Law Lexicon by P. Ramanatha Aiyar, 4th Edn., Vol. 5; College Law Dictionaries by Dr. Avtar Singh, 2nd Edn.]

(c)

"The 'receipt' of income refers to the first occasion when the recipient gets the money under his own control." [Keshav Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 230 (SC)].

Thus, the term "received" means an amount (money) actually received by the assessee during the previous year. The proviso contemplates actual receipt of amounts by the assessee during the previous year. So, in this context, the term "received" may not include "receivable". The Supreme Court in CIT v. Moon Mills Ltd. [1966] 59 ITR 574 (SC) held that there is no scope for holding that the expression "received" means "receivable".
