53. Allowing utilisation of the input tax credit ledger balance for reverse charge payments

Under the GST law, certain provisions result in cash blockages without yielding any incremental revenue to the Government. For instance, in the case of imports of services, the recipient of services is liable to discharge GST liability in cash under a reverse charge mechanism, which will then be available to him as ITC. The mandatory cash payment leads to cash blockage.

The Government should consider allowing taxpayers to use their GST ITC balance for payment of tax under the reverse charge mechanism. The ability to use the ITC balance to discharge the RCM liability would not only address the cash flow issues but also streamline the tax administration process, making it more business-friendly without compromising the tax revenues for the Government.

54. Transfer of Input Tax Credit from one State to another

Under the existing GST framework, Form ITC-02 facilitates the transfer of unutilised input tax credit only between GST registrations located within the same State. The law does not currently envisage or provide any mechanism for transferring accumulated ITC in cases of inter-State business movement. Consequently, in situations such as business reorganisation, merger or restructuring involving different States, closure of operations or a branch in one State, and continuation of the same business from another State, the accumulated ITC remains locked with the original registration. This results in a loss of credit, a blockage of working capital, and procedural hardship, despite no change in the underlying business or tax incidence.

Recently, the Bombay High Court in the case of Umicore Autocat India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2025) 32 Centax 416 (Bom.), pursuant to a scheme of amalgamation, held that the transfer of unutilized ITC lying in the electronic credit ledger of transferor company to amalgamated company is allowed irrespective of fact that companies are located in different States.

It is recommended that a procedure be devised to allow for the transfer of accumulated ITC in such inter-state business transfers, to ensure seamless credit flow and avoid loss of legitimate credits to taxpayers.

55. Refund of the closing balance of the Input Tax Credit

Under the erstwhile VAT regime, taxpayers were permitted to claim a refund of unutilized input tax credit (ITC) at the end of the financial year. This ensured that taxes already paid on inputs did not become a permanent cost to businesses and supported adequate working capital management.

Under the GST framework, the refund of accumulated ITC is currently available only in limited circumstances, such as for zero-rated supplies (exports and supplies to SEZs) and for inverted duty structures. In most other situations, unutilized ITC remains blocked, even though it represents taxes already paid to the Government.

A critical situation arises when a taxpayer decides to close or exit a business. Currently, the GST law does not explicitly provide for the refund of unutilized ITC upon business closure, leaving taxpayers unable to recover legitimate credits accumulated over the course of operations. This creates an unnecessary financial burden, as the unutilized credit represents tax that has already been paid and should rightfully be refundable.

It is therefore recommended that a provision be introduced under GST allowing:

Refund of unutilized ITC at the end of a financial year, to ease working capital constraints.

Refund of accumulated ITC on business closure, enabling taxpayers to recover input taxes legitimately paid, thereby reducing stranded credit and avoiding penalisation of businesses for exiting operations.

56. Legislative misalignment in the case of ECOs who are required to pay tax on supplies listed under section 9(5) as if they are the suppliers of notified services

The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has issued Circular No. 240/34/2024-GST, providing much-needed clarification regarding the Input Tax Credit (ITC) availed by E-Commerce Operators (ECOs) in scenarios where services specified under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, are supplied through their platform. This circular extends the principles previously clarified in Circular No. 167/23/2021, dated December 17, 2021, to restaurant services and other services notified under Section 9(5).

The circular draws upon the principles established in Circular No. 167/23/2021-GST, dated December 17, 2021, which clarified the ITC treatment for restaurant services provided through ECOs. These principles are now explicitly extended to other services notified under Section 9(5).

Section 158BC mandates that a person subjected to a search on or after 01-09-2024 must file a return of income in response to a notice issued by the Assessing Officer. The notice requires a person to furnish the return within the prescribed period but not exceeding 60/90 days2. Rule 12AE, which prescribes Form ITR-B for filing such returns, has been made applicable retrospectively from 01-09-2024. However, this Rule was notified only on 7th April 2025, and until this date, Form ITR-B did not exist in Income-tax Rules, 1962. Even after its notification, the form is not yet functional on the e-filing portal, creating a procedural gap in compliance with the requirement of Section 158BC.

This raises a critical issue if a notice under Section 158BC is issued on or after 01-09-2024 but before the notification of Rule 12AE, i.e., 07-04-2025, the assessee was legally required to file a return, but no prescribed form was available to comply with this obligation. This effectively places the assessee in a compliance dilemma, where a statutory obligation exists, but no practical mechanism to fulfill it has been provided.

The Rule fails to address how relief will be extended to taxpayers when a search is conducted after 01-09-2024 and a notice under Section 158BC is issued. Further, Rule 12AE does not provide any solution where an assessee is considered a defaulter because the due date for filing a return under Section 158BC had lapsed before the availability of an online mechanism to file Form ITR-B.

However, such deduction shall be allowed only if the assessee fulfils certain conditions. One of the conditions is that emoluments must be paid by any of the following modes:

An account payee cheque;

32. Seller for the purpose of TCS under Section 206C(1F) should include Individual or HUF

The Finance Act, 2016 inserted sub-section (1F) to Section 206C to bring high-value transactions within the tax net. This provision provides that every person, being a seller, who receives any amount as consideration for the sale of a motor vehicle of the value exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs, shall collect tax from the buyer at the rate of 1% of the sale consideration.

The term 'seller' has been defined under clause (c) of Explanation to Section 206C. This clause defines the meaning of seller with respect to sub-section (1) and sub-section (1F) of Section 206C. However, to include an individual or a HUF within the meaning of 'seller', it provides that total sales, gross receipts or turnover of such individual or HUF from the business or profession carried on by him should exceed Rs. 1 crore in case of business or Rs. 50 lakh in the case of the profession during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the goods of the nature specified in the Table in sub-section (1) are sold. This Explanation has inadvertently omitted to give a reference of sub-section (1F) of Section 206C.

It is recommended that clause (c) of the Explanation to Section 206C should be amended to mention the reference of sub-section (1F) also. This Explanation should read as under:

(a) "seller" with respect to sub-section (1) and sub-section (1F) means the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority or corporation or authority established by or under a Central, State or Provincial Act, or any company or firm or cooperative society and also includes an individual or a Hindu undivided family whose total sales, gross receipts or turnover from the business or profession carried on by him exceed one crore rupees in case of business or fifty lakh rupees in case of profession during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the goods of the nature specified in the Table in sub-section (1) or sub-section (1F) are sold.

The rendering or presentation of Para-10 as per costing taxonomy can be made as below: L. Para 11 - Reconciliation of Indirect Taxes (for the company as a whole)

(a) This Para is to be prepared for the company as a whole covering excise duty, service tax and VAT (including CST and any other State Tax) for all types of products whether or not covered under cost audit.

(b) The information of indirect taxes is to be given for current year and no previous year's figures are required.

(c) The format under para 11 is slightly modified to suit the requirement of taxonomy and furnish the details correctly.

(d) CST and Other State Taxes have been added in the costing taxonomy to show the details relating to them also.

(e) Assessable Value relating to all types of taxes should be taken from the respective Returns submitted with the tax authorities. For example, assessable value for excise duty should be taken from RT 12 (now ER-1), the gross amount (assessable value) for service tax should be taken as gross value of services as mentioned in ST-3 (under section 70 of Finance Act 1994).

(f) The duties and taxes Payable is based on clearances of goods and services against the respective heads.

(g) Duties/Taxes Paid include CENVAT/VAT Credit utilized on inputs, capital goods, input services and other utilization, if any.

(h) Taxes paid through PLA/Cash refer to the payment of Excise Duty, Service Tax, Cess & Others and VAT through debit in PLA account or deposit in to the PLA account or payment in to the bank account by way of cheque or cash through the GAR-7 Challan or the Challan for making the payment of VAT.

(i) Duties/Taxes Recovered should be taken from Books of Account of the company. It is necessary that the gross turnover or the gross billings should be duly accounted under various heads such as net sales, excise duty, sales tax, service tax, etc.

(j) Difference between duties/taxes paid and recovered refer to the amount of total duties/taxes paid and recovered. This may not match due to the following reasons -

♦ Excise duty element in stock of excise duty paid goods at depots, branches, and warehouse or with C & F agents.

♦ The goods lying at depots, etc. are duty paid goods which have not been sold to the customer. Hence, the duty has not been recovered from the customers.

♦ Excise duty/sales tax paid on free issues, samples, where the taxes are not recovered from customers.

♦ Excise Duty paid on inter factory transfers.

♦ Excise Duty paid on the goods captively consumed.

♦ Excise duty/sales tax/service tax/cess and other payments arising out of Order-in-Original or Order-in-Appeal, etc.

(k) The fines, penalties, interest etc. are not a payment of Excise Duty, Service Tax, Cess & Others and VAT. However, sometimes it is paid through PLA or Cash (deposit in to the bank account by way of cheque or cash through Challan) under the separate code as specified in the Challan. In these circumstances, the amount should be identified and shown separately. This amount can be tallied from Monthly ER-1 Return (Excise), Annual Financial Information Statement in ER-4 (Excise), Half Yearly ST-3 Return (Service Tax) and Monthly/Annual VAT return.

Diamond Dollar Account (DDA) Scheme

1. Firms and companies may open and maintain DDA with AD Category-I banks, subject to the following terms and conditions :—

(a)

The exporter should comply with the eligibility criteria stipulated in the Foreign Trade Policy of the Government of India, issued from time to time.

(b)

The DDA shall be opened in the name of the exporter and maintained in US Dollars only.

(c)

The account shall only be in the form of current account and no interest should be paid on the balance held in the account.

(d)

No intra-account transfer should be allowed between the DDAs maintained by the account holder.

(e)

An exporter firm/company shall be permitted to open and maintain not more than 5 DDAs.

(f)

The balances held in the accounts shall be subject to Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements.

(g)

Exporter firms and companies maintaining foreign currency accounts, excluding EEFC accounts, with banks in India or abroad, are not eligible to open Diamond Dollar Accounts.

(h)

The transactions in the DDA would be as under :

2. Permissible credits

(i)

Amount of pre-shipment and post-shipment finance availed in US Dollars.

(ii)

Realisation of export proceeds from shipments of rough, cut, polished diamonds and diamond studded jewellery.

(iii)

Realisation in US Dollars from local sale of rough, cut and polished diamonds.

3. Permissible debits

(i)

Payment for import/purchase of rough diamonds from overseas/local sources.

(ii)

Payment for purchase of cut and polished diamonds, coloured gemstones and plain gold jewellery from local sources.

(iii)

Payment for import/purchase of gold from overseas/nominated agencies and repayment of US Dollars loans availed from the bank.

(iv)

Transfer to rupee account of the exporter.

The above transactions are subject to the provisions of the Foreign Trade Policy of Government of India, issued from time to time.

4. Application procedure

The exporter firm/company shall make an application in the format annexed to the AD Category-I bank for opening of the DDA. AD Category-I banks should assess the track record of the firm/company at the end of every licensing year (April-March). In case any firm/company fails to meet the eligibility criteria, the account may be closed immediately.

5. AD Category-I banks shall submit a monthly report to the Chief General Manager-in-Charge, Foreign Exchange Department, Reserve Bank of India, Trade Division, Amar Building, Mumbai- 400 001, giving details of the name and address of the firm/company in whose name the Diamond Dollar Account is opened, along with the date of opening/closing the Diamond Dollar Account, by the 10th of the following month to which it relates.

8AB. (1) For the purposes of clause (iii) of section 48, where the amount is chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under sub-section (4) of section 45, the specified entity shall attribute such amount to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in a manner provided in this rule.

(2) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of the balance in his capital account, chargeable to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45, relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of clause (iii) of section 48 shall be the amount which bears to the amount charged under sub-section (4) of section 45 the same proportion as the increase in, or recognition of, value of that asset because of revaluation or valuation bears to the aggregate of increase in, or recognition of, value of all assets because of the revaluation or valuation.

(3) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 does not relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under sub-section (4) of section 45 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of clause (iii) of section 48.

specify the procedure for filing of Form No. 5C;

be responsible for formulating and implementing appropriate security, archival and retrieval policies in relation to the Form No 5C so furnished.

reranked.text: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]
[2026] 186 taxmann.com 345 (Delhi)[04-05-2026] Principal Commissioner of Income-tax  vs. Kross Diamonds (P.) ltd.
[2025] 181 taxmann.com 27 (Delhi)[24-11-2025] Kross Diamonds (P.) Ltd. vs. Income-tax Officer

1. All these appeals involve common facts and propose identical questions of law, for which we are deciding them by a common order. For the purpose of clarity and convenience, facts of ITA No. 675/2025 are however, being taken into consideration.

2. The respondent/assessee deals in diamonds, which he imports from various countries in accordance with the provision of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) found that the assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales (each being less than Rs.2 lacs in value), amounting to total of Rs. 97,12,70,670/-. This being the position, the AO was of the view that since the source of purchase was the cash received from these sales, the purchases amounting to Rs.97,13,70,670/-, (being the amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under Section 69C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act of 1961').

3. While passing the assessment order the AO clearly stated that he has no doubt so far as the genuineness of purchase is concerned and accepted the factum of purchase as such, but has taken recourse to Section 69 C of the Act of 1961 to disallow the expenses relating to such purchase, as according to him, the source of expenditure (being cash) not duly explained.

4. Against the assessment order so passed by the AO on 19.12.2016, the assessee preferred an appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) (hereinafter referred to as 'CIT(A)'), which was allowed by the Appellate Authority vide its order dated 10.01.2017.

5. Against the order of the Appellant Authority, the Income Tax Department preferred an appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (hereinafter referred to as 'Tribunal'), which was rejected by the Tribunal by its impugned order dated 18.12.2024.

6. While rejecting the appeal, the Tribunal has observed that all the purchases made by the assessee were made through proper banking channels and after paying applicable duties in accordance with provision of The Customs Act 1962 and other applicable rules. The Tribunal has also recorded that all the purchases were duly supported by bills/vouchers, import bills, bills of entry, airlines bills and custom documents etc. and such purchase cannot be disallowed. The Tribunal held that the AO has proceeded on mere assumption and conjuncture.

7. Having observed so, the Tribunal has also expressed its concern that when the AO had found the purchases to be genuine, how could he take the sale to be bogus without rejecting the books of account.

8. Mr. Guarav Gupta, learned Senior Standing Counsel for the appellants submitted that the Tribunal and the CIT(A) have erred in deleting the addition made by the AO, simply because the purchases were found to be through proper banking channels and supported by documents. He argued that it is an admitted case of the AO that purchases were genuine but what he had disallowed is the expenditure of the purchase itself, because source of purchase was unexplained. Explaining the arguments, Mr. Gaurav Gupta submitted that the amount in the bank account had come from the cash sales out of the transactions (6358) which were cash bills for less than Rs.2 lacs each. He read the order of the AO and showed that all the transactions have been made only in the span of 44 days with only 8 to 10 employees were engaged, which raises a doubt about the sales affected by petitioner.

9. Learned counsel for respondent/assessee, on the other hand, submitted that the assessee had an opening stock of Rs.114.62 crores to begin with and such stock has not been disputed by AO. He further submitted that all the purchases were from abroad and all the documents, bills, payment slips, bill of entry, courier receipts etc. have been produced and as a matter of fact, the purchases have been found to be genuine by the AO. He submitted that simply because the invoices were issued to the retailers and the sales were made in cash, which cash from time to time was deposited in the bank, it does not mean that the deposits were unexplained and hence, the source of purchase was not properly explained.

10. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

11. Both the Appellant Authorities namely the CIT(A) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the AO has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under Section 69C of the Act of 1961. Not only the Appellate Authority even the AO himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine.

■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

INCOME TAX: Where AO made addition for unexplained cash purchases in diamond trading business solely based on third-party software recovered from search on another entity without providing corroborative material or opportunity for cross-examination to assessee who maintained proper books and banking records, such addition under section 69C could not be sustained.

■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, diamond trader, imported diamonds and purchases were executed through banking channels and in compliance with statutory provisions, furthermore sine purchases were accepted as genuine with proper supporting documents, expenditure on such purchases could not be treated as unexplained merely because sales were made in cash or buyers could not be fully identified, and thus, disallowance under section 69C was unjustified

HEADNOTE: III. Section  69C,  read with section  56,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105,  read with section  92  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash payment) - Assessment year  2021-22  - A search was conducted on assessee company and its group - During search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced - Statements of assessee’s executives recorded under section 132(4) acknowledged planning a cash component of Rs.25 crores and indicated that Rs.7 crores had been paid, alongside Rs.75 crores towards share capital and unsecured loans - A cash receipt for Rs.5 crores dated 11-10-2020 signed by counterparty was also found - Relying on seized note, cash receipt and statements, AO held that Rs.7 crores had been paid in cash in connection with transaction and treated it as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - It was noted that respective statements made under section 132(4) were not shown to have any valid retraction and therefore, these statements were important and valid piece of evidence which could certainly be used while framing assessment particularly when same stood corroborated with seized material (cash receipt) during search on assessee - Whether therefore, impugned addition was to be confirmed - Held, yes [Paras 22 and 24] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: ■

During the search, a handwritten note referring to a Rs.150 crore overall deal surfaced. Statements of the assessee’s executives recorded under section 132(4) acknowledged planning a cash component of Rs.25 crores and indicated that Rs.7 crores had been paid, alongside Rs.75 crores towards share capital and unsecured loans. A cash receipt for Rs.5 crores dated 11-10-2020 signed by the counterparty was also found.

■

Relying on the seized note, the cash receipt and statements, the AO held that Rs.7 crores had been paid in cash in connection with the transaction and treated it as unexplained expenditure under section 69C. The assessee’s denial of cash exchange was not accepted, and the addition of Rs.7 crores was made. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition under section 69C.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Page as referred to by the AO, is a handwritten document dated 06-03-2021 which was confronted to Shri Navneet Gupta (VP, Finance). He stated that this was about deal between KBPL and the assessee. The total deal was for Rs.150 Crores. The cash involved was for Rs.25 Crores but in his presence, no cash was paid or delivered. This document was confronted to Shri AIS Bedi (Executive Director) who stated that Rs.25 Crores was planned to be paid in the form of cash. Out of the same, Rs.7 Crores had already been paid whereas they had no intention of paying the remaining amount in cash. Against this consideration, the receipt of Rs.5 Crores was found during search which was signed by Shri Harpal Singh. When confronted, Shri Harpal Singh admitted that the receipt of Rs.5 Crores was issued by him. However, he stated that this was a mere arrangement to raise capital to square-off the deal. There was no scope of cash transactions and nothing was transacted. The same stood rejected by the AO who made allegations of unaccounted cash expenditure for Rs.7 Crores and the same was consequently added to the income of the assessee as a separate addition. [Para 22]

■
Additions u/s 69C deleted as genuine diamond purchases can't be disallowed merely due to cash sales: HC

■

The Assessing Officer made additions on account of unverifiable purchases under section 69C and excess cash deposits.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer and restricted the addition by estimating commission/profit at 0.25 per cent on the alleged cash sales.

■

On further appeal, the Tribunal restored the addition, holding that the assessee failed to explain the source of excess cash deposits with any plausible evidence.

■

On appeal to the High Court:

HEADNOTE: IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

Following the search on 23-12-2023, the AO alleged that the assessee paid cash on-money for Halol land purchases and made additions under section 69C of Rs. 78.82 lakhs (AY 2016-17), Rs. 87.97 lakhs (AY 2018-19) and Rs. 30.20 lakhs (AY 2023-24), aggregating about Rs. 1.97 crores, by estimating cash payment at 20 per cent of the agreement value. The AO principally relied on the statement of Rakesh Talati, alleging a customary 15-20 per cent cash component and cash delivery through an employee, and certain WhatsApp chats with Dharendra Pathak.

■

Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that Talati's statement was general, devoid of transaction-specific details and later retracted; no seller was examined; no cash trail or seized material evidenced cash payment; and all purchases were registered, made through banking channels and at or above stamp duty values. It was further shown that the WhatsApp chats related to a proposed Valsad transaction, whereas the additions concerned Halol lands. The CIT(A) found no corroborative evidence of cash payment, noted the absence of enquiry from sellers, accepted that the registered values were not below stamp duty values, held the chats unrelated to Halol and found the uniform 20 per cent estimation to be without factual basis. The additions were deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and perused the material placed before it. The entire addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash payment for purchase of land rests on a very narrow foundation, namely the statement of Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications. If the statement of Rakesh Talati is examined closely, it is evident that the statement is general in nature and lacks all essential particulars which are necessary for treating it as evidence of actual expenditure. The statement does not identify the specific land parcel in respect of which cash was allegedly paid. It does not identify the survey number. It does not identify the seller who allegedly received cash. It does not mention the exact amount paid in cash. It does not mention the date of payment. It does not identify the source from which the cash was generated. It does not identify the person who physically delivered the cash to the seller in relation to any particular transaction. Such a statement, at the highest, may give rise to suspicion and may justify further enquiry, but it cannot by itself constitute proof of actual expenditure incurred by the assessee. [Para 96]

■

The evidentiary weakness becomes more pronounced because the statement of Rakesh Talati was subsequently retracted. It is true that a retraction by itself does not automatically wipe out an earlier statement; however, once a statement is retracted and the assessee contests the factual correctness of the alleged admission, the burden lies on the revenue to corroborate the original statement through independent material. In the present case, the Revenue has not brought any such corroborative material. No document found during search supports the alleged cash payment. No loose paper records the payment. No diary, receipt, acknowledgement, cash flow statement or electronic record has been found. No evidence has been brought on record showing that cash was withdrawn or generated by the assessee for making such alleged payment. Thus, the retracted statement remains uncorroborated at every material stage. [Para 97]

HEADNOTE: Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Sales during demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee was engaged in business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) - During demonetisation, assessee made cash sales of Rs. 10.28 crores on 08-11-2016 - Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to income of assessee under section 68 - It was noted that no specific transaction of sale, not even one, had been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue - Allegation of Revenue holding that cash sales of aforesaid amount claimed by assessee to be untrue, was without convincing materials - Aforesaid addition had been made by Revenue based merely on suspicion, doubt, conjecture and guess work - Assessee had provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.24 crores even after announcement of demonetisation - Moreover, assessee had shown sales in VAT returns, which had been accepted by VAT authorities - Whether, on facts, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Para E.2.1] [In favour of assessee]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

HEADNOTE: III. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Cash salary) - Assessment years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on basis of statements of Nisha Singh and Ramesh Kundnani and extrapolated alleged cash salary uniformly across Assessment Years 2015-16 to 2023-24 - It was noted that no parallel payroll, cash sheets, vouchers, approvals or cash withdrawal trail was found and existence of expenditure was sought to be inferred solely from retracted statements - Whether since revenue failed to prove actual expenditure incurred by assessee, invocation of section 69C failed at threshold - Held, yes - Whether further, extrapolation of alleged cash salary payments across all assessment years, without any material showing similar payments in each year, was unsustainable - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition under section 69C on account of alleged cash salary payments was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 82, 83 and 85] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

Pursuant to the search on 23-12-2023, the AO treated alleged cash salary as unexplained expenditure under section 69C solely on the basis of statements of Nisha Singh (Rs. 30,000 per month) and Ramesh Kundnani (Rs. 1 lakh per month). Treating the aggregate monthly cash salary at Rs. 1.30 lakhs (Rs. 15.60 lakhs annually), the AO extrapolated the addition uniformly from AY 2015-16 to AY 2023-24, relying on Nisha Singh's cash deposits and rejecting both retractions. No parallel payroll, cash salary records, vouchers or cash trail was found.

■

On appeal, the assessee submitted that the search yielded no evidence of cash salary payments; Nisha Singh's retraction explained that the Rs. 30,000 represented remuneration of her brother, Vishal Singh, under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani routed through her, which the AO never verified; and Kundnani's retraction remained unrefuted. The CIT(A) held that no contemporaneous evidence established cash salary payments, the explanation regarding Vishal Singh was not investigated, the foundational requirement of proving expenditure under section 69C was absent, and the uniform extrapolation across years lacked year-wise evidence. The addition was deleted.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal has carefully considered the rival submissions and examined the entire material available on record. At the outset, it would be appropriate to observe that the revenue's case, when reduced to its essential components, rests solely upon the statements of two employees recorded during the course of search proceedings. There is no dispute that no document evidencing payment of cash salary was found during the search. There is no dispute that no parallel payroll register was recovered. There is no dispute that no employeewise cash salary sheets were discovered. There is no dispute that no vouchers, approvals, authorisations, electronic communications, payroll records or cash disbursement statements were found. In other words, despite an extensive search operation conducted in the case of the assessee company, the revenue has not brought on record a single contemporaneous document indicating existence of a parallel salary structure. This factual background assumes considerable importance because the addition sought to be made is not in relation to an isolated cash payment but on the premise that the assessee was maintaining a recurring system of salary payments outside its books of account. [Para 78]

■

The Tribunal shall first deal with the statement of Nisha Singh. The revenue seeks to rely upon her original statement to establish that she received Rs.30,000 per month in cash. However, the matter does not end with the original statement. The record reveals that she subsequently filed a retraction affidavit furnishing a specific and verifiable explanation. According to her, the amount in question pertained to her brother Vishal Singh, who was working on a part-time basis under a personal arrangement with Inder Jaisinghani, and the amount was routed through her and deposited in her bank account. Once such a specific explanation came on record, it became incumbent upon the Assessing Officer to examine its correctness. The revenue could easily have verified the role of Vishal Singh. It could have examined Inder Jaisinghani. It could have brought material demonstrating that the amount actually emanated from the assessee company. None of these steps were taken. Instead, the explanation was rejected without investigation. In the Tribunal's considered view, rejection of a specific factual explanation without any enquiry cannot elevate the original statement into conclusive evidence against the assessee. [Para 79]

■
[2001] 116 Taxman 273 (Mumbai)[07-01-2000] Premier Diamonds vs. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in diamond trading, was subjected to addition under section 69C for alleged bogus purchases from a concern based solely on information from investigation into another group, but assessee denied transactions and purchase records showed no such entries, in absence of cogent evidence against assessee, addition was unsustainable and had to be deleted

There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section  68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Demonetization) - Assessment year  2017-18 - During demonetization period, assessee-jeweller deposited huge amount in three bank accounts - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had suddenly made cash sales to unidentifiable small customers during period from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - He, therefore, made addition under section 68 on account of such unexplained cash credit (sales) - It was noted that business of assessee was an expanding business and sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over years - Assessee had furnished before Assessing Officer month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and movement in stock position - Details of stock, purchases and sales that had been submitted by assessee before Assessing Officer had not been questioned or doubted in any manner by Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee had presented evidence of available stock and depletion of said stock on account of sales and Assessing Officer had not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of receipts on account of sale of that stock were unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 was made out - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, filed its return of income.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that during the demonetization period, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 3.80 crores in three bank accounts. He further noted that the assessee had made total sales of Rs. 49.99 crores during the financial year 2016-17 and the total cash sales during the year amounted to Rs. 4.94 crores. However, of the total cash sales, the assessee had made cash sales of Rs. 3.68 crores in October, 2016 and of Rs. 37.25 lakhs uptil 8.11.2016 i.e. in the period between 1.10.2016 to 8.11.2016, the assessee had suddenly made cash sales to the tune of Rs. 4.05 crores to unidentifiable small customers.He held that the assessee had not satisfactorily explained the credit of Rs. 3.68 crores recorded as cash sales in his books during the period 1.10.2016 to 30.10.2016, he held the same to be unexplained under section 68

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had not established that the assessee had accumulated cash in its books which was deposited on 10-11-2016. The assumptions made on the basis of comparison of sales figures of earlier years were not foolproof, as similar or higher sales had been made by the assessee in following financial year and the refusal to accept the sales shown by the assessee was not on account of any independent enquiry but only on the basis of assumptions/interpretations made by the Assessing Officer while comparing results of earlier years.

■

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition of Rs. 2.98 crores on account of unexplained cash deposit.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained moneys (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-firm, engaged in wholesale trading of sugar, regularly received cash from buyers and deposited it into its bank account - Assessee filed its return along with audit report under section 44AB and audited financial statements, disclosing turnover of Rs. 2.14 crores - Assessing Officer received information of cash deposits of about Rs. 19.02 lakhs linked to an individual who stated that bank account belonged to assessee-firm - HEADNOTE: I Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Sales) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was into business of trading and manufacturing of jewellery like gold and diamond, etc. - It had filed its return of income - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer formed a belief that there was an abnormal increase in percentage of cash sales during period 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - Further, sales did not have name of purchaser and PAN and that cash sales from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 amounting to Rs. 4.73 crores was added as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and accordingly, added to income of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to restrict addition to Rs. 3.25 crores - It was observed that assessee had furnished month-wise purchases, month-wise details, stock register, valuation of closing stock, month-wise details of cash sales, copies of VAT returns and not a single defect had been pointed out by Assessing Officer in these clinching evidences - Whether merely because there was a minor variation in cash sales during alleged period compared to previous year would not mean that assessee had inflated its sales to cover up demonetized currency - Held, yes - Whether since cash sales have already been offered as income, same could not be taxed in garb of inflation sales to cover up demonetization currency - Held, yes [Paras 22 to 27] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where cash sales were already offered as income, same could not be taxed in garb of inflation sales to cover up demonetization currency  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had claimed business promotion expenses, since all expenses were supported by bills and vouchers, duly recorded in books of account, addition by Assessing Officer in respect of said expenses was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals)  INCOME TAX : Where car running expenses were fully supported by bills and vouchers and were incurred towards petrol and regular repair and maintenance of cars, said expenses were rightly allowed by Commissioner (Appeals)

FACT: The assessee was into the business of trading and manufacturing of jewellery like gold and diamond, etc. The return for the year was electronically filed declaring income.

During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer formed a belief that there was an abnormal increase in the percentage of cash sales during the period 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016. Further, sales did not have the name of the purchaser and PAN. Cash sales from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 amounting to Rs. 4.73 crores was added as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and accordingly, added to the income of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to restrict the addition to Rs. 3.25 crores.

On cross appeal:

HELD: There is no dispute that the assessee was maintaining proper books of account which were produced before the Assessing Officer during the assessment proceedings. Month-wise details of cash deposited out of cash sale submitted during the assessment proceedings. [Para 15]

The entire quarrel revolves around the period 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 and cash sales during this period have been held to be unexplained credit under section 68. It is failed to understand how the cash sales for the period 1-10-2016 to 7-11-2016 be treated as inflated sales pursuant to demonetization, as not a single soul was aware that on 8-11-2016, the higher currencies will be demonetized. It was only on 8-11-2016 the Prime Minister announced the demonetization. [Para 16]

The only return which was revised was for the period 1-7-2016 to 30-9-2016 in which period there was no question of anybody being aware of demonetization. [Para 19]

The most peculiar fact is that on 23-12-2016, a survey operation under section 133A was carried out at the business premises of the assessee-company and not a single defect/discrepancy was found in the physical stock vis-a-vis book stock of the assessee. [Para 20]

If the allegation of the Assessing Officer is accepted that the assessee has inflated its sales during 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016, then there has to be some discrepancy in the book stock vis-a-vis physical stock, but no such discrepancy was found because no such sales were inflated by the assessee. [Para 21]

The nature of business of the assessee is not disputed that he is engaged in the wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. It is also not in dispute that in this line of business sale of jewellery in cash is normal trade practice. The books of assessee are audited by the independent Chartered Accountant and copy of audit report and statement of profit and loss account is filed by the assessee. It is noted from the record that the case of the assessee was taken up for scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) on the basis of CASS and desired information by the Assessing Officer were submitted by the assessee from time-to-time. After completion of assessment the Assessing Officer vide his order assessed the income of the assessee by making a single addition of Rs. 80 lakh out of the total cash deposited being the demonetized currency for an amount of Rs. 84 lakh. The assessee is selling the jewellery in cash in past year also and the assessee in his submission explained that in fact in the year under consideration the overall sales as per cent to total sales has reduced. [Para 9]

The said sum is picked as unexplained as the assessee has deposited a sum of Rs. 84 lakhs being the demonetized currency in the bank account considering the sales shown by the assessee as not genuine. Out of total sales of Rs. 1.86 crores made in the year under consideration only a sum of Rs. 80 lakh not considered as genuine. The only reasons that was advanced that the details of the buyers showing complete name, address and phone were not verifiable. The sales shown by the assessee is supported by the following documents which were not doubted by Assessing Officer :

(a)

Bill wise detail in respect of cash sales during the period from 03-11-2016 to 8-11-2016, along with the sales sills. (b) Copy of the monthly summary of stock register. (c) Copy of sales register from the books of account of assessee for the relevant previous year. (d) Copy of cash book for the relevant previous year. (e) Copies of VAT return filed by the assessee, for the year under consideration. (f) Tax Audit Report Audited Financial Statements. [Para 9.1]

The assessee by selling the goods in cash did not violate any provision of the Income-tax Act and even the. Assessing Officer has not mentioned any of the law provision to disbelieve the sales so made by the assessee. All the sales made by the assessee is supported by a commercial invoice duly complied with the value added tax (VAT) provision and the related VAT is also paid by the assessee. The invoices issued is also reported in VAT return filed and the sales has been accepted by the VAT authority without any adverse remark and in fact even the Assessing Officer has not made any adverse remark on the sales register and cash book submitted by the assessee to support the contentions of having been sold the goods/jewellery in cash. [Para 9.2]

The Assessing Officer accepted the opening stock, purchase, as well as the closing stock at the year-end to be genuine and correct. It is also worthwhile to mention that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and even there is no whisper in the order about any defects in the books of account. The Assessing Officer has not brought any material on record to establish that the sale bills were bogus or any evidences indicating that sales were bogus. The Assessing Officer is wrong in not accepting the declared cash sales as not verifiable which are recorded in books of account which were found to be correct and complete. It was also noted that the assessee has undertaken cash sales of Rs. 1.86 crores. Out of the total cash sales, cash sales amounting to Rs. 80 lakhs has been found to be non-genuine and added under section 68. Explanation offered to substantiate the cash sales has been arbitrarily rejected without holding that the sales is duly recorded in the books and is also supported by the various records produced in the assessment proceedings. [Para 9.5]

Respectfully following the consistent view and after considering the factual matrix of the cash on hand the addition made cannot be sustained and therefore, the addition of Rs. 80 lakhs made under section 68 is vacated as the same cannot be made without rejecting the books of account of the assessee regularly maintained by the assessee and the said cash deposited is duly supported by the entries passed in the books of account and part of the sale accepted by the Assessing Officer. [Para 9.8]

Even those persons who responded to notice under section 133(6) could not substantiate the source of funds. Therefore, he rejected cash sales made during demonetisation period and taxed cash deposits under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]
[2015] 59 taxmann.com 430 (Mumbai)[20-02-2015] Asht Laxmi Diamond & Jewellery  vs. Income-tax Officer, 21 (1) (1), Mumbai

HEADNOTE: Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh during demonetisation period - Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that there was abnormal increase in cash sales during October 2016 and some cash sales were made to unidentified persons - It was noted that no discrepancy was found in assessee's audited books of account, VAT returns, cash book, stock register, purchase register or sales register - It was further noted that assessee had established a direct nexus between cash sales, stock movement and cash deposits, and Assessing Officer had neither disturbed stock records nor rejected sales - Whether once AO had accepted sales and assessee had substantially established on basis of financials that there was a direct nexus of cash sales with closing stock, then addition under section 68 was not justified - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh in its bank account during the demonetisation period.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that there was an unusual increase in cash sales during October 2016 and held that the cash sales recorded immediately before demonetisation were non-genuine and represented unaccounted money introduced into the books.

■

After allowing credit for estimated cash-in-hand and estimated genuine cash sales, the Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 and taxed the same under section 115BBE.

■

On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

■

In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the cash sales were duly recorded in regular books of account and supported by VAT returns, cash book, ledger accounts, stock register, purchase register, sales register and audited financial statements. It was further submitted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor disputed purchases or stock movement.

HELD: ■

After taking into consideration the submissions and facts, there is substance in the contention of the Authorised Representative that without pointing out any discrepancy in the book of accounts as maintained by the assessee, the VAT returns, cash book, ledger, stock register, purchase register, sales register, sundry creditors and debtors, which were duly audited, the disallowance has been made. It is the considered view of the Tribunal that abnormal growth in the cash sales and that certain parties were not identified to whom the cash sales were made, are vague grounds, to make addition when assessee has demonstrated that there was direct co-relation cash outflow and from the books of account the cash deposits in the bank account were made. It is found outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected and was not inquired into or otherwise disturbed by the AO. Once the AO has accepted the sales and assessee had substantially established on the basis of financials that there is a direct nexus of the cash sales with the closing stock, then addition u/s 68 is not justified. During demonetization period it was quite possible that the cash sales would increase for the reason also that customers holding the demonetized currency wanted to use the same for making cash investment in gold.
