and had also pointed out that even prior to demonetization, the assessee had deposited substantial amount in cash in the bank to the tune of Rs. 20.32 crores from April to October, 2016. He had explained that being retailer in pan-masala products, their sales were mainly in cash, and therefore, the cash deposits was not only during the demonetization period, but also prior and post-demonetization also. [Para 9.1] It is evident from the above that the assessee had clearly demonstrated that the entire cash deposited during demonetization could not be treated as unexplained; that its scale of business operations was huge and nature of business was such that 90 per cent of its sales was done in cash, and even prior to demonetization, the assessee had made huge cash sales commensurate to the sale made during the demonetization period. All these explanation given by the assessee was rightly taken note of by the Assessing Officer and finding anomaly to the extent of substantial increase in sales during the demonetization period, he considered it fit to treat 20 per cent of the sales as unexplained credits. The Pr. Commissioner's view that entire cash deposits during this period is to be treated as unexplained, is contrary to the facts on record, wherein the assessee has demonstrated the factum of huge turnover prior to and post-demonetization in the preceding year, and even in the succeeding year, and also factum of majority of the sales being in cash. Therefore, there was no occasion at all for the Assessing Officer to treat the entire cash deposited during the demonetization period, as unexplained credits. The facts on record could not have led to the inference that entire sales made by the assessee during the demonetization period were bogus. In fact, the inference drawn by the Assessing Officer, that only a portion of it could be treated as bogus/unexplained, was not incorrect. Therefore, the Pr. Commissioner's finding of error is based on incorrect appreciation of the facts before it, and his finding that the assessee had not been able to substantiate its explanation for cash sales completely is also not correct. In fact, as rightly found by the Assessing Officer, to a great extent his explanation was substantiated that the majority of sales made by the assessee was in cash, but it was only vis-à-vis abnormal incremental sales made during the demonetization period, the Assessing Officer refused to agree with the assessee. Also the finding of the Pr. Commissioner therefore that the Assessing Officer completely disagreed with the assessee regarding its explanation and found the explanation of the assessee to be unsatisfactory for the entire cash deposits, is also incorrect. As noted above, the Assessing Officer was dissatisfied not with the explanation of the entire cash deposits, but only partially in view of the abnormal increase in the sales shown by the assessee during that period. [Para 10]

In view of the above, the finding of the Pr. Commissioner that the entire cash deposits during the demonetization ought to have been treated as unexplained credit under section 68 could not have been inferred from the facts on record, and there is no error as such in the order of the Assessing Officer in this regard. The order passed by the Pr. Commissioner under section 263 holding the assessment order erroneous so as to cause prejudice to the revenue is therefore not sustainable in law and is set aside. The grounds raised by the assessee are allowed in above terms. [Para 11]

Investigations following a search on a land aggregator (LCPL) led to seizure of electronic Evernote records and statements indicating cash payments to landowners at Madambakkam. A search at the assessee’s premises followed. In relation to the 1.41-acre sale registered at about Rs.1.27 crores, the assessee’s statement under section 132(4) acknowledged total consideration of about Rs.5.99 crores including about Rs.4.72 crores in cash; during cross-examination on 10.08.2021 of the aggregator’s director, he maintained cash payment of Rs.4.72 crores, while the assessee disputed the quantum and, in a revised computation, admitted only Rs.84.60 lakhs as cash. In another Madambakkam sale of about 2.12 acres registered at about Rs.1.91 crores, the assessee’s statement recorded cash receipt of about Rs.6.78 crores.

■

For the 1.41-acre sale, the AO issued a show-cause to tax about Rs.4.72 crores cash and, relying on the assessee’s section 132(4) admission, corroborative seized materials and the cross-examined witness’s confirmation, added the full Rs.4.72 crores to the consideration. For the 2.12-acre sale, based on seized material and statements, the AO concluded total consideration at about Rs.8.91 crores (about Rs.1.91 crores by banking channels and about Rs.6.99 crores in cash) and made a corresponding addition to long-term capital gains.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A), for the 1.41-acre sale, relied on Evernote entries identifying the assessee and quantifying cash at about Rs.4.72 crores, the aggregator’s statements explaining contemporaneous recording and cash flows, and the assessee’s section 132(4) statement and subsequent admission letter; treating the later claim of only Rs.84.60 lakhs as a belated, unsupported retraction, the CIT(A) confirmed inclusion of about Rs.4.72 crores as on-money. For the 2.12-acre sale, the CIT(A) confirmed inclusion of about Rs.6.99 crores cash over the registered amount.

■

In instant appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that search statements were made under stress and later retracted. Evernote data were unilateral third-party records without proof of actual cash movement. It further contended that cross-examination clarified that only Rs.84.60 lakhs was received in the first sale and that no assets/investments/expenditure traceable to the larger sums were found despite investigation.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of gold bullion/jewellery. A search under section 132 was carried out on 22-12-2016 at the residential premises of ‘K’ and ‘A’, partners of JMK Export. Consequently, a search and seizure operation was also carried out in the residential premises of ‘M’, erstwhile director of ‘RBPL’ on 23-12-2016. Simultaneously, survey action under section 133A was conducted at the business premises of some other entities namely, JMK Exports, Harrison Diamonds Pvt. Ltd., JMK Jewels Pvt. Ltd. and RBPL.

During the course of search and survey operations, a large number of incriminating materials including E-mail and SMS conversations amongst parties was found. During the course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of ‘M’, statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he stated that cash deposits amounting to Rs. 32.82 crores made in the bank accounts of RBPL post-demonetization, was given to him by ‘R’, one of the directors of assessee company, for depositing in the bank accounts and thereafter transferring funds to specified bank accounts on commission basis. Based on the statement of ‘M’ and other incriminating materials allegedly found in course of search and survey operations, the Assessing Officer, in the course of assessment proceedings of ‘M’, recorded a satisfaction note for initiation of proceedings under section 153C in the case of assessee for assessment years 2011-12 to 2016-17.

For the impugned assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 143(2) requiring assessee to furnish certain information regarding the alleged cash deposits of Rs. 32.82 crores in the bank accounts of RBPL and commission of Rs. 1.52 crore paid to ‘M’ for depositing the cash. In response to the query raised, the assessee furnished detailed submissions completely denying the allegation of cash deposits made into the bank accounts of RBPL through ‘M’.

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified

3. With respect to the deposit of the cash on hand with the various bank, the explanation of the assessee that no such bank was accepting such a huge cash at one go and therefore assessee had to deposit the cash in various banks.

The assessee also submitted that that in the same bank assessee has deposited cash in its 2 different branches which itself proves that the banks were not accepting such a huge deposit. Even otherwise, it was submitted correctly that merely because the cash holding as on 8/11/2016 was not deposited immediately cannot lead to conclusion that assessee did not have that cash.

It can merely lead to a suspicion but based on this addition cannot be made without making further enquiry and conclusively proving that assessee did not have that kind of cash available with it.

Even otherwise, if the assessee had to introduce his unaccounted money he would have deposited it at the first instance.

4. ITAT observed that assessee also filed its VAT returns, which are not found to be in variance with the accounting and tax records. Therefore, it cannot be substantiated that the assessee has backdated the transactions of the sale.

5. ITAT further observed that CBDT had issued various standard operating procedures under 'Operation Clean money'. Unsatisfactory/no explanation - In the absence of any cogent evidence, a bald explanation furnished by the assessee about the source of the credits in question, viz., realisation from the debtors of the erstwhile firm, in the opinion of the AO, was not satisfactory [Vijay Kumar Talwar v. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 264/[2011] 196 Taxman 136 (SC)]. Where the appellant has not been able to prove either the identity or the existence of the parties who had advanced money to it and because the defence of trade credit set up by the appellant is against the normal human conduct as no petty supplier/commission agent/fruit vendor would give money four to nine months in advance for supply of vegetables like cabbage, thus, additions held to be justified [Hacienda Farms (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 9 taxmann.com 306/198 Taxman 509 (Del.)].

Mere filing of PAN, acknowledgement of ITRs of the entry providers and bank account statement is not sufficient to discharge the onus on the assessee [CIT v. Nova Promoters & Finlease (P.) Ltd. [2012] 18 taxmann.com 217/206 Taxman 207 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. N. Tarika Properties Investment (P.) Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 525/[2014] 221 Taxman 14 (Delhi), SLP dismissed inN. Tarika Property Investment (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 51 taxmann.com 387/227 Taxman 373 (SC).

Where assessee had sold a new product launched by it on test market basis over and above its counter sale but failed to explain as to how and why such cash sales of huge amount effected only in one month of a year, AO was justified in making additions in respect of such unexplained sales [J. M. J. Essential Oil Co. v. CIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 181/259 Taxman 546 (HP), SLP dismissed inJ. M. J. Essential Oil Co. v. CIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 463/269 Taxman 202 (SC)].

Department need not to locate source of receipt - Where the assessee has failed to prove satisfactorily the source and nature of a credit entry in his books, and it is held that the relevant amount is the income of the assessee, it is not necessary for the department to locate its exact source [A. Govindarajulu Mudaliar v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 807 (SC); CIT v. M. Ganapathi Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 623 (SC)].

The above principle applies alike to cases in which an entry is found in the books of account of the assessee and to cases in which no such entry is found. If the amount represented the income of the assessee of the previous year, it was liable to be included in the total income and an enquiry whether for the purpose of bringing the amount to tax it was from a business activity or from some other source was not relevant [CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1969] 72 ITR 807 (SC)].

Mere unsatisfactory explanation does not result in treating cash credits as income - In the absence of a satisfactory explanation, the unexplained cash credit may be charged to income-tax, therefore, the unsatisfactoriness of the explanation would not automatically result in deeming the amount credited in the books as income of the assessee [CIT v. Smt. P. K. Noorjahan [1999] 103 Taxman 382 (SC)]. The word 'may' indicate that the intention of the Legislature is to confer a discretion on the AO in the matter of treating the source of investment or credit which had not been satisfactorily explained as income of an assessee, but it is not obligatory to treat such source as income in every case where the explanation offered was found to be not satisfactory [CIT v. Pragati Co-operative Bank Ltd. [2005] 149 Taxman 149 (Guj.)].

Even after rejecting the explanation given by the assessees if found unacceptable, the crucial aspect, whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, it should be inferred the sums credited in the books of the assessees constituted income of the PY must receive the consideration of the authorities provided the assessees rebut the evidence and the inference drawn to reject the explanation offered as unsatisfactory [CIT v. P. Mohanakala [2007] 161 Taxman 169 (SC)].

Alternative explanations - The provision does not debar the assessee from offering alternative explanation and if either of them is accepted, the cash credit cannot be charged as the income of the assessee [Addl. CIT v. Ghai Lime Stone Co. [1982] 11 Taxman 58 (MP)]. Also see, Dhansiram Agarwalla v. CIT [1995] 81 Taxman 1 (Gauh.).

As far as the sales alleged to have been made to bogus entities controlled by entry operator Sonu Punjabi is concerned it is observed that in course of assessment proceeding as well as before the first appellate authority the assessee has furnished various documentary evidences, such as, party-wise details of purchase and sale for the entire year, VAT returns and VAT assessment orders, item-wise stock register and purchase invoices, confirmation from the suppliers, audited books of account, quantitative tally of purchase and sale, etc. It is also a fact that the suppliers from whom the assessee purchases gold/bullion confirmed the transactions in response to notices issued under section 133(6). Pertinently, no deficiency or discrepancy was found either in the books of account maintained by the assessee or the documentary evidences furnished. This is so because, neither the Assessing Officer nor the first appellate authority have returned any adverse inference, either in relation to the books of account maintained by the assessee or the documentary evidences furnished. Merely because the notices issued under section 133(6) and summons issued under section 131 returned unserved or remained unanswered, cannot lead to the conclusion that sales are bogus, when there are overwhelming documentary evidences brought on record in the form of audited books of account, stock register, item-wise purchase and sales, VAT return, VAT assessment order accepting the sale transactions to demonstrate that the assessee indeed has effected the sales. [Para 13]

Similarly, in respect of sales made to RBPL the addition was made purely on conjectures and surmises. The Assessing Officer has attempted to treat the sales made by the assessee as non-genuine only because of statement recorded on oath from M stating that cash amounting to Rs. 32 crores was given to him by DL Jewellers for depositing in the bank account of RBPL. The purported cash deposit in the bank account of RBPL, even assuming it to be correct, cannot prove that the sales effected by the assessee to RBPL is non-genuine. On the contrary, it proves availability of fund with RBPL to effect the purchases from the assessee. Even in respect of the sales made to RBPL the assessee has furnished all documentary evidences including audited books of account, item-wise purchase and sales, VAT return, VAT assessment orders, stock register, etc, to prove the genuineness of sales. Admittedly, the Assessing Officer has not found any discrepancy or deficiency in the books of account and stock register maintained by the assessee. Thus, when the assessee has maintained item wise purchase and sale details as well as stock register and, moreover neither in course of survey any stock discrepancy was found nor any unaccounted cash was found, certain sales cannot be treated as bogus. More so, when one of the directors of RBPL has stated before the Assessing Officer that he had taken delivery of gold/bullion purchased from assessee. [Para 14]

Similar is the factual position qua the sales effected to Olivia and S.S Overseas, as the assessee has furnished all documentary evidences to prove the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of transaction. Thus, the assessee has sufficiently discharged the initial burden cast upon it to prove the credit entries appearing in the books of account. In fact, the first appellate authority has accepted the fact that the assessee has discharged the initial burden cast upon it. Once it is established that the initial burden cast upon the assessee has been discharged, the burden shifts to the Assessing Officer to conclusively prove that the credit entries appearing in the books of account are unexplained in terms with section 68. In the facts of the instant appeal, the Assessing Officer has failed to do so. Therefore, the amount in dispute cannot be treated as unexplained cash credit under section 68. [Para 15]

AY 2017-18 and onwards, incomes in the nature of section 68 to 69D has been made liable for being taxed at higher rate @ 60% plus surcharge of 25% making the effective tax rate at about 78% u/s 115BBE, irrespective of whether such unexplained income is suo moto offered by an assessee as income in the return of income filed u/s 139(1) or in response to notice u/s 142(1)/ 148/ 153A/ 153C, etc. The same tax rate is applicable for unexplained bullion/ jewellery/ stock/ other investment in shares and property etc. found during search or survey and offered in statement u/s 132(4) or 133A.

Prior to 01 April 2017, the question whether the undisclosed income sought to be taxed was in nature of income u/s 68 to 69D or not, or the question with regards to nature of activity from which such undisclosed income was derived, was not at all relevant as the rate of taxation was same in either case i.e. @30% only. But in view of the substantial increase of the tax rate @ 78%, this issue now has assumed huge tax implications from AY 2017–18 onwards.

Prohibition of Receipts of Cash in excess of Rs. Two Lakhs (Section 269ST of the Income Tax Act, 1961)

3. A new Section 269ST has been inserted by the Finance Act, 2017, w.e.f. 1.4.2017, for the AY 2017-18 and onwards, which provides as under:

No person shall receive an amount of two lakh rupees or more—

(a)

in aggregate from a person in a day; or

(b)

in respect of a single transaction; or

(c)

in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account.

Therefore, w.e.f. AY 2017-18 and onwards, any person who receives cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs, in aggregate from a person in a day or in respect of a single transaction or in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person shall be liable to a penalty of an amount equivalent to the amount of such cash transaction.

Certain entities/transactions have been kept outside the purview of the above provisions of section 269ST as under:

The provisions of the section 269ST shall not apply to—

(i)

any receipt by—

(a)

Government;

(b)

any banking company, post office savings bank or co-operative bank;

(ii)

transactions of the nature referred to in section 269SS;

(iii)

such other persons or class of persons or receipts, which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify.

Assessments in OCM/ Demonetisation Cases

4. The demonetisation period i.e. period from 9.11.2016 till 30.12.2016, fell in the FY 2016-17 corresponding to the AY 2017-18. So, in the regular assessments for the AY 2017-18, a large number of scrutiny cases were pertaining to the issue of huge and abnormal cash deposits during the demonetisation period.

The earlier deadline for completing regular assessments for OCM/demonetisation cases was 30.9.2019. However, due to the paucity of time, the CBDT has extended the deadline for assessing officers to complete and conclude the assessments of such OCM/demonetisation cases by December 31, 2019, which in any case was the time barring deadline for completion of regular assessment cases for the AY 2017-18, other than transfer pricing cases.

The assessing authorities have segregated such OCM cases separately for business cases and non-business cases and have analysed these in terms of various criterion.

Further, cash deposits made in a financial year have been segmented into three parts, i.e. pre demonetisation period (1.04.2016 till 8.11.2016), post demonetisation period (9.11.2016 till 31.12.2016) and total in the financial year 016-17 and corresponding period in FY 2015-16. The assessing authorities have subjected these data to analytics and have worked out the percentage increase in cash deposits against all the three combinations to derive the meaningful inferences. The analysis of month wise cash sales and deposits for demonetisation period and also the corresponding period in the FY 2015-16 have also been undertaken.

If they declare their unaccounted cash/bank deposits in PMGKY, then obviously, there would be no question of reopening their past assessments of income-tax or indirect taxes. If they do not declare in PMGKY and opt to show it as current year's turnover, then they should be able to justify it. If taxpayers are not able to justify the spurt in turnover as current year's turnover duly supported by increased purchases/stock and /or expansion of facilities, the same will be treated as unexplained income under sections 68 to 69D of Income-Tax Act, 1961 and will be taxed at proposed rate of 77.25% under section 115BBE along with penalty of 10% under proposed new section 271AAC.

There would be no need to reopen past income-tax assessments in such cases under section 147 of the Income-Tax Act, 1961. However, they could face problems in indirect taxes as they have explained it as "current turnover" and if explanation falls flat then past assessments could be reopened.

A prudent course of action for businesses/businessmen would be as follows:

To the extent the spurt in turnover is due to increase in digital sales, there is nothing to worry

There is nothing to fear if a spurt in cash sales is explainable by adequate purchases/stock/adequate expansion of facilities /increase in manpower

In both the above cases, show turnover in books and returns and pay normal taxes as usual and relax.

If unaccounted money available in the form of cash or deposits in bank accounts, better not to show it as current year's cash sales if one cannot satisfactorily explain as above the resulting increase in turnover. In such cases, better to show, declare such cash in PMGKY by paying 49.9% (tax, surcharge and penalty) and depositing 25% in PMGKY bonds.

During assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer after recording the assessee's statement regarding source of purchase of drafts amounting to Rs. 4,49,527, observed that the assessee claimed to have purchased drafts from cash available during normal business transactions, but it had made credit sales to almost all the parties whose accounts were obtained under section 133(6) and, therefore, there was no possibility of the assessee having heavy cash in hand. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed (a) that the assessee was doing very good business in garments and had also daily sale proceeds, (b) goods released by custom authorities, after payment of customs duty and demurrage charges, were indeed available for sale and (c) the assessee utilised the sale proceeds for making further remittances to the Customs Collector for releasing more goods. Therefore, the according to the Tribunal, the entire amount of Rs. 4,49,527 representing the five drafts could not be said to be available in the hands of the assessee at a time; the drafts having been sent during the course of four months, the money must have rotated and it was appropriate to at best adopt the peak amount of Rs. 1,95,000 as money available from unexplained sources. "Cash" has been defined by the dictionaries as under:

"Money in the form of notes and coins, rather than cheques or credit cards" [dictionary.cambridge.org]. "Money in the form of coins or banknotes, especially that issued by a government" [dictionary.com].

Unlike the proviso to section 44AD(1), which prescribes the permissible mode of the receipt for 6% presumptive income, the first proviso to Explanation (b)(ii) to section 44AD explicitly uses the term "cash" and the second proviso to said Explanation provides a deeming fiction to treat the non-account payee cheque and draft as cash. The intention to use the "cash" in the first proviso, in a negative sense, is to discourage the cash transactions. Thus, to compute the 5% threshold, only cash receipts should be considered, and any receipts by way of journal entry should not be considered in the 5% threshold. Similarly, sales made on a credit basis, even if funds are not realised, should not form part of the 5% threshold.

Inter-bank transfers

■ The Tribunal now deals with the component claimed to represent inter-bank transfers between the assessee's own accounts. The assessee submitted a detailed bifurcation of these transactions before the Commissioner (Appeals), supported by date-wise entries drawn from the Axis Bank statement, clearly identifying them as internal fund movements between current and savings accounts held by the assessee in the same bank. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the appellate order, has accepted this explanation after noting that these transactions are duly recorded as contra entries and correspond to internal transfers, with no third-party involvement. The entries are supported by bank statements, do not involve any unexplained cash or credit from external sources, and are verifiable from the assessee's own records. It is also noted that no adverse finding has been recorded by the Assessing Officer in respect of this component, as the source-wise bifurcation was not before him at the reassessment stage. During appellate proceedings before the Tribunal, no material has been brought on record by the Departmental Representative to controvert the assessee's explanation or to dispute the conclusion drawn by the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 31]

■

Accordingly, no infirmity is found in the conclusion of the Commissioner (Appeals) in treating the amount of Rs.12.04 crore as explained inter-bank transfers. The same does not attract the mischief of section 68, and the deletion to this extent is upheld. [Para 32]

■

The assessee claimed that a substantial portion of cash deposits aggregating to Rs 31.75 crore made in the account with Multi-State Urban Co-operative Credit Society Ltd. were sourced from cash sales carried out in the normal course of business and, in part, by redepositing earlier cash withdrawals. In support, the assessee submitted a tabular reconciliation, extracts from the cash book, and bank statements as part of reply dated 05.02.2024, which were placed on record for the first time before the Commissioner (Appeals). These documents sought to demonstrate the trail of cash withdrawals from Axis Bank and its subsequent redeposit into the Society's account. The Commissioner (Appeals), acknowledged that the assessee had placed on record a summary chart and cash book evidencing cash withdrawals and re-deposits. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) also expressly recorded that the assessee failed to give a specific breakup as to which portion of the available cash was deposited with the Society and which part constituted current cash receipts. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that this bifurcation was material and that the claim was not conclusively established. Nevertheless, while finalizing the computation of unexplained income, the Commissioner (Appeals) appears to have treated Rs. 31.75 crore as explained, without subjecting the claim to independent verification, third-party cross-check, or reconciliation with stock records or VAT returns. [Para 33]

■

At the outset, it is noted that the explanation regarding cash deposits is based entirely on internal documents such as the cash book and bank statements. No primary evidence has been placed on record to prove that actual sales took place against which cash was received. The supporting invoices are VAT-free and no VAT returns or sales tax records were submitted either before the AO or the Commissioner (Appeals). Further, no stock register or inventory movement summary has been filed to establish that there was actual movement of goods justifying such cash sales. It is also not demonstrated whether the goods sold were exempt under VAT laws, or if any exemption certificate was filed. [Para 34]

There is no dispute with regard to the amount of cash deposits into her bank account during the demonetization period and the explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of opening cash balance available as on 8-11-2016 as per the cash book maintained for the relevant financial year. In fact, the Assessing Officer never disputed the fact that the assessee has explained the cash deposit into the bank account out of cash balance available as per books of account. The Assessing Officer disbelieved the arguments of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits out of sales declared from 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016 and claimed that, there is abnormal deviation in the sales declared by the assessee for the above period when compared to the earlier months and subsequent months. The Assessing Officer further noted that, the assessee has furnished VAT returns belatedly to cover up the backdated sale bills issued to the customers to show sufficient cash balance in the books of account to explain cash deposits into the bank account. Therefore, he disbelieved the evidences filed by the assessee and assessed the cash deposits as unexplained money under section 69A. [Para 19]

■

There is no dispute with regard to the fact that, the cash balance shown in the books of account as on 8-11-2016 is supported by necessary sales bills issued towards sale of jewellery from 1-11-2016 to 7-11-2016. It is also not in dispute that, the assessee was having sufficient stock-in-hand to explain the sale bills issued to the customers between 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016. The sales declared by the assessee are recorded in the books of account and also part of the turnover declared for the year under consideration which suffered taxation. Once the assessee has recorded sales in the books of account, which is supported by necessary sales bills with a corresponding stock-in-hand, the Assessing Officer ought not to have made additions towards cash deposits as unexplained money only on the ground that, there is abnormal variation in cash sales during the demonetization period when compared to earlier or subsequent periods. It was a well-known fact during the demonetization period that, there was a mad rush in jewellery shops for purchasing gold jewellery out of demonetized currency when the demonetization was announced on 8-11-2016. In the instant case, going by the facts available on record, the assessee has reported major sales on 7-11-2016, which is the previous day of the demonetization was announced, and from the details furnished by the assessee, it is very clear that, the assessee has made sales of gold jewellery in cash which is the source for cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period on 14-11-2016. Since the cash deposited into the bank account is supported by necessary cash balance available as per books of account maintained by the assessee which was further supported by necessary sales bills, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards cash deposits under section 69A as unexplained money cannot be sustained. Although the Assessing Officer has disbelieved the sales on the basis of VAT returns submitted by the assessee for the month of November, 2016 and claimed that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover backdated sales, but going by the history of the assessee in filing the VAT returns, it is evident that, for all the months in the financial year 2016-17, the assessee has filed VAT returns belatedly and from the above, it is very clear that, the argument of the Assessing Officer that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover up backdated sales, is contrary to the evidence available on record and cannot be accepted. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A. Thus, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made under section 69A. [Para 20]

The assessee was engaged in the business of gold bullion/jewellery. A search under section 132 was carried out on 22-12-2016 at the residential premises of ‘K’ and ‘A’, partners of JMK Export. Consequently, a search and seizure operation was also carried out in the residential premises of ‘M’, erstwhile director of ‘RBPL’ on 23-12-2016. Simultaneously, survey action under section 133A was conducted at the business premises of some other entities namely, JMK Exports, Harrison Diamonds Pvt. Ltd., JMK Jewels Pvt. Ltd. and RBPL.

During the course of search and survey operations, a large number of incriminating materials including E-mail and SMS conversations amongst parties was found. During the course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of ‘M’, statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he stated that cash deposits amounting to Rs. 32.82 crores made in the bank accounts of RBPL post-demonetization, was given to him by ‘R’, one of the directors of assessee company, for depositing in the bank accounts and thereafter transferring funds to specified bank accounts on commission basis. Based on the statement of ‘M’ and other incriminating materials allegedly found in course of search and survey operations, the Assessing Officer, in the course of assessment proceedings of ‘M’, recorded a satisfaction note for initiation of proceedings under section 153C in the case of assessee for assessment years 2011-12 to 2016-17.

For the impugned assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 143(2) requiring assessee to furnish certain information regarding the alleged cash deposits of Rs. 32.82 crores in the bank accounts of RBPL and commission of Rs. 1.52 crore paid to ‘M’ for depositing the cash. In response to the query raised, the assessee furnished detailed submissions completely denying the allegation of cash deposits made into the bank accounts of RBPL through ‘M’.

However, the Assessing Officer was not convinced with the submissions of the assessee. Heavily relying upon the statement of ‘M’ recorded under section 132(4) and some CCTV footages obtained from the Kotak Mahindra Bank, wherein, some close associate/relatives of ‘R’ purportedly were seen carrying bags full of old currency, the Assessing Officer ultimately held that cash amounting to Rs. 32.82 crores deposited in various bank accounts of RBPL post-demonetization was actually given by assessee. He also held that for depositing cash in the bank accounts of RBPL through ‘M’, assessee had paid commission of Rs.1.52 crores to ‘M’. The Assessing Officer made addition of alleged cash deposits of Rs. 32.82 crores and alleged commission paid of Rs.1.52 crores under section 69A for the impugned AY. Besides the aforesaid additions, the AO made a couple of other additions amounting to Rs. 6.66 Lac representing labour expenses and Rs.1.17 cr representing unexplained liability on account of sundry creditors and unexplained purchases.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) called for a remand report and held that since the date of recording of satisfaction had to be construed as the date of search and seizure operation as contemplated under section 153C, the Assessing Officer was justified in initiating proceedings under section 153C and passing the assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 153C. So far as merits are concerned, Commissioner (Appeals) restricted the addition under section 69A to Rs. 4.68 crores. Consequently, he proportionately reduced the addition made on account of commission expenditure from Rs.1.52 crores to Rs. 21.63 lakhs. and confirmed the rest of the additions.

A search and survey action under section 133A was carried out on the premises of assessee-company, engaged in the business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery and bullion. It was noticed that the assessee had deposited huge amounts in its bank account after demonetization was announced.

During the course of survey, a statement of the company's MD was recorded wherein he stated that the amount deposited was received from 2153 customers on 8-11-2016 and each customer had paid an advance of less than 2 lakhs for purchase of bullions. Said bullions were to be purchased from ALG, owned by one NS. He thus filed a declaration of Rs. 40 crores under the PMGKY scheme, however, withdrew same later on.

Subsequently, the assessee filed its return admitting an income of Rs. 1.42 crores after adjustment of certain brought forward losses. The case was selected for scrutiny and certain statutory notices were issued on it.

The Assessing Officer completed assessment by making addition of Rs. 40.11 crores under section 68 and assessed the assessee's income at the rate of 60 per cent as per section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the additions made under section 68 to the extent of Rs. 28.37 crores on various ground; firstly, that the statement of third party given before police/E.D. was not contradicted by the AO; secondly, no inquiry was made from the parties whose details had been given by third party and thirdly, the deposit of cash by the third party in the account of the assessee has not been disputed by the Assessing Officer.

A search and seizure action under section 132 was carried out in the case of the ''Rubberwala Group'', including RHIL, its promoters and directors TS and key employee of the group, IA. For the assessment year 2017-18, an addition of Rs. 1 lakh was made under section 69C.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected the contentions of the assessee, holding that the right of cross-examination was not absolute, that adequate opportunity had been granted, and that the material relied upon constituted corroborated digital evidence supported by sworn statements and disclosure by the developer group.

48.4.5-9 How to reckon the limit of Rs. 2,00,000? - Section 269ST is applicable when any payment is received of Rs. 2,00,000 or more

(a)

in aggregate from a person in a day;

(b)

in respect of a single transaction; or

(c)

in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person. Illustration 1 - Suppose Mr. X had made credit sales of Rs. 1,00,000, Rs. 1,50,000 and Rs. 50,000 on three different dates against different orders and different bills to Mr. Y. Mr. Y pays Rs. 3,00,000 by cash on 01.04.2023 against these bills. This will amount to receiving Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in aggregate from a person in a day" and thus violate section 269ST. If suppose Rs. 1,00,000 cash is paid on 01.04.2023 and Rs. 1,00,000 cash is paid on 02.04.2023 and Rs. 1,00,000 cash on 03-04-2023, it will not amount to a violation of section 269ST as Rs. 2,00,000 limit is not made up in either of the three ways in (a) or (b) or (c) above.

Illustration 2 - Suppose a caterer takes an order for a wedding and receives Rs. 15,00,000 in cash from his customer and gives item-wise bills for various services, and each bill doesn't exceed Rs. 2,00,000 and Rs. 15,00,000 is received in cash on different dates and cash received on any one day is less than Rs. 2,00,000. This splitting of bills and payments day-wise will not help as all these payments are "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person".

Illustration 3 - Suppose a credit sale of Rs. 2,00,000 is made, and the buyer makes two cash payments of Rs. 1,00,000 per day to the seller on two different dates. Section 269ST is attracted as Rs. 2,00,000 cash limit is reached "in respect of a single transaction".

Illustration 4 - Suppose X, a contractor, undertakes a contract for the renovation of a house and charges Rs. 5,00,000 (Rs. 2,00,000 related to civil work and remodelling, Rs. 2,00,000 related to woodwork, Rs. 50,000 for plumbing and Rs. 50,000 related to electrical work). He bills separately for each of these and receives three cash payments of Rs. 1,50,000 each on 2-9-2023, 3-9-2023 and 4-9-2023 and balance Rs. 50,000 in cash on 5-9-2023. Section 269ST is attracted as the sum received in cash is Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person"

Illustration 5 - Suppose in Illustration 4 above the contractor receives Rs. 1,99,000 in cash and a balance Rs. 3,01,000 in cheque. In this case, section 269ST is not attracted as the cash receipt is less than Rs. 2,00,000.

Illustration 6 - Suppose the owner of a house demolishes it and sells the resulting debris (malba) for cash amounting to Rs. 3,00,000. Section 269ST is attracted whether the transaction is business or personal.

Illustration 7 - Suppose I sell my old car for Rs. 2,50,000 and receive a cash advance of Rs. 75,000 on 2-10-2023 and Rs. 1,75,000 in cash on 3-10-2023 on delivery. Section 269ST is contravened here as the sum received in cash is Rs. 2,00,000 or more "in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person" as also "in respect of a single transaction" even though aggregate sum received in cash in a single day is less than Rs. 2,00,000.

Cash deposits made out of cash sales recorded in post demonetisation period treated as unexplained cash credits u/s 68 of the Income Tax Act. The text of section 68 of the Income Tax Act is being reproduced as under:

68. Cash Credits

Where any sum is found credited in the books of an assessee maintained for any previous year, and the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source thereof or the explanation offered by him is not, in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, satisfactory, the sum so credited may be charged to income-tax as the income of the assessee of that previous year:"

From the plain reading of the above section 68, it is abundantly clear that the essential and mandatory pre-requisite for making an addition under this section is that the unexplained sum must be found credited in the books of an assessee maintained by him for any previous year. If the assessee is not maintaining any books of accounts, then addition u/s 68 is unsustainable. The existence of books of account is a condition precedent for invoking of the power u/s 68 of the Act.

The reliance in this regard is placed on the following Judicial Pronouncements viz.

(i)

Judgement of Hon'ble Guwahati High Court in the case of Anand ram Raytani v. CIT, [1997] 223 ITR 544;

The relevant extract of the aforesaid judgement (para 8) is reproduced below for Your Honours' ready reference,

"8. ............We have gone through Section 68 of the Act. The Assessing Officer before invoking the power under Section 68 of the Act must be satisfied that there are books of account maintained by the assessee and the cash credit is recorded in the said books of account and if the assessee fails to satisfy the Assessing Officer, the said sum so credited has to be charged to income-tax as the income of the assessee of that previous year. The existence of books of account is a condition precedent for invoking of the power. Discharging of burden is a subsequent condition. If the first point is not fulfilled the question of burden of proof does not arise."

Whether Bank Pass Book can be considered as Books of Accounts u/s 68?

In several judicial pronouncements especially in the case of CIT v. Bhaichand N. Gandhi [1983] 141 ITR 67/11 Taxman 59 (Bom.), it has been held that the bank statement can't be considered as books of accounts, for the purpose of making addition u/s 68 of the Income Tax Act.

(iii)

Rejection of assessee's claim of cash deposits out of earlier cash withdrawals due to time gap between such withdrawal and the cash deposits

In a recent decision the Hon'ble ITAT Delhi, in the case of "Gordhan, Delhi v. Dy. CIT dated 19/10/2019, have held that no addition can be made u/s 68 on the sole reason that there was a time gap of five months between the date of withdrawals from bank account and redeposit of the same in the bank account, unless the AO demonstrates that the amount in question has been used by the assessee for any other purpose.

Similarly, in the case of 'Asstt. CIT v. Baldev Raj Charla [2009] 121 TTJ 366 (Delhi)' also it has been held that merely because there was a time gap between withdrawal of cash and cash deposits, explanation of the assessee could not be rejected and addition on account of cash deposit could not be made particularly when there was no finding recorded by the assessing officer that apart from depositing this cash into bank as explained by the assessee, there was any other purpose, for which it was used by the assessee

One can also place his reliance on the decision of Ld. Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Kulwant rai [2007] 291 ITR 36/163 Taxman 585 wherein the honourable Delhi High Court has held as under:-

As regards the first and second statements of VDT, the same having been recorded not during the proceedings pertaining to the assessee, but during survey in the case of VDT, the copies of the same having not been supplied to the assessee prior to assessment and supplied only as attached with the assessment order and opportunity for cross-examining VDT in respect of those statements having not been accorded to the assessee, the same could not be read/used against the assessee. The question of the assessee's self asking for cross examination of VDT in respect of those two statements, dated 30/31-3-2000 did not arise when the copies of the same had not been supplied to the assessee before making assessment. Besides, it is the basic principle of law that without affording opportunity of cross-examination, a statement recorded at the back of the assessee will not partake of the nature of evidence against the assessee and cannot be read/used against the assessee. Even apart, the said statements had been retracted by VDT vide his letter dated 4-4-2000. In the said retraction VDT had mentioned that those statements were given by him as directed by the department and he was under a state of total confusion. He had also mentioned in the said retraction letter that he had made the purchases, correctly issued bills, accounted for in his books and also furnished to the Sales-tax Department. He had supported the purchase of 71 carats of diamonds from the assessee by his affidavit and statement dated 25-10-2002 recorded by the Assessing Officer when he made his attendance before the Assessing Officer in response to the summons issued to him by the Assessing Officer during assessment proceedings pertaining to the present assessee. The sale of diamonds by the present assessee to VDT was also supported by VDT's purchase bill; the payments had been made by VDT to the assessee by account payee cheques and the same was corroborated by bank statement. That transaction of sale of 71 carats of loose diamonds by the assessee to VDT had already been accepted in the assessee's original assessment under section 143(3). There was no evidence on record that any cash amount was paid back by the assessee to VDT. The possession of loose diamonds by the assessee was proved by the assessee's declaration under VDIS. As such, there was no justification for holding the sale of loose diamonds by the assessee to 'DD' as bogus sale or as a mere paper transaction and not genuine, and in turn for making/sustaining addition. The addition of Rs. 11,18,250 made in the income of the assessee was, therefore, liable to be deleted.

Addition u/s 69A & tax u/s 115BBE are justified w.r.t. unexplained cash equal to cash seized introduced by assessee in the books on the date of the search

In K.Gomathi v. DCIT, Central Circle-2(3), Chennai ; ITAT order, dated 19-10-2022, it was held that addition u/s 69A & tax u/s 115BBE are justified w.r.t. unexplained cash equal to cash seized introduced by assessee in the books on the date of the search. The Tribunal held as follows:

Where cash seized of Rs. 1,73,40,790 seized during the search was explained by assessee as repayments by borrowers in his financing business and same was shown in P& L account as amounts accepted as income during search with corresponding entry in balance sheet of cash seized but assessee continued with same cash balance as on date of search with reducing cash seized from cash in hand, it amounts to introduction of cash in books of an amount equal to cash seized on date of search for which source is to be explained satisfactorily.

Where assessee failed to explain satisfactorily the source of the cash, addition of the amount under section 69A and tax on the addition under section 155BBE by AO were justified and such action did not amount to treating the seized cash as unexplained income as action was with reference to fresh cash introduced in the books as on date of search. The explanation of cash so introduced was business income was rightly not accepted by AO and CIT(A) as business income was subsumed in the cash seized duly accounted in Profit and loss account with corresponding entry as cash seized in the balance sheet.

In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and we find that there is no abnormal deviation in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the AO that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The AO could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, in our considered view, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. In our considered view, there cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, yearend sales, etc. Therefore, in our considered view, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable.

16. Coming back to second observation of the AO in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crs. from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crs. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. We have perused relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, we find force in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of accounts of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of accounts as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, in our considered view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, in our considered view, there is no reason for the AO to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account.

■ The Commissioner (Appeals) has sought to distinguish the co-ordinate Bench decision in Rajesh Jain v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal Nos. 3841 and 3842, dated 26/11/2024] primarily on the ground that the assessee therein was subjected to search, whereas the present assessee was not. This distinction is wholly irrelevant to the core issue of evidentiary reliance on third-party material without cross-examination. Considerable reliance has been placed on the alleged admission by the Rubberwala Group that it received on-money and offered the same to tax. This, however, cannot be determinative of the assessee's liability. The ratio of Rajesh Jain rests squarely on two pillars: absence of corroborative material against the assessee, and denial of cross-examination despite specific request. [Para 8.14]

■

Both these features are present in the instant case. Judicial discipline mandates that a co-ordinate Bench decision on identical facts be followed unless shown to be per incuriam, which is not the case here. [Para 8.15]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) relied on various decisions to contend that providing cross examination of IA was not required. These authorities do not lay down a blanket proposition dispensing with cross-examination. On the contrary, they consistently hold that the requirement depends on the nature of evidence, its role in the adjudication, and the prejudice caused. In the present case: the assessee has categorically denied having made any cash payment; no cash, diary, or corroborative document was found from the assessee; the alleged diary, though repeatedly referred to in statements, was never recovered; and the entire edifice of the addition rests on third-party statements and electronic data interpreted by those very persons. [Para 8.16]

■

In such circumstances, denial of cross-examination causes manifest prejudice and cannot be brushed aside as a mere procedural irregularity. [Para 8.17]

■

It is found that, in identical factual circumstances relating to alleged cash ''on-money'' payments for purchase of shops in Platinum Mall from the Rubberwala Group, the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Praveen Khetaramm Purohit v. DCIT (ITA Nos. 4742 to 4744/Mum/2025) has deleted similar additions. The Bench also placed reliance upon another decision of the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Akhraj Pukhraaj Chopra v. DCIT and Lilaram v. DCIT in ITAs No.5553 and 5554/Mum/2025, vide order dated 12-11-2025, wherein similar addition was made on the basis of search and seizure action on Rubberwala Group. [Para 8.18]

■

The consistent factual matrix emerging from above decisions is that the additions were made solely on the basis of (i) statements of IA, an employee of the Rubberwala Group, recorded during the course of search, and (ii) data contained in an Excel sheet retrieved from a pen drive found from his possession. No incriminating material was found from the assessee. The assessee, from the inception, categorically denied having paid any cash over and above the documented consideration. [Para 8.19]

■

The Co-ordinate Bench, after an exhaustive examination of the facts, has held that such third-party statements and electronic records, uncorroborated by any independent evidence and not directly linking the assessee to the alleged cash payment, do not constitute credible evidence for sustaining an addition under section 69. The Bench further noted that, despite specific requests, the assessee was neither confronted with the complete adverse material nor afforded an opportunity to cross-examine IA or any other person whose statements were relied upon. [Para 8.20]

■

It is well settled that while the rigours of the Evidence Act do not strictly apply to income-tax proceedings, additions must nevertheless be founded on material which is reliable, cogent, and has a direct nexus with the assessee. Third-party statements, cannot be treated as conclusive unless supported by independent corroborative evidence. At best, such material may give rise to suspicion, but suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of proof. [Para 8.21]

The main issue in instant appeal is addition made under section 69. [Para 15]

■

It is clear from decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that he has adopted theory of peak credit to sustain addition of Rs.4 crore and allowed relief of Rs.32.17 crores. Peak credit theory applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) is not acceptable since the Commissioner (Appeals) has not brought on record peculiar facts of case which compelled him to apply peak credit theory in picture. The Commissioner (Appeals) has simply taken amount of highest balance in the bank account and has treated it as ''''peak credit'''', which is not correct. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to take note that from 17 date-wise transactions, it can be observed that the cash deposits were made and then cheques were issued. It is not the case that cash was first deposited from which cash was withdrawn and same remained unutilized for subsequent deposit. The determination of the peak credit cannot be applied in case of appellant because of following reasons: (i) where there are cash deposits but withdrawals are through the cheques then benefit of the peak credit cannot be allowed for the cash deposit so made in bank account. In the assessee''''s case, against the cash deposits cheques were issued to some other entities. (ii) As amount of the cash credits were standing in the names of different persons which all along assessee had been claiming as genuine deposit, withdrawal/payment of amount to different set of persons would not at all entitle applicant to claim benefit of peak credits. [Para 15.1]

■

While determining the peak credit, the withdrawal of cash, if not utilized elsewhere, is considered as available for making the deposits. The highest unexplained cash deposit is considered as the peak credit. determination of the peak credit reduces taxable income. However, where withdrawal are through cheques, the benefits of those withdrawals will not be available to explain deposits. Therefore, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) to allow the peak credit to the assessee was not correct. [Para 15.2]

■

The appellant claimed to have sold gold bullion during demonetization period and demonetized currency was deposited in bank account of ''''N''''. The Commissioner (Appeals) has formed a hypothesis to decide case on the peak credit principle and restrict the addition to Rs.4 crore and delete the addition of Rs.32.17 crores. However, on facts of the case nowhere the assessee had been able to conclusively establish that he had made genuine sales during demonetization period from 10-11-2016 till date of survey on 23-12-2016 nor names have been furnished by the assessee before the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals)/CBI/ED. Significantly, neither revenue nor the appellant have requested to apply principle of the peak credit inthe instant case. In fact, the assessee itself has raised a ground to delete addition of Rs.4 crore based on peak credit principle. [Para 15.3]

■

The revenue took plea that survey by Department has established that the falsification of accounts had happened because the sale invoices were booked in the name of NC which was proved to be a bogus entity during survey proceedings and in subsequent proceedings before department. Further, mere payments made by cheques or RTGS does not establish that said gold was received immediately and same was serially and genuinely sold to unknown 2200 purchasers against demonetized currency notes. Even survey could not find evidence of such series of sale by the assessee or commensurate stock of gold and silver at known business premises. The net effect of cash deposited in the bank account of NC and subsequent cheques/RTGS payment is nothing but attempt to convert hoarded undisclosed income of the assessee into the stock of gold for future sales. Under these circumstances, granting benefit of peak credit to the assessee is not warranted. [Para 15.4]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) has considered that the transaction in the bank account of NC relates to the assessee and has accordingly, given benefit to the assessee by restricting the addition in the case. The assessee has not been able to explain as to how almost all cash deposited in bank account of NC were immediately transferred to bank account of assessee. [Para 15.5]

■

The Commissioner (Appeals), whose powers are co-terminus with that of the Assessing Officer should have examined the facts of case, which he failed to do. Considering totality of facts and circumstances of the case and once it is established that the assessee cannot be allowed benefit of the peak credit, the cash deposited in bank account of the assessee remains unexplained as the assessee has not been able to explain nature and source of such cash deposits along with the documentary evidence either before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 15.6]

Further, as per rules 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, if sale value of jewellery is in excess of Rs. 2 lakhs to a single person, then, it is required to collect PAN. Since, there is no requirement of collecting PAN, the assessee does not having details of PAN and correct postal address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery. Therefore, assessee submitted that the question of filing confirmation letter from the parties, from whom, it has collected advance for sale of jewellery does not arise, and consequently, cash receipts cannot be assessed under section 68. The assessee had also explained the Assessing Officer that it has sufficient cash balance as on 8-11-2016 as per books of account maintained for that assessment year and argued that the total cash deposits into bank account is explained out of cash in hand. The assessee has also made an alternative submission that it has sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account on various dates, which has been recorded in books of account of the assessee and source for cash deposits is also out of cash withdrawal from very same bank account. The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. During search, a desktop computer (PC-3) yielded an Excel file titled “1. Pay-Exp”, containing cheque and cash payment details for land purchases under projects including Royal Residency Phase I & II.

■

The Assessing Officer matched cheque entries with ledger/bank records and, treating the Excel sheet as authentic, worked out total alleged cash payments of Rs. 56.31 crores to the seller group.

On a proportional basis, cash of Rs. 37,43,82,651 was attributed to the assessee–HUF and allocated as Rs. 16.22 crores, Rs. 17.81 crores and Rs. 3.40 crores for assessment years 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19 respectively.

After show-cause and rejection of the assessee’s denial, the Assessing Officer treated these amounts as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE, with an alternative observation that, if section 68 was held inapplicable, the sums would be treated as part of sale consideration for capital gains.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the substantive addition on merits, accepted the receipts as part of capital gains computation in place of section 68, and upheld the department’s stand on invoking section 115BBE while rejecting objections regarding reliance on third-party electronic data and cross-examination.

Thus, to compute the 5% threshold, only cash receipts should be considered, and any receipts by way of journal entry should not be considered in the 5% threshold. Similarly, sales made on a credit basis, even if funds are not realised, should not form part of the 5% threshold. The term "receive" or "received" has been judicially explained as follows:

(a)

"To come into possession of, get, acquire, or the like, from any source outside of oneself." [In re McCullough's Estate, 193 Wash. 145, 74 P.2d 877 (1928)]

(b)

"To receive means to get by a transfer, as, to receive a gift, to receive a letter, or to receive money and involves an actual receipt." [The Major Law Lexicon by P. Ramanatha Aiyar, 4th Edn., Vol. 5; College Law Dictionaries by Dr. Avtar Singh, 2nd Edn.]

(c)

"The 'receipt' of income refers to the first occasion when the recipient gets the money under his own control." [Keshav Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 230 (SC)].

Thus, the term "received" means an amount (money) actually received by the assessee during the previous year. The proviso contemplates actual receipt of amounts by the assessee during the previous year. So, in this context, the term "received" may not include "receivable". The Supreme Court in CIT v. Moon Mills Ltd. [1966] 59 ITR 574 (SC) held that there is no scope for holding that the expression "received" means "receivable".

The Finance Act, 2016 inserted sub-section (1F) to Section 206C to bring high-value transactions within the tax net. This provision provides that every person, being a seller, who receives any amount as consideration for the sale of a motor vehicle of the value exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs, shall collect tax from the buyer at the rate of 1% of the sale consideration. 31. Need for an enabling provision to deduct tax under Section 194N as cash withdrawn is not an income

Section 194N was introduced by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, which was subsequently substituted with a new provision by the Finance Act, 2020. This provision requires deduction of tax at source from the cash withdrawn by a person from his account maintained with a bank, cooperative bank or a post office.

Section 194N is covered under Chapter XVII which relates to the collection and recovery of tax. Section 4 and Section 190 contain the enabling provisions for the deduction and recovery of tax.

Section 4(1) provides that income tax shall be levied in respect of the total income of the relevant year. Section 4(2) provides that in respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income tax shall be deducted at the source or paid in advance, where it is so deductible or payable under any provision of this Act.

Section 190 relates to the deduction/collection of tax and payment of advance tax. Sub-section (1) of the said section provides that:

"Notwithstanding that the regular assessment in respect of any income is to be made in a later assessment year, the tax on such income shall be payable by deduction or collection at source or by advance payment or by payment under sub-section (1A) of section 192, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter."

This provision explicitly provides that the collection and deduction of tax shall be made in respect of the income of the assessee. If the amount received cannot be categorised as income in the hands of the receiver on which tax is leviable, no tax can be deducted/collected at source.

TDS on cash withdrawal was introduced to promote a cashless economy and discourage payments in cash. Section 194N requires tax deduction from the amount withdrawn from the accounts. However, it contradicts with provisions of Section 4 and Section 190. There is no income component in cash withdrawn from a bank account, thus, the question of TDS should not arise.

The Supreme Court has affirmed this proposition in the case of CIT v. Eli Lilly & Co. (India) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 178 Taxman 505 (SC) that if a particular income falls outside section 4(1), then TDS provisions cannot come in. The Madras High Court, in the case of Tirunelveli District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. JCIT [2020] 119 taxmann.com 21 (Madras),has also held that tax cannot be deducted under Section 194N if cash withdrawn is not an income of the account holder.

Thus, it is expected that Govt. may bring a suitable amendment under the law to end any possible litigation on this provision.

There was another search action carried out under section 132 in the case of Badalia Gems Pvt. Ltd., wherein, the assessee had been a director. However, statement of the assessee, was recorded under section 132(4) on 8-8-2019. In the course of his statement, the assessee was confronted with some loose sheets which were brought by the investigation wing with themselves from their office record. The said loose sheets as per the revenue authorities were found and seized during the course of a past search action carried out in the case of third parties 'Kasera Group', on 30-11-2018. The name of the assessee was found mentioned, relating to certain cash amount transactions, in the said loose sheets.

No further action was carried out against the assessee either under the provisions of section 153C or under section 147 relating to the said incriminating material/loose sheets found during the past search action carried out on 30-12-2018 in the 'Kasera Group of cases'. However, the said loose sheets were brought by the revenue along with them to the business premises of Badalia Gems Pvt. Ltd. and the assessee was confronted with the said looses sheets. Abstract

Gold has regained prominence as a universal store of value amid rising geopolitical uncertainty, inflation, and distrust in fiat currencies. Its surge to record highs in 2025 reflects both legitimate economic behaviour and increasing compliance challenges. This article analyses how global gold dynamics intersect with taxation, money-laundering laws, and white-collar crime, particularly within India's regulatory ecosystem. It also examines cross-border trade complexities, enforcement coordination, and the evolving standards of global financial governance. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for policymakers and corporate stakeholders to balance economic opportunity with legal responsibility.

Keywords: Gold, Taxation, Compliance, PMLA, FATF, GAAR, Cross-Border Trade, Corporate Governance, White-Collar Crime

I. Research Objective and Context

Gold remains more than a commodity. It is an emotion, a financial anchor, and a barometer of public confidence. In 2025, its value has soared not only because of market mechanics but also due to geopolitical tension and financial distrust. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the legal, tax, and compliance implications of gold's renewed prominence in the global economy.

The research aims to:

1.

Examine the global and Indian gold market trends shaping 2025.

2.

Analyse the legal and regulatory architecture governing taxation, anti-money-laundering, and cross-border transactions.

3.

Identify vulnerabilities that enable gold to be used for white-collar crime.

4.

Recommend policy and governance strategies that uphold transparency and accountability without impeding legitimate trade.

Gold's unique attributes such as liquidity, anonymity, and universal acceptance make it both an asset of stability and a tool of concealment. Understanding this duality is essential for designing laws that protect integrity while enabling commerce.

II. The Global Gold Surge: Economics, Emotion and Law

A. Price Trends and Market Forces

According to Reuters and the World Gold Council, gold prices in 2025 have risen nearly 50 percent year-on-year, reaching around US $3,950 per ounce internationally and crossing Rs. 1,25,000 per 10 grams in India. This dramatic rise stems from persistent inflation, high global debt, and growing investor preference for tangible assets.

Central banks across Asia and the Middle East have purchased record quantities of gold to diversify reserves. Goldman Sachs has forecast prices could approach US $4,900 per ounce by 2026 if inflation remains elevated and interest rates stabilise.

This global pattern underscores gold's transformation from a passive store of value into a geopolitical hedge. It reflects both market sentiment and institutional strategy.

B. India's Domestic Context

India's relationship with gold is historical and deeply cultural. Demand peaks during festivals and marriage seasons, creating a recurring impact on trade balances. India imports nearly all its gold, which has implications for the current account deficit and currency stability.

High import duties and fluctuating exchange rates have incentivised smuggling and under-invoicing. In March 2025, the government discontinued parts of the Gold Monetisation Scheme to limit fiscal exposure. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has since reported a notable increase in illegal inflows through land and maritime borders.

C. Geopolitical Context

Gold's rally cannot be separated from the global political landscape. The continuing Russia–Ukraine conflict, instability in the Middle East, and trade tensions between the United States and China have disrupted global supply chains. Sanctions against Russian bullion refineries have redirected trade to Asian hubs such as Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

As trade flows realign, enforcement agencies must address differing compliance standards among jurisdictions. Some free-trade zones have become conduits for gold trading with limited regulatory oversight, increasing risks of mis-invoicing and money laundering.

III. Legal Framework Governing Gold and Financial Compliance

A. Income-Tax and Disclosure Laws

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, unexplained gold holdings can be taxed as income under Sections 69 and 69B. High-net-worth individuals and corporations are required to declare gold holdings accurately to avoid reassessment and penalty.

Cross-border transactions in gold attract transfer-pricing scrutiny under Section 92F. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued guidelines requiring documentation that justifies arm's-length pricing.

Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor.
